Now that we have each flight duration and a key that identifies flights between a certain pair of cities, we can assign a ranking to each flight pair based on the magnitude of its flight duration. Since we want the second longest flight between each pair of cities we filter for the records where the ranking equals 2.


```sql
WITH flight_details AS (
    SELECT
        f.*,
        EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (f.flight_end - f.flight_start)) AS flight_duration,
        CASE 
            WHEN f.takeoff_location > f.arrival_location 
            THEN f.takeoff_location || '-' || f.arrival_location
            ELSE f.arrival_location || '-' || f.takeoff_location
        END AS flight_key
    FROM 
        flights f 
), flight_duration_rankings AS (
    SELECT 
        fd.*,
        RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY fd.flight_key ORDER BY fd.flight_duration DESC) AS rnk
    FROM 
        flight_details fd 
)

SELECT 
    fdr.id,
    fdr.arrival_location,
    fdr.takeoff_location,
    fdr.flight_start,
    fdr.flight_end
FROM 
    flight_duration_rankings fdr 
WHERE 
    rnk = 2
ORDER BY 
    fdr.id ASC 
```

title: Bank Arbitrage
statement: You have a bond and bank account that pay 5% and 3% compounded annually. You are allowed to buy or borrow the bond (needing to repay it back later). Similarly, you are able to borrow money from the bank (needing to pay the principal and interest at the end) or deposit money into the bank. There is an arbitrage opportunity. How much profit will you receive at the end of 11 year if you have $200 total?
solution:
To make an arbitrage profit, you'll borrow at the lower bank rate (3%) and invest in the higher-yielding bond (5%), using your \$200 as collateral, then repay the loan with interest and keep the difference.

With \$200 at 3% for 11 years, you owe \$200*(1.03)^11 â‰ˆ \$276.85, while your \$200 invested at 5% earns \$200*(1.05)^11 â‰ˆ \$342.07, yielding a net profit of \$342.07 - \$276.85 = $\boxed{65.22}$ at the end of year 11, demonstrating a risk-free gain.

title: Sharing a Secret
statement: A group of 5 people want to keep their secret document in a safe. They want to make sure that in the future, only a majority (>=3) of people can open the safe. To accomplish this they want to put some locks on the safe, whereby each of the locks have to be opened to access the safe. Each lock can have multiple keys; but each key only opens one lock. How many locks are required at minimum? How many keys will each member carry?
solution: For each group of 2 people, there must be a lock which none of them have a key to. But the key of such a lock will be given to the remaining 3 people of the group. Thus, we must have at least 5C2 = 10 Locks. Each lock has 3 keys, which is given to unique 3-member subgroup. So each member should have 10*3/5 = $\boxed{6 \ \text{keys}}$

title: Flipped in Succession
statement: Five fair coins are flipped in succession. What is the probability that the number of heads in the first three coin flips is equal to the number of heads in the last two coin flips?
solution:
We want the # of heads in the first three flips to equal the # of heads in the last 2 flips.

For $r = 0, 1, 2$ the events can match.

Probability = $\sum_{r=0}^2{P(\text{first 3 have} \ r}) \cdot P(\text{last 2 have} \ r)$

$$
P(\text{first 3 have} \ r) = \frac{3\choose r}{2^3}, \ P(\text{last 2 have} \ r) = \frac{2\choose r}{2^2}
$$

So 

$$ 
P = \sum_{r=0}^2 \frac{{3}\choose{r} }{8} \cdot \frac{{2}\choose{r} }{4} = \frac{1 + 6 + 3}{32} =  \boxed{\frac{5}{16}}
$$

title: Collecting Coupons
statement: Coupons in cereal boxes are numbered 1 to 5, and a set of one of each is required for a prize. With one coupon per box, how many boxes on the average are required to make a complete set?
solution:
We get one of the numbers in the first box. Now the chance of getting a new number from the next box is $\frac{4}{5}$. The second new number requires $1 / (4/5) = \frac{5}{4}$ boxes. The third number requires an additional $1 / (3/5) = \frac{5}{3}$; the fourth $\frac{5}{2}$, the fifth $\frac{5}{1}$. Thus the average number of boxes required is:

$$
5(\frac{1}{5} + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{2} + 1) \approx 11.42
$$

title: 8 Clubs
statement: 8 cards are dealt out from a standard deck. Find the variance of the number of clubs in the 8 cards.
solution:
Let $X$ be the number of clubs in 8 cards dealt from a standard 52-card deck.

$X$ has a hypergeometric distribution with parameters:
$$
N = 52,\quad K = 13,\quad n = 8
$$

The variance of a hypergeometric random variable is
$$
\operatorname{Var}(X)
= n \frac{K}{N}\left(1 - \frac{K}{N}\right)\frac{N-n}{N-1}.
$$

Substitute the values:
$$
\operatorname{Var}(X)
= 8 \cdot \frac{13}{52} \cdot \frac{39}{52} \cdot \frac{44}{51}.
$$

Simplify:
$$
\frac{13}{52} = \frac{1}{4}, \quad \frac{39}{52} = \frac{3}{4}.
$$

Thus,
$$
\operatorname{Var}(X)
= 8 \cdot \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{44}{51}
= \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{44}{51}
= \frac{66}{51}
= \frac{22}{17}.
$$

$$
\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(X) = \frac{22}{17}}
$$

title: German Tanks
statement: Suppose that German tanks are assigned distinct serial numbers $1,2,\dots, N$. You observe $6$ tanks with serial numbers $38,17, 59, 42, 97,$ and $120$. Under a frequentist approach, what is the best guess for $N$?
solution:
We need to find $N$ such that the expected value of the $X_{(6)}$, the maximum among $6$ distinct uniform random draws from $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$ is $120$. 

Intuitively, if $120$ is the $6$th order statistic, then in expectation, there are 5 other tanks before it that should partition $\{1,2,\dots,120\}$ into 6 equal length parts. This means that besides all of tanks that are the order statistics themselves (since we have discrete values), there are $114$ other serial numbers. 

The spacings between these tanks should be equal in expectation, so the average distance between them should be $\frac{114}{6} = 19$. Therefore, as $120$ is the $6$th order statistic and we know each order statistic on average has a spacing of $19$, the maximum tank number should just be $120 + 19 = 139$.

title: The Clumsy Chemist
statement: In a laboratory, each of a handful of thin 9-inch glass rods had one tip marked with a blue dot and the other with a red. When the laboratory assistant tripped and dropped them onto the concrete floor, many broke into three pieces. For these, what was the average length of the fragment with the blue dot?
solution: Assuming these rods broke at random, the principle of symmetry says that each fragment-blue-dotted, middle, and red-dotted segment-would have the same distribution and the same mean. Since the means have to add to 9 inches, the blue-dotted segments average about 3 inches.

title: Illegible Dice
statement: You are given two fair dice: one is a normal six-sided die and the other is an illegible, six-sided die. Whenever you toss the two dice, it is equally likely for the sum of the faces to be any integer between 1 and 12, inclusive. What is the sum of the sides of the illegible die?
solution: There are 36 possible face combinations of two six-sided dice rolls. In order for each of the twelve outcomes to be equally likely, each must be able to occur exactly three times. In order for 1 to occur three times, there must be three 0's on the illegible die. Furthermore, in order for 12 to occur three times, there must be three 6's on the illegible die. Hence, we have solved the sides of the illegible die and the sum of its sides is 18.

title: Rubik's Cube Stickers
statement: A $4 \times 4 \times 4$ Rubik's Cube is composed of $1 \times 1 \times 1$ mini-cubes. The Rubik's Cube has stickers on its outer layer to denote the colors of the cube. How many mini-cubes have at least one sticker on them?
solution:
There are a total of $4^3$ mini-cubes that compose the Rubik's Cube. Of these, the core $2^3$ mini-cubes that make up the inside of the cube and that are not showing do not have stickers on it. Thus, the total number of mini-cubes that do have stickers on it is:

$$
4^3-2^3=56
$$

title: 17 Balls
statement: There are 18 beans, 17 of which are identical and one is heavier. What is the minimum number of weighings using a balance scale to guarantee finding the heavier bean?
solution:
A balance scale has three outcomes:
1. Left side heavier
2. Right side heavier
3. Both sides equal

Each weighing can give us at most 3 outcomes, so in general, if we have n items and k weighings:

$$
3^k \geq n
$$

is the minimum requirement to guarantee identification of one odd item. This is a standard approach from "coin weighing problems."

We have $n=18$ beans. We want the smallest integer $k$ such that:

$$
3^k \geq 18
$$

So the minimum number of weighings is $\boxed{3}$

title: Forwards and Futures
statement: What's the difference between futures and forwards? If the price of the underlying asset is strongly positively correlated with interest rates, and the interest rates are stochastic, which one has higher price: future or forwards? Why?
solution:
Futures contracts are exchange-traded standardized contracts; forward contracts are over-the-counter agreements so they are more flexible. Futures contracts are marked-to-market daily; forwards contacts are settled at the end of the contract term.

If the interest rate is deterministic, futures and forwards have the same theoretical price: $F = Se^{(r+u-y)\tau}$, where $u$ represents all the storage costs and $y$ represents dividend yield for investment assets, convenience yield for commodities and foreign risk-free interest rate for foreign currencies.

The mark-to-market property of future makes their values differ from forwards when interest rates vary unpredictably. As the life of a futures contract increases, the differences between forward and futures contracts may become significant. If the futures price is positively correlated with the interest rate, the increases of the futures price tend to occur the same time when interest rate is high.

Because of the mark-to-market feature, the investor who longs the futures has an immediate profit that can be reinvested at a higher rate. The loss tends to occur when the interest rate is low so that it can be financed at a low rate. So a futures contract is more valuable than the forward when its value is positively correlated with interest rates and the futures price should be higher.

title: Infinite Maturity
statement: What's the value of a vanilla European call option of infinite maturity, and a given strike, volatility, interest rate, and spot price?
solution:
If the underlying pays no dividends (continuous dividend yield $q=0$), the Black-Scholes value of a European call with strike $K$, spot $S$, interest rate $r$, and volatility $\sigma$ tends to:

$$
\boxed{C_{T \to \infin} = S}
$$

With no dividends, owning a very long-dated call is almost as good as owning the stock: over an arbitrarily long horizon the stock will â€” with high probability â€” reach levels far above any fixed strike and, importantly, the present value of paying the fixed strike at that very far future time is essentially zero (because $Ke^{-rT} \to 0$ according to the Black-Scholes model). So the call's price approaches the stock price $S$.

---

If the underlying pays a continuous dividend yield $q > 0$, the call price instead tends to

$$
\boxed{C_{T\to\infin} = 0}
$$

With positive dividends the stock pays out value over time that the call-holder does not receive, and the present value of those foregone dividends over an infinite horizon wipes out the option's value â€” the call tends to zero.

title: R Squared Range
statement: Using OLS, we regress $y$ onto $X_1$ and find that the model has an $R^2$ of 0.15.  We also regress $y$ onto $X_2$ but this time the model has an $R^2$ of 0.2. Let $[\text{min}, \text{max}]$ denote the lower and upper-bound of the $R^2$ of a model which regresses $y$ onto $X_1, X_2$. Express your answer as $\frac{\text{max}}{\text{min}}$.
solution:
Let $R_1^2 = 0.15$ be the $R^2$ from regressing $y$ on $X_1$ alone, and
$R_2^2 = 0.20$ be the $R^2$ from regressing $y$ on $X_2$ alone.

Lower bound:
Adding regressors in OLS cannot reduce $R^2$. Therefore, the $R^2$ from
regressing y on $(X_1, X_2)$ must be at least as large as the larger of the
two individual $R^2$ values:
$$
\min R^2 = \max\{R_1^2, R_2^2\} = 0.20.
$$

Upper bound:
There is no restriction that prevents $X_1$ and $X_2$ together from
perfectly explaining $y$, even if each variable alone explains little.
For example, $y$ could lie in the span of $(X_1, X_2)$ while being poorly
aligned with each variable individually. Hence, the $R^2$ of the joint
regression can be as high as 1:
$$
\max R^2 = 1.
$$

Therefore,
$$
\frac{\max}{\min} = \frac{1}{0.20} = 5.
$$

title: Trailing Zeros
statement: How many trailing zeros are there in 100!
solution:
A trailing zero occurs with each factor of 10, and so we know that every pair of 2 and 5 will give a trailing zero. Intuitively, the frequency of 2 in the prime factorization of 100! is far greater than the frequency of 5, and thus the number of 5s limits and determines the number of trailing zeros. 

Among the numbers 1, 2, ..., 100, there are 20 numbers that are divisible by 5 (5, 10, ..., 100). Among these numbers, 4 are divisible by 5 twice (25, 50, 75, 100). Therefore, the frequency of 5 is 24, and thus there are $\boxed{24}$ trailing zeros in 100!.

title: Remainders
statement: What is the smallest positive integer that has a remainder of 1 when divided by 2, a remainder of 2 when divided by 3, ..., and a remainder of 9 when divided by 10?
solution:
Let $X$ denote the smallest positive integer we are solving for. We can further define $X_2, X_3, ..., X_{10}$ as positive integers such that:

$$
X = 2 \times X_2 + 1 \\
X = 3 \times X_3 + 2 \\
\vdots \\
X = 10 \times X_{10} + 10
$$

Let $X'_i = X_i + 1 \forall i \in \{2, 3, ..., 10\}$. 

Then, adding $1$ to both sides of each equations:

$$
X + 1 = 2 \times X'_2 \\
X + 1 = 3 \times X'_3 \\ 
\vdots \\ 
X + 1 = 10 \times X'_{10}
$$

In other words, we are now looking for $X$ such that $X+1$ is perfectly divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10. The least common multiple of these numbers is 2520, and thus $X$ is $\boxed{2519}$

title: Adjacent Evens
statement: How many permutations of $\{1, 2, \dots, 7\}$ have no adjacent even digits?
solution:
We start by determining how many ways we can arrange the odd digits (1, 3, 5, 7). There are $4! = 24$ ways to arrange them.

This creates a gap where event digits can be placed.

_ O _ O _ O _ O _

Here O are the odd digits, _ are gaps where event digits can go. The number of gaps = the number of odd digits + 1 = 5.

We have 3 even digits to place into these 5 gaps. Since no two even digits can be in the same gap, we have ${5}\choose{3}$ $=10$ ways. Arranging the even digits amongst themselves gives $3!=6$.

Putting it together

$$
4! \times {5\choose 3} \times 3! = \boxed{1440}
$$

title: Uniform Sum Probability
statement: Is it possible to have two non-fair 6-sided dice, with sides numbered 1 through 6, with a uniform sum probability?
solution:
$\boxed{No}$ 

Let $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4,p_5$ and $p_6$ be the probabilities for one 6-sided die, and $q_1,q_2,q_3,q_4,q_5$ and $q_6$ be the probabilities for another. Suppose that these dice together yield sums with uniform probabilities. That is, suppose $P(\text{sum} = k) = \frac{1}{11}$ for $k=2,...,12$. Then:

$$
p_1q_1 = \frac{1}{11} \quad \text{and} \quad p_6q_6 = \frac{1}{11}
$$

Also,

$$
\frac{1}{11} = P(\text{sum} = 7) \geq p_1q_6 + p_6q_1
$$

so:

$$
p_1\frac{1}{11p_6} + p_6\frac{1}{11p_1} \leq \frac{1}{11}
$$

i.e

$$
\frac{p_1}{p_6} + \frac{p_6}{p_1} \leq 1
$$

Now, if we let $x=\frac{p_1}{p_6}$, then we have

$$
x + \frac{1}{x} \leq
$$

which is impossible, since for positive real $x, x + \frac{1}{x} \geq 2$. Thus, no such dice are possible.

title: Sequential Six
statement: On average, how many times must a 6-sided die be rolled until a 6 turns up twice in a row?
solution:
We can solve this using a recurrence relation on, $E$, the expected number of rolls. When we start rolling, we expect, on average 6 rolls until a 6 shows up. Once that happens, there is a 1/6 chance that we will roll once more, and a 5/6 chance that we will be, effectively, starting all over again, and so have as many additional expected rolls as when we started. As a result, we can say:

$$
E = 6 + \frac{1}{6} \times 1 + \frac{5}{6}(E+1)
$$

Solving this, we find that $\boxed{E=42}$

title: Color Elimination
statement: Jane offers to play the following game with you. Starting with a standard deck of 52 cards, you take turns drawing two cards. Jane goes first. If the two cards are black, Jane keeps them. If the cards are red, you keep them. If there is one red and one black card, the cards are discarded. When you have gone through the deck, you and Jane combine your cards, shuffle them, and resume, playing until one of the colors is eliminated. If there are red cards remaining, you win $100. What is a fair price to pay to play this game?
solution: This is a trick question. The cards are always discarded by pair (red, black) so the number of discarded red cards and discarded black cards is always equal. Thus the red and black colors will be eliminated only when the whole deck is eliminated, and there will be no red cards remaining. Therefore, there is no way to win the \$100, so the fair price is $\boxed{0 \ \text{dollars}}$

title: Space Station
statement: The population of a space station on a recolonization mission is kept alive by its expandable life support system. Given they are trying to repopulate, the population aboard the station quadruples every 54 years, but the life support system capacity can only be doubled every 54 years. Suppose the initial population is 2 people and the initial life support system has a capacity for 16384 people. How many years will pass before the population reaches the capacity of the support system?
solution:
Our goal is to find the time (in years) when the population first reaches the systemâ€™s capacity. To do this, we compare the exponential growth of the population and the exponential growth of the capacity.

### Step #1: Define the number of growth periods

Because both the population and capacity grow in discrete 54-year cycles, we define:

$$
k = \frac{t}{54}
$$

where
- $k$ is the number of 54-year periods
- $t$ is the total number of years

This allows us to write both quantities as exponential functions of $k$

### Step #2: Write the population as a function of $k$

The population starts at 2 and quadruples every period, so:

$$
P(k) = 2 \cdot 4^k
$$

In each 54-year interval, the population is multiplied by 4. After $k$ intervals, this gives $4^k$. Multiplying by the initial population gives the full expression.


### Step #3: Write the life support capacity as a function of $k$

The capacity begins at 16,384 and doubles every period, so:

$$
C(k) = 16384 \cdot 2^{k}
$$

Each period multiplies the capacity 2. After $k$ periods, this produces $2^k$. Again, multiplying by the initial capacity gives the full capacity after $k$ growth cycles.

### Step #4: Set population equal to capacity and solve for $k$

$$
2 \cdot 4^{k} = 16384 \cdot 2^{k} \\ 
4^{k} = (2^{2})^{k} = 2^{2k} \\
2 \cdot 2^{2k} = 16384 \cdot 2^{k} \\
16384 \cdot 2^{k} = 2^{14} \cdot 2^{k} = 2^{k + 14} \\
2^{2k + 1} = 2^{k + 14} \\
2k + 1 = k + 14 \\
k = 13
$$

### Step #5: Convert number of periods back to years

Each period is 54 years, so:

$$
t = 54k = 54 \cdot 13 = \boxed{702 \ \text{years}}
$$

title: Dice Coin Paradigm
statement: We flip a fair coin until we obtain our first heads. Given the first heads occurs on the $n$th flip, we roll a fair $6-$sided die $n$ times. Find the probability that the die value 1 is observed in the rolls.
solution:
Let N be the flip on which the first heads appears.

Step 1: Distribution of N.
Since the coin is fair,
$$
\mathbb{P}(N = n) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n, \quad n = 1,2,\dots
$$

Step 2: Conditional probability given $N = n$.
If we roll a fair six-sided die n times, the probability of observing no 1's is
$$
\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^n
$$
Therefore, the probability of observing at least one 1 is
$$
1 - \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^n
$$

Step 3: Unconditional probability.
$$
\mathbb{P}(\text{at least one 1})
= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left[1 - \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^n \right]
\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n
$$

$$
= 1 - \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{5}{6} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\right)^n
= 1 - \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{5}{12}\right)^n
$$

The remaining sum is geometric:
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(\frac{5}{12}\right)^n
= \frac{\frac{5}{12}}{1 - \frac{5}{12}} = \frac{5}{7}
$$

Final answer:
$$
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{at least one 1}) = 1 - \frac{5}{7} = \frac{2}{7}}
$$

title: Little End of the Stick
statement:
**Part 1:** If a stick is broken in two at random, what is the average length of the smaller piece?

**Part 2:** What is the average ratio of the smaller length to the larger?
solution:
**Part 1:**

Breaking "at random" means that all points of the stick are equally likely as a breaking point (uniform distribution). The breaking point is just as likely to be in the left half as the right half. If it is in the left half, the smaller piece is on the left; and its average size is half of that half, or onefourth the length of the stick. The same sort of argument applies when the break is in the right half of the stick, and so the answer is $\boxed{\text{one-fourth of the length}}$

---

**Part 2:**

We might suppose that the point fell in the right-second half. Then $(1-x)/x$ is the fraction if the stick is of unit length. Since $x$ is evenly distributed from $1/2$ to $1$, the average value, instead of the intuitive $1/3$ is:

$$
2 \int_{\frac{1}{2}}^1\frac{1-x}{x}dx = 2 \int_{\frac{1}{2}}^1(\frac{1}{x} - 1)dx  =2\log_e2 - 1 \approx \boxed{0.386}
$$

title: Curing the Compulsive Gambler
statement:
Mr. Brown always bets a dollar on the number 13 at roulette against the advice of Kind Friend. To help cure Mr. Brown of playing roulette, Kind Friend always bets Brown $20 at even money that Brown will be behind at the end of 36 plays. How is the cure working? 

(Most American roulette wheels have 38 equally likely numbers. If the player's number comes up, he is paid 35 times his stake and gets his original
stake back; otherwise he loses his stake.)
solution:
If Mr. Brown wins once in 36 turns, he is even with the casino. His probability of losing all 36 time is $(\frac{37}{38})^{36} \approx 0.383$. In a single turn his expectation is:

$$
35 (\frac{1}{38}) - 1(\frac{37}{38}) = -\frac{2}{38} (\text{dollars})
$$

and in 36 turns

$$
- \frac{2(36)}{38} \approx -1.89 (\text{dollars})
$$

Against Kind Friend, Mr.Brown has an expectation of 

$$
20(0.617) - 20(0.383) \approx 4.68 (\text{dollars})
$$

And so all told Mr.Brown gains $4.68 - 1.89 = 2.79$ dollars per 36 trials; he is finally making money at roulette. Possibly Kind Friend will be cured first. Of course, when Brown loses all 36, he is out $56, which may jolt him a bit.

title: Dollar Cent Confusion
statement: A man went to his local bank to cash a check. When giving his money to the cashier, by mistake, gave him dollars as cents and cents as dollars. He didn't examine the money and just walked home and spent a nickel on some candy. He then found that he possessed exactly twice as much money as the check was worth. He had no money in his pocket before going to the bank. How much was the check for?
solution:
He should have received
$$
D + \frac{C}{100}
$$
Instead, dollars and cents were swapped, so he received
$$
C + \frac{D}{100}
$$

He spent 5 cents, so the amount left was
$$
C + \frac{D}{100} = 0.05
$$

After spending the nickel, he had exactly twice the value of the check

$$
C + \frac{D}{100} - 0.05 = 2(D + \frac{C}{100})
$$

Multiply both sides by 100 and rearrange:

$$
100C + D - 5 = 200D + 2C \\
98C = 199D + 5
$$

Now look for integer solutions with $0 \leq C \leq 99$

Trying values of $D$, we find

$$
D = 31 \quad C = 63
$$

Therefore the check was for $\boxed{31.63}$ dollars

title: Dice Labeling
statement: How many distinct ways can you label a 6 sided dice if you wipe off all the numbers? Arrangements that can be formed by rotating the die around are not considered distinct.
solution:
First, notice that there are $24$ ways of turning the die. This is because if you consider one particular face of the die, there are exactly $4$ ways of turning it so that this face is always in the same place. Then do the same for the other faces, and get $4 \times 6=24$

$6!$ is the number of ways to number the die but this also counts the $24$ possible turns of the die. So the answer is $\frac{6!}{24}=\boxed{30}$

title: 4Head I
statement: Varun has $4$ fair coins. He flips all $4$ at once and notes the parity of each. After seeing the outcomes, he may $\textbf{turn over}$ (rather than flip) any pair of coins. Note that this means a heads becomes a tails and vice versa. Varun may not turn over a single coin without turning over another. He can iterate this process as many times as he would like. If Varun plays to maximize his expected number of heads, find the expected number of heads he will have.
solution: The key item to note here is that Varun will always end up with either $3$ or $4$ heads. The final amount that he can obtain is going to depend on how many heads he obtains initially. If Varun obtains an even number of heads, he can select a pair of tails and turn both of them over. He can do this with any amount of tail pairs, so Varun will eventually end up with all heads. However, if Varun obtains either $1$ or $3$ heads on the first turn, he can't do any better than $3$ heads, as any pair of coins that he would select to attempt to do better would consist of one head and one tail. This implies that Varun will obtain $4$ heads precisely when his initial flipping yields an even number of heads, while he obtains $3$ heads precisely when his initial flipping yields an odd number of heads. The probability that Varun obtains an even number of heads from the $4$ flips is $$\dfrac{1 + 6 + 1}{16} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$ The above was obtained via the Binomial distribution. Therefore, the probability Varun obtains an odd number of heads from the $4$ flips is $1/2$. The expected number of heads Varun obtains is $$\dfrac{4+3}{2} = \dfrac{7}{2}$$
hints: Varun will either end up with $3$ or $4$ heads in the end. In what cases would he end up with $3$?

title: 4Head II
statement: Varun has $4$ fair coins. He flips all $4$ at once and notes the parity of each. After seeing the outcomes, he may flip any pair of coins again. Varun may not flip a single coin without flipping another. He can iterate this process as many times as he would like. If Varun plays to maximize his expected number of heads, find the expected number of heads he will have.
solution: For each pair we flip again, we always have a positive probability ($1/4$ on each flip) of obtaining $2$ heads. Since there is a positive probability per trial of obtaining two heads, regardless of the initial outcome, if the pair is flipped enough times, Varun will end with a pair heads. This can be rigorously proven by the Borel-Cantelli lemma. If he repeats this for the two pairs, he will eventually have $4$ heads. Therefore, the answer is just $4$, as with probability $1$, Varun will obtain $HHHH$ at some point.
hints: Can you iterate through the pairs until they are all heads?

title: 4Head III
statement: Varun has $4$ fair coins. He flips all $4$ at once and notes the parity of each. After seeing the outcomes, he may flip any pair of tails again. Varun may not flip a single coin without flipping another. He can iterate this process as many times as he would like. Under a strategy that maximizes his expected number of heads, what is the expected amount of heads that Varun observes at the end?
solution:
The expected number of heads that Varun will obtain is dependent on how many heads he observes at the first flip. Afterwards, the number of heads that Varun has is best modelled as a Markov Chain, as his current number of heads influences how many heads he can have after the reflip.    

$$$$

Let $T$ be the total number of heads Varun has when he stops. As per the discussion above, let $X$ be the number of heads that appear on the first flipping of the coins. By the Law of Total Expectation, we have that $\mathbb{E}[T] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[T \mid X]] = \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{4}\mathbb{E}[T \mid X =k]\mathbb{P}[X = k]$. As $X$ counts the number of successes (in this case, heads) appearing in a fixed number of independent trials (flips), $X$ follows a binomial distribution. In particular, $X \sim \text{Binom}\left(4,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, as there are $4$ flips of a fair coin. Now, we need to consider each individual case of the values for $X$.

$$$$

If $X = 4$, Varun already has heads on all coins, so he can't obtain any more heads. Therefore, $\mathbb{E}[T \mid X = 4] = 4$. Similarly, if $X = 3$, Varun is unable to flip just one tails, so $\mathbb{E}[T \mid X = 3] = 3$.

$$$$

If $X = 2$, then Varun is going to continually flip the two tail coins again until he doesn't obtain $TT$. Since the coin is fair, conditioned on the coins not appearing $TT$, each of the outcomes that are not $TT$ are equally likely. There are $3$ outcomes that are not $TT$, which would be $TH, HT,$ and $HH$. Conditioned on the fact that Varun doesn't obtain $TT$, $2$ of the $3$ equally-likely outcomes result in him having $3$ heads, while the last one allows him to obtain $4$ heads, so $$\mathbb{E}[T \mid X = 2] = \dfrac{2}{3} \cdot 3 + \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot 4 = \dfrac{10}{3}$$

We now use similar logic for when $X = 1$. If $X = 1$, then Varun flips the two tails until they don't appear $TT$. With probability $\dfrac{2}{3}$, he obtains a single head on the two coins, leaving him with $2$ heads. However, as per the above, from the state of having $2$ heads, the expected number of heads that Varun ends with is $10/3$. With probability $\dfrac{1}{3}$, Varun obtains $HH$ on the two coins, giving him $3$ heads. He can't flip anymore from that state, so he is done. Therefore, by Law of Total Expectation, $$\mathbb{E}[T \mid X = 1] = \dfrac{2}{3} \cdot \dfrac{10}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot 3 = \dfrac{29}{9}$$

$$$$

Lastly, if $X = 0$, with probability $\dfrac{2}{3}$, Varun obtains $1$ head, so the expected number of heads that Varun obtains from the state of $1$ head is $\dfrac{29}{9}$ by the above. With probability $\dfrac{1}{3}$, Varun obtains $2$ heads, which gives Varun an expected amount of $\dfrac{10}{3}$ heads by the end of the game. Therefore, by Law of Total Expectation, $$\mathbb{E}[T \mid X = 0] = \dfrac{2}{3} \cdot \dfrac{29}{9} + \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{10}{3} = \dfrac{88}{27}$$

To avoid plugging into the expression at the beginning, we can note that $\ev{T \mid X = 0} = \ev{T}$, as we can view his initial state as one where he has not flipped yet, which means that he has $0$ heads obtained. Therefore, given that he obtained $0$ heads on the initial flip, it is the same scenario as if he was before the initial flip. Therefore, we get that $\ev{T} = 88/27$. One can also verify the validity of this quantity by plugging into the Law of Total Expectation expression from the start of the question.
hints: The expected number of heads that Varun will obtain is dependent on how many heads he observes at the first flip. Afterwards, the number of heads that Varun has is best modelled as a Markov Chain, as his current number of heads influences how many heads he can have after the reflip.

title: 4Head IV
statement: Varun has $4$ fair coins. He flips all $4$ at once and notes the parity of each. After seeing the outcomes, he may flip any pair of tails again. Varun may not flip a single coin without flipping another. He can iterate this process as many times as he would like, as long as he has less than $3$ heads obtained (otherwise, no pair of tails exists, and the game ends). Find the expected number of flips that Varun performs. Note that the initial $4$ flips are still flips, and each pair counts as $2$ flips!
solution:
The expected number of flips that Varun will have to perform is dependent on how many heads he observes at the first flip. If he obtains either $3$ or $4$ heads, he doesn't have to perform any additional flips. Otherwise, there are additional flips that will need to be performed. Therefore, it is best to model this as a Markov Chain, where there is dependency between states based on how many heads Varun currently has.

$$$$

Let $T$ be the total number of flips that Varun needs to perform. As per the discussion above, let $X$ be the number of heads that appear on the first flipping of the coins. By the Law of Total Expectation, we have that $\mathbb{E}[T] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[T \mid X]] = \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{4}\mathbb{E}[T \mid X =k]\mathbb{P}[X = k]$. As $X$ counts the number of successes (in this case, heads) appearing in a fixed number of independent trials (flips), $X$ follows a binomial distribution. In particular, $X \sim \text{Binom}\left(4,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, as there are $4$ flips of a fair coin. Now, we need to consider each individual case of the values for $X$. To set our notation, let $e_i$ represent the additional number of flips needed to stop our process once we have $i$ heads. Since there are $4$ flips that Varun has to do on the initial term, $\ev{T \mid X = k} = 4 + e_k$. We have to set up the problem like this, as the $4$ flips only occur on the first turn, and not on any additional turns.

$$$$

If $X = 4$, there are no additional flips that can be performed, so $\mathbb{E}[T \mid X = 4] = 4$. This would mean $e_4 = 0$. Similarly, if $X = 3$, no additional flips can be performed, so $\mathbb{E}[T \mid X = 3] = 4$. This would mean $e_3 = 0$.

$$$$

If $X = 2$, then Varun will continually flip the two tail coins again until he doesn't obtain two tails. From the two coins, Varun can obtain either $0,1,$ or $2$ heads from it. Since each coin is independent, with probability $1/2 \cdot 1/2 = 1/4$, two tails are obtained, in which $2$ additional coin flips are performed, and Varun still has $2$ heads. With probability $1/2 \cdot 1/2 = 1/4$, Varun obtains $2$ heads, which means that Varun performed $2$ flips, and then he is done. Lastly, with probability $1/2$, Varun obtains $1$ head from the $2$ flips, and he is done. Therefore, we have derived the recurrence $$e_2 = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (2 + e_4) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (2 + e_3) + \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (2 + e_2)$$ Solving for $e_2$ here by plugging in $e_3 = e_4 = 0$ is $e_2 = \dfrac{8}{3}$, so $\mathbb{E}[T \mid X = 2] = 4 + \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{20}{3}$.

$$$$

We repeat this logic when $X = 1$. Varun flips two tails until they don't appear $TT$. The calculations are the exact same as the above, except $e_2,e_3,$ and $e_4$ are now $e_1,e_2,$ and $e_3$, as we start with one head less. The equation becomes $$e_1 = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (2 + e_3) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (2 + e_2) + \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (2 + e_1)$$ Plugging in $e_3 = 0$ and $e_2 = \dfrac{8}{3}$ yields that $e_1 = \dfrac{40}{9}$. Therefore, $\mathbb{E}[T \mid X = 1] = \dfrac{40}{9} + 4 = \dfrac{76}{9}$.

$$$$

Using the exact same logic with $X = 0$, we get $$e_0 = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (2 + e_2) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (2 + e_1) + \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (2 + e_0)$$ Solving for $e_0$ by plugging in $e_2 = \dfrac{8}{3}$ and $e_1 = \dfrac{40}{9}$ yields $e_0 = \dfrac{176}{27}$. We can compute $\mathbb{E}[T \mid X = 0] = \dfrac{176}{27} + 4 = \dfrac{284}{27}$.

$$$$

Plugging the values and the PMF of $X$ into our expression from the beginning, we get that $$\mathbb{E}[T] = \dfrac{1}{16} \cdot 4 + \dfrac{4}{16} \cdot 4 + \dfrac{6}{16} \cdot \dfrac{20}{3} + \dfrac{4}{16} \cdot \dfrac{76}{9} + \dfrac{1}{16} \cdot \dfrac{284}{27} = \dfrac{176}{27}$$ It makes intuitive sense that $\ev{T} = e_0$, as Varun initially has no heads, and if $X = 0$, $e_0$ is the additional number of flips that Varun must perform before stopping when he obtained $0$ heads on the initial flips. Since $e_0$ is the additional amount of flips needed, this doesn't count for the initial $4$ flips needed, so $\ev{T}$ and $e_0$ are counting the expected number of coin flips for the same scenario. Additionally, this answer is exactly twice as much as the previous answer, which isn't coincidence! This comes from the fact that each head, on average, takes $2$ flips to obtain, as the coin is fair.
hints: The expected number of flips that Varun will have to perform is dependent on how many heads he observes at the first flip. If he obtains either $3$ or $4$ heads, he doesn't have to perform any additional flips. Otherwise, there are additional flips that will need to be performed. Model this as a Markov Chain in some sense, where there is dependency between states based on how many heads Varun currently has. Make sure to add $4$ to account for the initial flips!

title: See All Sides I
statement: On average, how many times do you need to roll a standard fair $6-$sided die to see all of the sides at least once?
solution:
The idea here is to use linearity of expectation by decomposing into the number of rolls between each consecutive new value. We can see this since the number of rolls needed between observing new values is a geometric random variable, as it measures the number of trials needed to observe the occurrence of some event. 

$$$$

In particular, let $X_i$ be the number of rolls needed to observe the $i$th distinct value given that we have already observed $i-1$ distinct values on the die. Then $T = X_1 + \dots + X_6$ gives the total number of rolls needed to observe all $6$ sides. For example, if our sequence of rolls is $1131344213456$, then $X_1 = 1, X_2 = 2, X_3 = 3, X_4 = 2, X_5 = 4,$ and $X_6 = 1$. By linearity of expectation, we have that $$\mathbb{E}[T] = \mathbb{E}[X_1] + \mathbb{E}[X_2] + \dots + \mathbb{E}[X_6]$$ Let's interpret each random variable separately. $X_i$ is the number of rolls needed to observe the $i$th distinct value on the die, given that $i-1$ distinct values have already been observed. This means that $i-1$ of the $6$ sides on each turn do not give us a new value. This means that $6 - (i-1) = 7-i$ of the sides do yield a new value. Therefore, the probability on each roll that a new value is observed is $$\dfrac{7-i}{6}$$ Since this is a waiting time until some event, we should employ a geometric random variable. In particular, $X_i \sim \text{Geom}\left(\dfrac{7-i}{6}\right)$, so $\mathbb{E}[X_i] = \dfrac{6}{7-i}$. This implies that $$\mathbb{E}[T] = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^6 \dfrac{6}{7-i} = \dfrac{6}{1} + \dfrac{6}{2} + \dots + \dfrac{6}{6} = \displaystyle 6\sum_{i=1}^6\dfrac{1}{i} = \dfrac{147}{10}$$
hints: Use linearity of expectation by decomposing into the number of rolls between each consecutive new value.

title: First Ace
statement: Scott turns over cards one-by-one from a standard deck of cards without replacement. Find the expected number of cards Scott needs to turn over to observe the first ace.
hints: Use linearity of expectation by decomposing into the regions between aces, before the first ace, and after the last ace.
Alternatively, define an appropriate indicator random variable whose sum is equal to the total number of cards you must pull.

title: Roll Again I
statement: Kelly rolls a fair standard $6-$sided die. She observes the value on the face. Afterwards, she is given the option to either receive the upface (in dollars) as a payout or to roll again. If she rolls again, she receives the upface of the second roll (in dollars) as payout, regardless of what she rolled on the first turn. If Kelly plays optimally, what is her expected payout?
solution:
The idea here is that Kelly wants to maximize her expected value at each step. Therefore, Kelly should only roll again when she receives a value on the first roll than is smaller than the expected value rolling again.

$$$$

The expected value of a standard die is $3.5$, so if Kelly receives any value less than $3.5$, which would be $1,2,$ or $3$, she should roll again. This is because she would have another roll, which has expected value $3.5$, which is larger than the value currently showing on her die. Otherwise, if Kelly rolls a $4,5,$ or $6$, she should keep her value and cash out. We now need to compute a conditional expectation, conditioning on the value that Kelly observes on her first roll. Let $P$ be her payout and $X_1$ be the value on the first roll. By Law of Total Expectation, we have that $$\mathbb{E}[P] = \mathbb{E}[P \mid X_1 \leq 3]\mathbb{P}[X_1 \leq 3] + \mathbb{E}[P \mid X_1 > 3]\mathbb{P}[X_1 > 3]$$ The two probabilities are each $1/2$, as they cover $3$ of the $6$ possible values of the die. If $X_1 \leq 3$, Kelly rolls her die again, so her expected payout in this scenario is $3.5$, as it is the expected value of the second die roll. If Kelly receives larger than $3$ on the first roll, she stays with her current value, so the value she rolled is uniformly random among $\{4,5,6\}$, which has mean $5$. Her expected payout in this case would be $5$. Therefore, putting it all together, $$\mathbb{E}[P] = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 3.5 + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 5 = \dfrac{17}{4} = 4.25$$ Note that this is an improvement by $0.75$ over just a standard die roll.
hints: What is the expected value of a die? When is her expected value of a re-roll greater than what she rolled?

title: Roll Again II
statement: Kelly rolls a fair standard $6-$sided die. She observes the value on the face. Afterwards, she is given the option to either receive the upface (in dollars) as a payout or to roll again. If she rolls again, she faces the same decision to either receive the upface of the second roll (in dollars) as payout or roll a third time. If she chooses to roll for the third time, she receives a payout equal to this final roll, regardless of what she rolled previously. If Kelly plays optimally, what is her expected payout?
solution:
The idea here is that Kelly wants to maximize her expected value at each step. Therefore, Kelly should only roll again when she receives a value on the roll that is smaller than her expected payout in the remaining rolls.

$$$$

When Kelly rolls for her first time, she will have the opportunity to roll up to two more times afterwards. In those remaining two rolls, if she chooses to re-roll, under optimal play, her payout would be $17/4$ by Roll Again I, as it reduces to the same problem once there are two remaining rolls. Therefore, if Kelly observes a value that is at most $17/4$ on the first roll, then she should roll again, as her expected value by rolling again and playing optimally is higher than her current roll. Therefore, with probability $2/3$, Kelly will roll again, and her expected payout would be $17/4$. Otherwise, with probability $1/3$, Kelly receives a $5$ or $6$ on the first roll, and those would occur with equal probability. Therefore, conditional on Kelly observing a $5$ or $6$ on the first roll, her expected payout is $11/2$. By Law of Total Expectation, Kelly's expected payout on this strategy is $$\dfrac{2}{3} \cdot \dfrac{17}{4} + \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{11}{2} = \dfrac{14}{3}$$
hints: What is the expected value of a die? When is her expected value of a re-roll greater than what she rolled?

title: Coinsecutive I
statement: Daniel flips a fair coin until he obtains $2$ consecutive heads. Find the expected number of flips that Daniel performs.
solution:
The idea here is to condition on what happens at the first flip and set up a Markov Chain. 

$$$$

We need to think about our intermediate states that can occur before hitting $HH$. We could have no part of the sequence or one $H$ before hitting the sequence $HH$. Therefore, let $e_0$ be the expected number of flips needed to observe two consecutive heads given that no heads have been observed in our sequence yet. Similarly, let $e_H$ be the expected number of flips needed to observe two consecutive heads given that the previous flip was $H$. By conditioning on the first flip, we have that $$e_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (e_0 + 1) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (e_H + 1)$$ This is because if we obtain a tails (which occurs with probability $1/2$), it is as if we are still in a "nothing" state, but the number of flips we have performed now is $1$ instead of $0$. Therefore, our process is in the same state, but now we add $1$ to the counter. If we flip a heads on the first flip (also occurring with probability $1/2$), then we are in the state where our previous flip was $H$. We have to add $1$ for the same fact that we have now flipped and it must be added to our running total. 

$$$$

We now need to compute $e_H$ in terms of $e_0$. Conditioning on the next flip, we have that $$e_H = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1 + e_0) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1)$$ If we obtain a tails on the next flip, then we go back to a "nothing" state, as we don't have any part of the sequence $HH$ presently. Therefore, we add $1$ to our counter and have expected time $e_0$ to obtain $HH$. If we obtain a heads on the next flip, then we now have the sequence $HH$, which means it took $1$ flip from our current state to obtain $HH$. We now have  a system of two equations with two unknowns. By substituting in $e_H = \dfrac{1}{2}e_0 + 1$ into the first equation, we can solve for $e_0 = 6$.

$$$$

On an intuitive level, it should make sense that the sequences $HH$ (and also $TT$, assuming a fair coin) is the "most difficult" $2$ flip sequence to obtain consecutively. This is because of the fact that even if you have flipped a heads, flipping a tails restarts your sequence, whereas if your sequence is $HT$, if you flip a heads and then flip another heads, you don't have to restart your sequence. Therefore, it should take longer (on average) to see the sequence $HH$ than $HT$.
hints: Condition on what happens at the first flip and set up a Markov Chain.

title: Coinsecutive II
statement: Daniel flips a fair coin until he obtains a heads immediately followed by a tails. Find the expected number of flips that Daniel performs. For example, if the sequence Daniel flips is $THHT$, then it took him $4$ flips total.
solution:
The idea here is to condition on what happens at the first flip and set up a Markov Chain. 

$$$$

We need to think about our intermediate states that can occur before hitting $HT$. We could have no part of the sequence or one $H$ before hitting the sequence $HT$. Therefore, let $e_0$ be the expected number of flips needed to observe $HT$ given that no part of our sequence has been observed yet. Similarly, let $e_H$ be the expected number of flips needed to observe $HT$ given that the previous flip was $H$. By conditioning on the first flip, we have that $$e_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (e_0 + 1) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (e_H + 1)$$ This is because if we obtain a tails (which occurs with probability $1/2$), it is as if we are still in a "nothing" state, but the number of flips we have performed now is $1$ instead of $0$. Therefore, our process is in the same state, but now we add $1$ to the counter. If we flip a heads on the first flip (also occurring with probability $1/2$), then we are in the state where our previous flip was $H$. We have to add $1$ for the same fact that we have now flipped and it must be added to our running total. 

$$$$

We now need to compute $e_H$ in terms of $e_0$. Conditioning on the next flip, we have that $$e_H = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1) + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (1 + e_H)$$ If we obtain a tails on the next flip, then we have obtained the sequence $HT$. Therefore, it would have only taken one flip from $H$ to obtain our sequence of interest. If we obtain a heads on the next flip, then we remain in the state where the previous flip was a heads, but must add $1$ to our counter to account for the fact that we performed an additional flip. The above provides two equations with two unknowns, which we can solve for $e_0$. Solving for $e_H = 2$ in the second equation, we can solve for $e_0 = 4$ by substituting in $2$ for $e_H$ in the first equation.

$$$$

On an intuitive level, it should make sense that the sequences $HH$ (and also $TT$, assuming a fair coin) is the "most difficult" $2$ flip sequence to obtain consecutively. This is because of the fact that even if you have flipped a heads, flipping a tails restarts your sequence, whereas if your sequence is $HT$, if you flip a heads and then flip another heads, you don't have to restart your sequence. Therefore, it should take longer (on average) to see the sequence $HH$ than $HT$.
hints: Condition on what happens at the first flip and set up a Markov Chain.

title: Groggy Froggy
statement: A frog starts at the center of a circular lily pad of radius 1 meter. The frog hops to a uniformly random point on the lily pad. Find the expected radial distance of the frog from the center of the lily pad.
hints: Let $R$ be the radial distance of the frog from the center. Consider using the tail probability formula for expected value $\ev{R} = \ctailsum{R}$.
Alternatively, use the definition of expected value directly. How do you find the pdf of the distance from the frog to the center?

title: BOOLAH
statement: Find the number of anagrams of $BOOLAHUBBOO$ that have all of the $B$'s before the first $O$.
solution:
There are $3$ $B$s and $4$ $O$s in the word above. For the moment, ignore all of the other letters, as we only are concerned with the orderings of $B$ and $O$. First, we can select the locations of the $B$s and $O$s in our word. There are $\displaystyle \binom{11}{7}$ ways to pick the locations of these $7$ letters in our anagram, as there are $11$ total letters and $7$ must be reserved for these two characters. However, there is only one anagram of $BBBOOOO$ that has all of the $B$'s before all of the $O$'s. Namely, it is the one listed there. Therefore, we don't need to consider any further arrangements on the spots for the $B$s and $O$s. Afterwards, the other $4$ letters $LAHU$ can be arranged in the remaining $4$ spots completely at will in $4!$ ways. This is because of the fact that their relative orders are irrelevant. Therefore, the answer is $$4! \cdot \displaystyle \binom{11}{7} = \dfrac{11!}{7!} = 7920$$

 A second solution to this problem is to consider the total number of anagrams that can be made by this word and compute the probability that the anagram satisfies our condition. Namely, there are $\binom{11}{3,4,1,1,1,1} = \dfrac{11!}{3!4!}$ total anagrams of $BOOLAHUBBOO$, as it contains the repeated letters of $B$ and $O$. Once again, consider the orderings of the $B$s and $O$s relative to one another. If we are looking at only the $7$ blanks that correspond to $B$ and $O$, there are $\binom{7}{3}$ distinct ways to arrange the $3$ $B$s and $4$ $O$s on the blanks, as once the locations of the $B$s are fixed, the $O$s must go in the remaining $4$ blanks. Only one of these arrangements satisfies our condition, so the probability of this occurring is $$\dfrac{1}{\binom{7}{3}} = \dfrac{3!4!}{7!}$$ This means that the total number of anagrams that satisfy our condition is just the total number of anagrams multiplied by the probability of a given anagram satisfying our condition. This yields the answer $$\dfrac{3!4!}{7!} \cdot \dfrac{11!}{3!4!} = \dfrac{11!}{7!} = 7920$$
hints: There are $3$ $B$ and $4$ $O$ in the word above. How many ways are there to pick the locations of these $7$ letters in our anagram?
After the $B$s and $O$s are placed, how many ways are there to arrange the remaining letters?

title: Two Four Ace
statement: Suppose we deal out cards from a standard deck. Find expected number of cards after the first $2$ and before the first ace given that the first $2$ appears before the first ace.
hints: Use the idea of the "first ace" paradigm twice: First, apply it to find the expected number of cards between any rank $2$ or $A$ card. Afterwards, apply it a second time to find the expected number of regions.
Alternatively, condition on the position of the first $2$ and use the law of total probability.

title: Bowl of Ramen
statement: You have $n$ noodles in your soup bowl. Viciously, you are randomly blindfolded and told to take two ends of some noodles uniformly at random in your bowl and connect them. You are told to repeat this process until there are no free ends left to connect. Find the expected number of circles that will be formed by the end of this process when $n = 60$. Round to the nearest hundredth.
hints: Consider some basic cases of $1,2,$ and $3$ noodles. Then, try to derive a recurrence relation for general $n$.
Alternatively, can you think of an appropriate indicator random variable to define and then use the indicator trick?

title: True Equation
statement:
Dan has a fair $6$-sided die with faces labeled $1,2,3,4,+,$ and $-.$ In order to complete the equation
    \[ \underline{\qquad} \ \underline{\qquad} \ \underline{\qquad}=\underline{\qquad}, \]
    Dan repeatedly rolls his die and fills in a blank with the character he obtained, starting with the leftmost blank and progressing rightward. Find the probability that, when all blanks are filled, Dan forms a true equation.
solution:
We know that the first, third, and last digits must be numerical values, as the expression would not make sense otherwise. If the second digit is also numerical, then the statement can't be true, as Dan would have a $3-$digit integer equal to a $1-$digit integer, which is not valid. Therefore, the second roll must be either a $+$ or $-$. This gives us two cases to consider. 

$$$$

If the second roll is a $+$, then by fixing the first roll as a $1$, we can see the triples $(1,1,2), (1,2,3),$ and $(1,3,4)$ are the only valid roll combinations. Similarly, if $2$ is the first roll, then $(2,1,3)$ and $(2,2,4)$ are the only valid roll combinations. Lastly, if $3$ is the first roll, then $(3,1,4)$ is the only valid combination. This implies that there are $6$ combinations that are valid with a $+$.

$$$$

However, if the second roll is a $-$, we can see symmetry in this problem. If $a+b = c$ if valid, then $c-b = a$ is also a valid combination with a $-$. Therefore, we can match up the valid triples $(a,b,c)$ for $+$ with the triple $(c,b,a)$ for $-$ to get all of the valid combinations for $-$. This implies there are also $6$ triples with a $-$ in the middle that make a valid equation. 

$$$$

Therefore, there are $6 + 6 = 12$ total roll combinations that are valid. Since there are a total of $6^4 = 1296$ total rolls that can be obtained, as there are $6$ outcomes per roll, so the probability of a valid equation is $$\dfrac{12}{1296} = \dfrac{1}{108}$$
hints: Consider how the statement could be true. In particular, what must go in the second spot of the expression? Afterwards, what can go in the other spots?

title: Slow Ferry I
statement: You are waiting for a ferry to go to the Statue of Liberty! The ferry runs on a fixed schedule of appearing every $10$ minutes. If you arrive at a uniformly random time throughout the day, what is the expected time until the next ferry arrives (in minutes)?
solution: The key observation here is that since the ferry runs on a fixed schedule of appearing every $10$ minutes, the only quantity that matters is how many minutes before the next multiple of $10$ minutes did you appear. Since you arrive at the ferry stop at a uniformly random time throughout the day, the time until the next ferry (and also the time since the last ferry) is $\unif{0}{10}$ distributed. Therefore, this distribution has mean $5$, which means that you will have to wait $5$ minutes for the next ferry on average.
hints: Suppose that the ferry comes on minutes $10,20,\dots$ throughout the day. Since you arrive at a uniformly random time, the number of minutes after midnight you arrive, say $X$, will satisfy $X \ \text{mod} \ 10 \sim \unif{0}{10}$. Convince yourself of this intuitively.

title: Disco Squares I
statement: $n$ adjacent colorless squares are linear arranged. Each individual square is colored black or white with equal probability, independent of all other squares. A connected component is a maximal sequence of adjacent squares all with the same color. For example, BBWWBBBWBWWW has $6$ connected components. Find the expected number of connected components in the line after coloring the squares when $n = 100$.
solution:
It is best to derive a recurrence relation for the quantity of interest. This approach makes sense, as when we add on another square to the line, we get another line of squares that is directly related to what already was there. In particular, suppose $C_n$ is the expected number of connected components in a line of $n$ squares. We can find the expected number of connected components that the $n$th square brings in addition to the first $n-1$. Since we have an equal probability of black or white at each step, the symmetry here makes this work nicely.

$$$$

The color of the $(n-1)$st square here is irrelevant, as each is equally likely. Therefore, we can fix the color of it arbitrarily. There is probability $1/2$ that the $n$th square will match in color with the $(n-1)$st square. In this case, the expected number of connected component we would have in our line is $C_{n-1}$, as having another square of the same color does not add a new connected component. With probability $1/2$ as well, the color of the $n$th square differs from the previous one, which means that we obtain $C_{n-1} + 1$ connected components on average, as we have $C_{n-1}$ on average from the first $n-1$ squares and an additional $1$ component from the change in color. Putting this together, we obtain the recurrence $$C_n = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot C_{n-1} + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (C_{n-1} + 1) = C_{n-1} + \dfrac{1}{2}$$ We have a boundary condition that $C_1 = 1$, as there will always be exactly one connected component in one square. We can quickly see a closed-form for $C_n$ by recursing backwards $n-1$ times. In particular, $$C_n = C_{n-1} + \dfrac{1}{2} = C_{n-2} + 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dots = C_{1} + \dfrac{n-1}{2} = \dfrac{n+1}{2}$$ With $n = 100$ for our question, the answer is $C_{100} = 101/2 = 50.5$. 

$$$$

Intuitively, this formula makes a lot of sense. The first square will always give a new connected component, as there is nothing coming before that. Afterwards, each square differs from the color of the previous square with probability $1/2$, so each additional square contributes (on average) $1/2$ of a connected component, as it contributes $0$ or $1$ with equal probability. Therefore, the expected number of connected components total would be $1 + 1/2 \cdot (n-1)$, as there are $n-1$ squares beyond the first.
hints: Let $C_n$ be the expected number of connected components there are with $n$ squares in the line. Condition on the color of the $n-1$st square.

title: Birthday Squad
statement: $n$ friends in the squad sit around a circular table of $n$ seats uniformly at random. Assume that each of the friends has a distinct age. Find the probability that they sit down at the table in age order when $n = 6$. This means that either clockwise or counter-clockwise, the ages of the people are in strictly increasing order.
solution: The key here is to consider the number of ways that the people can distinctly sit at the table, and then count the number of ways that the people actually sit in increasing order of birthday. If this were a line of seats, there would be $n!$ distinct ways to sit the people at the table. However, the key issue with this is that rotations of the table really yield the same order of seats, so we are over-counting here by the number of rotations of the table that don't change the order. There are $n$ rotations of the table, as we can rotate by $1,2,\dots, n$ seats and obtain the same ordering of people, so there are a total of $n!/n = (n-1)!$ arrangements at the table that are distinct. Of those arrangements, only $2$ of them satisfy our event at hand: The people must either be going in increasing order counter-clockwise or clockwise. We don't have to consider rotations of these arrangements, as we have removed those rotations in the denominator. Therefore, our answer is simply $\frac{2}{(n-1)!}$. With $n = 6$, the answer is $1/60$.
hints: How many distinct ways can the people be sat at the table, where arrangements that can be obtained by rotations of the table are not considered distinct?
How many of those arrangements from the previous hint abide by the condition in the question? Read the condition again closely.

title: Quartic Normal I
statement: Let $X \sim N(0,1)$. Compute $\mathbb{E}[X \mid X^4]$.
solution:
The key fact to notice here is that if $X \sim \norm{0}{1}, -X \sim \norm{0}{1}$ as well. This arises from the fact that the PDF of a standard normal distribution is symmetric about $0$, so $X$ and $-X$, which really is a reflection about $x = 0$ in terms of the PDF, are identically distributed. Using this fact, we can replace $X$ by $-X$ in the expression and obtain $$\mathbb{E}[X \mid X^4] = \mathbb{E}[-X \mid (-X)^4] = - \mathbb{E}[X \mid X^4]$$ This can only occur when $\ev{X \mid X^4} = 0$. 

$$$$

This answer should make intuitive sense. Since $f(x) = x^4$ is even in $x$, the value of $x^4$ could be generated by $x$ or $-x$. By the symmetry of the standard normal distribution about $0$, $x$ and $-x$ have equal probability density, so the conditional mean in that pair is $0$. Since this "pairing" idea can hold for any value of $x$, the answer should be $0$.
hints: The key fact to notice here is that if $X \sim \norm{0}{1}, -X \sim \norm{0}{1}$ as well. Consider the fact the information given is even in $X$.

title: Blind Die
statement: Alan has two $6-$sided dice. One of the dice is a standard fair $6-$sided die with the values $1-6$ on the sides. Alan does not know the values on the other die. Note that the values on this other die do not necessarily need to be $1-6$ and can also potentially be repeated. Whenever Alan tosses both dice, each of the integer sums $1-12$, inclusive of both, are equally likely. What is the sum of the values on the sides of the die Alan doesn't know?
solution: We know that the distribution of the sum of the two dice is uniformly distribute on the first $12$ positive integers. The key here is to consider the expected value of the sum, as we can use this to find the expected value of the second die. Afterwards, since the die has $6$ times, we can take the expected value of the second die and multiply it by the number of times to get the sum of all of the sides. We know that the expected value of the sum of the two dice is $\dfrac{12+1}{2} = \dfrac{13}{2}$, as the sum is uniform on $\{1,2,\dots,12\}$. We also know that the expected value of a fair die is $\dfrac{7}{2}$, so by linearity of expectation, if $V$ is the expected value of the second die, then $$\dfrac{7}{2} + V = \dfrac{13}{2} \iff V = 3$$ This implies that the average value of the sides on the second die is $3$. Since there are $6$ sides on the second die, it must be the case that the sum of those sides is $3 \cdot 6 = 18$.
hints: Consider taking the expected value of the sum of the two dice. How can you relate that to the sum?

title: Jenga Stack
statement: Jenga blocks are either $1$ unit or $2$ units tall. Assuming you have at least $10$ of each type of block, how many distinct ways can a $10$ unit tall tower be built?
solution:
This has a recursive flavor to it, as the number of ways that the tower can be built depends on the last block in the tower. Therefore, it is appropriate to break this up into two cases: the last block is $2$ tall vs. $1$ tall. Let $T_n$ be the number of ways to build a tower of height $n$. If the last block in the tower is $1$ unit tall, then there are $T_{n-1}$ ways to build the tower that is $n-1$ units tall and add a $1$ unit tall block on top of it. If the last block in the tower is $2$ units tall, there are $T_{n-2}$ ways to build the tower that is $n-2$ units tall and add a $2$ unit tall block on top of it. These two cases are disjoint, as the last block in the tower can't be both $1$ unit and $2$ units tall.

$$$$

With this, we obtain a recurrence relation for $T_n$ given by $$T_n = T_{n-1} + T_{n-2}$$ The initial conditions on this are $T_1 = 1$ (only the $1$ tall block works here) and $T_2 = 2$ (either $2$ $1$ unit blocks or $1$ $2$ unit block). We can see that this looks very similar to the Fibonacci numbers. This is actually exactly the Fibonacci numbers shifted by $1$ term, as the initial two terms in Fibonacci are typically $F_1 = F_2 = 1$, so we are one term ahead with $T_n$. Therefore, the solution is $T_n = F_{n+1}$. This means that $T_{10} = F_{11} = 89$.
hints: This has a recursive flavor to it, as the number of ways that the tower can be built depends on the last block in the tower. Break this up into two cases: the last block is $2$ tall vs. $1$ tall.

title: Die Expected Value
statement: A fair standard $6-$sided die is rolled once. What is the expected value of the face that appears?
solution: The approach here is to apply the fundamental definition of expected value. The die can take $6$ possible values that are equally likely, which are the integers $1-6$, inclusive of both. In this scenario, the random variable $X$ is the value of the side that appears on the die. We know that $\prob{X = k} = \frac{1}{6}$ for each integer $1 \leq k \leq 6$, as each of the $6$ sides are equally likely. Therefore, $$\ev{X} = \sum_{k=1}^6 k\prob{X = k} = \dfrac{1 + 2 + 3+4 + 5 + 6}{6} = \dfrac{7}{2}$$
hints: Use the fundamental definition of expected value. There are $6$ possible values that the die can take, which are $1-6$. Each of them is equally likely.

title: Picky Subset
statement: How many subsets of $\{1,2,\dots, 12\}$ contain exactly $2$ elements from $\{1,2,3,4\}$?
solution: There are two steps to creating a valid subset here. We must first count the number of ways that $2$ elements from $\{1,2,3,4\}$ can be selected. As we are selecting $2$ elements from $4$, there are $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ ways to pick the two elements that are included in the subset that we are forming. After we have selected the two elements from $\{1,2,3,4\}$, there are no more restriction on what needs to be included in our subset. Therefore, for each of the remaining $8$ elements $\{5,6,\dots, 12\}$, they are free to be included or excluded from the subset being formed. In other words, once we have selected $2$ values from $\{1,2,3,4\}$, we can append to those two values any subset of the values $\{5,6,\dots, 12\}$ to create a subset that satisfies our original condition. There are $2^8 = 256$ such subsets of $\{5,6,\dots,12\}$, as that is a set of $8$ elements. Therefore, the total number of ways to form a satisfactory subset of $\{1,2,\dots, 12\}$ is $6 \cdot 256 = 1536$.
hints: There are two steps to creating a valid subset here. You must first count the number of ways that $2$ elements from $\{1,2,3,4\}$ can be selected. Afterwards, you must count the number of ways that the rest of the set can be formed.

title: Pair of Cards
statement: A standard deck of cards is shuffled uniformly at random and the top $2$ cards are dealt from the deck. Find the probability that the cards have the same rank.
solution:
The key here is to note that each rank is equally likely on the first card dealt, so we can fix the rank of this card arbitrarily. This is because the calculation will be exactly the same for each of the $13$ ranks, so we can just fix one of them and work with that for the calculation. 
$$$$

Once we have fixed this rank, we need to find the probability that we obtain a pair, which means that the second card dealt needs to match in rank to the first card. Once we have dealt out the first card, there will be $3$ more cards of that same rank left in the deck, as there were originally $4$ cards of each rank and we removed one card without replacement. There will be $51$ cards left in the deck, so the probability that the second card matches in rank to the first is $$\dfrac{3}{51}  =\dfrac{1}{17}$$
hints: Since all of the different ranks are equally likely, fix the first card's rank arbitrarily. What does this tell you about the second card?

title: Cordial Handshake I
statement: A business meeting begins with $2$ representatives from $5$ different companies. If every person at the meeting shakes hands with every other person at the meeting, how many handshakes occur total?
solution: The key to this question is to think about what constitutes a handshake. A handshake is exactly a pair of people coming together, so counting the number of pairs of people that can be formed at the meeting is exactly the same as counting the number of handshakes that occur. This question now becomes how many pairs of people can be formed? Since there are $5 \cdot 2 = 10$ people at the meeting and we want to form pairs of people, the answer is just $\binom{10}{2} = 45$, as each handshake consists of people two people from $10$ to shake hands.
hints: A handshake involves a pair of people, so it would be beneficial to count the number of pairs of people that can be formed.

title: Sturdy Roof I
statement: $100$ students are walking on the roof of a house. The weight of each student is random with mean $70$ kg and standard deviation $15$ kg, independently between students. The house roof is approved to withstand loads of up to $7500$ kg before failure. Approximate the probability that the total weight of the students exceeds the failure load of the roof. The answer will be in the form $\Phi(a)$ for some real $a$. Find $a$.
solution: The first item to determine is the appropriate theorem(s) that should be used here. Let $T$ be the total weight (kg) of all of the students and $W_i$ be the weight (kg) of the $i$th student, $1 \leq i \leq 100$. The total weight is just the sum of the weights of all students, so $T = W_1 + \dots + W_{100}$. We want to approximate the probability $\prob{T \geq 7500}$, as $7500$ is the threshold. This is a classic question that the central limit theorem (CLT) solves. We first need to standardize our random variable $T$ (subtract mean and divide by variance), and then we can apply CLT since $T$ is the sum of a large number of IID random variables. Therefore, the answer is $a = -10/3$.
hints: Since we are looking at the distribution of a sum of a large number of IID random variables, what theorem is most applicable here? Find the mean and variance of the sum and then standardize.

title: Sturdy Roof II
statement: $100$ students are walking on the roof of a house. The weight of each student is random with mean $70$ kg and standard deviation $15$ kg, independently between students. Approximate the probability that the mean weight of the students exceeds $73$ kg. The answer will be in the form $\Phi(a)$ for some real $a$. Find $a$.
solution:
The first item to determine is the appropriate theorem(s) that should be used here. Let $T$ be the total weight (kg) of all of the students and $W_i$ be the weight (kg) of the $i$th student, $1 \leq i \leq 100$. The total weight is just the sum of the weights of all students, so $T = W_1 + \dots + W_{100}$. Therefore, the mean of all of the weights is $\dfrac{T}{100}$, as we are summing up $100$ weights. We want to approximate the probability $\prob{\dfrac{T}{100} \geq 73}$, as we want the mean to be at least $73$ kg. This is the same as saying $\prob{T \geq 7300}$ after multiplying by $100$ on both sides of the interior. This is a classic question that the central limit theorem (CLT) solves. We first need to standardize our random variable $T$ (subtract mean and divide by variance), and then we can apply CLT since $T$ is the sum of a large number of IID random variables.

$$$$

By linearity of expectation and the fact that the $W_i$ random variables are IID, $\ev{T} = 100\ev{W_1} = 100 \cdot 70 = 7000$. Since the random variables are IID, we can say that $\var{T} = 100\var{W_1} = 100 \cdot 15^2 = (150)^2$, so $\sigma_T = \sqrt{\var{T}} = 150$. Standardizing, we get $$\mathbb{P}\left[\dfrac{T-7000}{150} \geq \dfrac{7300-7000}{150}\right]$$ We can approximate the LHS as a $Z \sim N(0,1)$ random variable by CLT, so we approximate the above probability by $$\mathbb{P}\left[T \geq 2\right]$$ This is just $1 - \Phi\left(2\right) = \Phi\left(-2\right)$ by the symmetry of the standard normal CDF. Therefore, the answer is $a = -2$.
hints: Since we are looking at the distribution of a sum of a large number of IID random variables, what theorem is most applicable here? Find the mean and variance of the sum and then standardize.

title: Scholastic Books
statement: Tesfa is a scholar, so he is reading a book that's $400$ pages long for fun. The amount of time it takes him to read each page (in minutes) is $\exponential{0.2}$ distributed, independent between pages. Find the approximate time $t$ so that the probability Tesfa finishes reading the book by time $t$ is $97.5\%$. Use the values $\Phi^{-1}(0.95) = 1.65$ and $\Phi^{-1}(0.975) = 1.96$.
solution:
The amount of time it takes for Tesfa to read the entire book is the sum of the times it takes for him to reach each of the pages. You are looking to compute some probability involving the sum of a large number of IID random variables here, so central limit theorem (CLT) would be most applicable to this question.

$$$$

Let's first construct the framework for this problem. Let $T_i$ be the amount of time it takes for Tesfa to read page $i$. Then $T = T_1 + \dots + T_{400}$ gives the total amount of time it takes for Tesfa to read the entire book. We know that $\mathbb{E}[T_1] = 5$ and $\var{T_1} = 5^2 = 25$ from properties of exponential random variables. By linearity of expectation and the fact that the $T_i$ random variables are IID, $\mathbb{E}[T] = 400\mathbb{E}[T_1] = 2000$. Similarly, since the $T_i$ random variables are IID, $\var{T} = 400\text{Var}(T_1) = 10000 = (100)^2$. Our goal in this question is to find a value $t$ so that $\mathbb{P}[T \leq t] = 0.975$, as there must be a $97.5\%$ chance that Tesfa finishes reading the book by time $t$, meaning the time he took, $T$, is at most $t$. 

$$$$

To apply CLT, we first need to standardize. By standardizing, the LHS of the equality above is the same as $\mathbb{P}\left[\dfrac{T-2000}{100} \leq \dfrac{t-2000}{100}\right]$. We can approximate $\dfrac{T-2000}{100}$ as a $Z \sim N(0,1)$ random variable by CLT. Thus, the LHS becomes $\Phi\left(\dfrac{t-2000}{100}\right)$. We need to solve the equality $$\Phi\left(\dfrac{t-2000}{100}\right) = 0.975$$ Using the inverse standard normal CDF and rearranging, we get that $t = 2000 + 100\Phi^{-1}(0.975)$. You can verify from the table that $\Phi^{-1}(0.975) = 1.96$, so we have that $t = 2196$ minutes.
hints: The amount of time it takes for Tesfa to read the entire book is the sum of the times it takes for him to reach each of the pages. You are looking to compute some probability involving the sum of a large number of IID random variables here, so which theorem(s) would be appropriate?

title: Contained Origin
statement: Let $X,Y \sim \unif{-2}{4}$ IID. Find the probability that origin lies between $X$ and $Y$.
solution:
We want to find the probability that the origin lies between the two random points that are selected. For this to happen, it must be the case that one of the two random variables takes a negative value, while the other takes a positive value. If this isn't the case, the region between the two will either be strictly positive or strictly negative in value, meaning $0$ would not be contained inside. 

$$$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, we can just consider one arrangement of $X$ and $Y$ being positive/negative and multiply this probability by the number of permutations of $X$ and $Y$ that there are. We will consider $\prob{X > 0, Y < 0}$. There are $2! = 2$ permutations of the values of $X$ and $Y$, so our answer to this question will just be $2 \prob{X > 0, Y< 0}$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables, we can say $\prob{X > 0, Y < 0} = \prob{X > 0}\prob{Y < 0}$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are uniform random variables, we can very easily compute these probabilities by computing the portion of the total support that our respective events cover. The event $\{X > 0\}$ is of length $4$ inside the support, as it is the interval $(0,4)$, while our total interval is of length $6$, so $\prob{X > 0} = 4/6 = 2/3$. Similarly, the event $\{Y < 0\}$ in our support is $(-2,0)$, which is of length $2$, so $\prob{Y < 0} = 2/6 = 1/3$. Therefore, our answer is $$\dfrac{2}{3} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot 2 = \dfrac{4}{9}$$
hints: For the origin to lie between the two points, it must be the case that one of them is negative and the other is positive.

title: Jar Match
statement: Bob has $2$ jars in front of him, say A and B. Jar A has $4$ blue and $6$ red marbles. Jar B has $5$ blue and $3$ red marbles. If Bob selects a uniformly random marble from each jar, find the probability that they match in color.
solution:
We want to compute the probability that Bob selects matching color marbles from each jar. Bob can obtain matching color marbles by either selecting a red marble or a blue marble from both jars. Since there are not identical amounts of blue and red marbles per jar, we should break this up into computing each case separately. 

$$$$

The probability that Bob selects a red marble from Jar A is $6/10 = 3/5$, meaning that he selects a blue marble from Jar A with probability $1 - 3/5 = 2/5$. This is because he selects uniformly at random from the jar. Similarly, from Jar B, the probability a red marble is selected is $3/8$, meaning the probability a blue marble is selected is $1 - 3/8 = 5/8$.

$$$$

By the independence of the two draws, the probability that Bob draws a red marble from both is the product of the individual probabilities that he draws a red marble from each jar, which is $3/5 \cdot 3/8 = 9/40$. The probability that Bob draws a blue marble from both is the product of the individual probabilities that he draws a blue marble from each jar, which is $2/5 \cdot 5/8 = 10/40$. Adding these two together, we get a total probability of drawing the same color from both jars as $19/40$.
hints: Bob can select matching color marbles by either selecting a red marble from each jar or a blue marble from each jar. Break up into the two cases.

title: Group Project I
statement: A class of $12$ students must divide up into $4$ groups of size $3$ with group numbers $1-4$ for a class project. How many distinct ways can the class perform this task?
solution: This is a classic problem of dividing distinct objects (in this case, people), into groups. In this case, the groups are distinct, which makes this problem easier. Since all the groups are distinct, all that matters is the group label for a given person. Each assignment of the $12$ people to the groups corresponds to an anagram of the $12$ character string consisting of $3$ of each integer $1-4$. For example, the anagram $123412341234$ corresponds to people $1,5,$ and $9$ going to group $1$, $2,6,$ and $10$ going to group $2$, and so on. This implies that counting the number of group arrangements is equal to counting the number of anagrams of the string above. The number of such anagrams is $\binom{12}{3,3,3,3} = 369600$.
hints: Imagine that the groups were distinct for the time being. How many ways could they arrange into groups? How do you account for the fact that they are not distinct afterwards?

title: Almost Squares
