The total area of the support of $X$ and $Y$ is $1$, so the probability of forming a right triangle given $Z = z$ is $\dfrac{z^2}{2}$. Plugging this in, we get that $$\prob{T} = \displaystyle \int_0^1 \dfrac{z^2}{2}dz = \dfrac{1}{6}$$ As per the first paragraph, we must multiply by $3$ to account for the number of ways that the maximum can be selected, so the answer is $3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. 

An alternative geometric solution goes as follows: Plot the joint support of $(X,Y,Z)$ in $3-$space. This forms the unit cube. The three conditions that must be satisfied are $X+Y> Z, X+Z>Y,$ and $Y+Z>X$. 

$$$$

Plot the planes $x+y=z, x+z=y,$ and $y+z=x$. Each of these planes cuts off a tetrahedron in the corner of the cube. For example, with $x+y=z$, the vertices of this tetrahedron are $(1,0,1), (0,0,0), (0,1,1),$ and $(0,0,1)$. This is a right tetrahedron with a base that is a triangle of side lengths $1$ in the $xy-$plane and height $1$. The area of this triangle is $1/2$, so the volume of the tetrahedron is $\dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 = \dfrac{1}{6}$. 

$$$$

These tetrahedra are also all disjoint, as only the largest number can be larger than the sum of the other two numbers, so there can't be any intersection between them. Thus, to find the probability of the event of interest, note that the region above these planes i.e. the tetrahedra are where $X+Y<Z$, and so on. Thus, we must consider the complement of these tetrahedra as the region where our event is satisfied. 

$$$$

The combined volume of these tetrahedra is $3 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ by the fact that they are disjoint, so the volume lying outside the tetrahedra is also $1/2$. 

$$$$

As the random variables are uniform, we can take ratios of volumes to compute probabilities. The volume of the unit cube is obviously 1. Thus, the probability of being able to form a triangle is $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
hints: There are three sources of randomness here, so it's best to fix one of them to remove a source of randomness and reduce this to a two-dimensional problem. Note that the condition for a triangle to exist is that the sum of the lengths of any two sides must be larger than the third side.

title: Subtract 1 I
statement: A fair standard $n-$sided die, where $n$ is even, is rolled. The outcome is recorded, and $1$ is subtracted from the result. Find the probability that the result is even when $n = 12$.
solution: An odd value must be rolled for the result to be even after subtraction. On this die, since $n$ is even, there are $n/2$ even values and $n/2$ odd values on the die. As the die is fair, the probability of obtaining an odd value on the die, and hence an even result after subtraction, is $1/2$, regardless of $n$.
hints: An odd value must be rolled for the result to be even after subtraction.

title: Subtract 1 II
statement: A fair standard $n-$sided die, where $n$ is odd, is rolled. The outcome is recorded, and $1$ is subtracted from the result. Find the probability that the result is even when $n = 11$.
solution: An odd value must be rolled for the result to be even after subtraction. On this die, since $n$ is odd, there are $(n-1)/2$ even values and $(n+1)/2$ odd values on the die, as there is one extra odd value. As the die is fair, the probability of obtaining an odd value on the die, and hence an even result after subtraction, is $\dfrac{n+1}{2n}$. With $n = 11$, the answer is $\dfrac{6}{11}$.
hints: An odd value must be rolled for the result to be even after subtraction.

title: Prime Sum I
statement: $1 \leq k \leq n - 1$ integers are selected uniformly at random from the set $S_n$ of the $n$ prime integers, where $k$ is even. Find the probability that the sum all of $k$ integers is even when $n = 10$ and $k = 4$.
solution: Note that $2$ is the only even prime integer. Since $k$ is even, to obtain an even sum, we must have all of the selected integers be odd, as if we select $2$, there would be an odd amount of odd integers selected, which results in an odd sum. Thus, we must select all $k$ integers from the other $n-1$ prime integers that are not $2$. In other words, we just need to not select $2$. Since we pick uniformly at random, each integer is equally likely to either be or not be selected. As $k$ of the $n$ integers are selected, the probability that any particular integer is selected is $k/n$. Thus, the probability any given element is not selected is $1 - k/n$. This can also be computed by noting that there are $\binom{n-1}{k}$ ways to pick $k$ integers from the other $n-1$ integers that are not the one that we desire to exclude, and there are $\binom{n}{k}$ ways to pick a subset of $k$ elements from $n$, so the probability that, so the probability of excluding a given element is $$\dfrac{\binom{n-1}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}} = \dfrac{\frac{(n-1)!}{k!(n-k-1)!}}{\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}} = \dfrac{n-k}{n} = 1 - \dfrac{k}{n}$$ With these values, the answer is $\dfrac{3}{5}$.
hints: Note that $2$ is the only even prime integer. Since $k$ is even, we must select all $k$ integers that are odd.

title: Prime Sum II
statement: $1 \leq k \leq n - 1$ integers are selected uniformly at random from the set $S_n$ of the $n$ prime integers, where $k$ is odd. Find the probability that the sum all of $k$ integers is even when $n = 10$ and $k = 5$.
solution: Note that $2$ is the only even prime integer. Since $k$ is odd, we must select $2$ so that there are an even number of odd integers selected. Since we pick uniformly at random, each integer is equally likely to either be or not be selected. As $k$ of the $n$ integers are selected, the probability that any particular integer is selected is $k/n$. This can also be computed by noting that to pick $2$, we fix $2$ in our selection. Afterwards, we must select $k-1$ integers from the other $n-1$. There are $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ ways to do this. There are $\binom{n}{k}$ ways to pick a subset of $k$ elements from $n$ without restriction, so the probability that, so the probability of excluding a given element is $$\dfrac{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}{\binom{n}{k}} = \dfrac{\frac{(n-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!}}{\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}} = \dfrac{k}{n}$$ With these values, the answer is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
hints: Note that $2$ is the only even prime integer. Since $k$ is odd, we must select $2$ so that there are an even number of odd integers selected.

title: Below Diagonal
statement: A square has vertices at $(0,0), (0,4), (4,4),$ and $(4,0)$. A bug starts at $(3,2)$ on the interior of the square. The bug moves in each of the $4$ cardinal directions with equal probability at each step. The bug stop when it crashes into one of the sides of the square. Find the probability that the bug ends up crashing into the square on a vertical side.
solution:
The key to note here is that if the bug is on a diagonal of the square, it is equally likely to end up on either a horizontal or vertical side. This is because any path that leads to a vertical side could be reflected about the diagonal to result a path that is equally likely (since each movement is uniformly at random) to yield a path that ends up on a horizontal side. Therefore, the best approach here is to condition on where the bug moves in $1$ step from $(3,2)$. 

$$$$

From the bug's current position, if it moves $1$ unit right, it hits a vertical side. This occurs with probability $1/4$. Otherwise, any other move that the bug takes from this current position puts it on a diagonal. If it does this, there is probability $1/2$ that it ends up on a vertical side. The bug moves in such a way with probability $1 - 1/4 = 3/4$. Therefore, the total probability that the bug reaches a vertical side is $$\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{5}{8}$$
hints: The key to note here is that if the bug is on a diagonal of the square, it is equally likely to end up on either a horizontal or vertical side. This is because any path that leads to a vertical side could be reflected about the diagonal to result a path that is equally likely (since each movement is uniformly at random) to yield a path that ends up on a horizontal side.
Condition on the move of the bug at the first step.

title: Set Combo I
statement: Let $1 \leq k \leq n$ be fixed. How many subsets of $[n] = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$ contain exactly one of the elements in $\{1,2,\dots, k\}$ when $n = 8$ and $k = 3$?
solution: To create a valid subset, you must choose one element of $\{1,2,\dots, k\}$ and any other subset of $\{4,5,\dots, n\}$. These can be appended together to form a subset with exactly one element from $\{1,2,\dots, k\}$, as there are no restrictions on what else there is in the subset. There are $k$ ways to pick the element from $\{1,2,\dots, k\}$, and there are $2^{n-k}$ ways to pick a subset of $\{k+1,\dots, n\}$, as there are $n$ elements total and the part removed has $k$ elements, so there are $n-k$ elements in the remaining set. A subset of size $r$ has $2^r$ subsets, so there are $2^{n-k}$ such subsets of this set. Thus, there are $k \cdot 2^{n-k}$ subsets total satisfying this condition. With the specified values, the answer is $96$.
hints: To create a valid subset, you must choose one element of $\{1,2,\dots, k\}$ and any other subset of $\{k+1,\dots, n\}$.

title: Set Combo II
statement: Let $1 \leq k \leq n$ be fixed. How many subsets of $[n] = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$ contain exactly one of the elements in $\{1,2,\dots, k\}$ and only contains odd integers when $n = 8$ and $k = 3$?
solution:
To create a valid subset, you must choose one odd element of $\{1,2,\dots, k\}$ and any subset of the odd integers in $\{k+1,\dots, n\}$. This problem now boils down to counting the number of odd integers in a set of the form $[r]$. We can see that there is one odd integer for $r = 1,2$, two for $r = 3,4$, and so on. Thus, a good guess is $\ceil{r/2}$, the smallest integer at least $r/2$. This is indeed the answer, as the first positive integer is odd, so the number of odd positive integers will be equal to the number of even positive integers when $r$ is even i.e. $\ceil{r/2} = r/2$, as $r/2$ is an integer. Otherwise, when $r$ is odd, there will be one more odd integer than even integer, so the ceiling actually comes into play. 

$$$$

Using this, there are $\ceil{k/2}$ ways to pick the odd integer from $[k]$ that is included in our subset. There are $\ceil{n/2}$ odd integers in $[n]$ total, and $\ceil{k/2}$ of them were in $[k]$, which we can no longer pick from. Therefore, there are $\ceil{n/2} - \ceil{k/2}$ odd integers left in $\{k+1,\dots, n\}$ to select from. We can select any such subset among these $\ceil{n/2} - \ceil{k/2}$ integers, so there are $2^{\ceil{n/2} - \ceil{k/2}}$ subsets of these integers that can be selected from. By the multiplication principle, this implies that there $\ceil{k/2} \cdot 2^{\ceil{n/2} - \ceil{k/2}}$ such subsets that are valid, as we have $\ceil{k/2}$ ways to pick one element from $[k]$. With the specified values, the answer is $8$.
hints: To create a valid subset, you must choose one odd element of $\{1,2,\dots, k\}$ and any subset of the odd integers in $\{k+1,\dots, n\}$.

title: Equal Ends
statement: Amber and Billy each have a fair $n-$sided die, where $n \geq 2$. If Amber rolls a strictly larger value than Billy, she wins. If Amber and Billy roll equal values, Billy wins. Otherwise, both of them roll their die again. The game continues until there is a winner declared. Find the probability that Amber is the winner when $n = 10$.
solution:
For a winner to have been declared in the game, it must be the case that Amber and Billy rolled either the same value or Amber rolled higher than Billy. In other words, Amber's roll was at least as high as Billy's roll. All of the other outcomes that came before the end of the game don't influence the end state, as each roll is independent. Thus, on the roll that ends the game, condition on Amber rolling at least as high as Billy, we must find the probability that Amber rolled strictly higher than Billy. Since the dice are fair, we can take the ratio of the number of outcomes that have Amber win to the total number of outcomes that end the game.$$$$ 

There are $n^2$ total outcomes for the two dice with no restrictions. Of those, $n$ of those outcomes have Amber and Billy with the same value, as these are all the pairs $(i,i)$ for $1 \leq i \leq n$. Removing these, there are $n^2 - n$ outcomes left where Amber and Billy don't have the same value. These are all the pairs $(a,b)$ for $a \neq b$. Exactly half of these pairs have Amber winning i.e. $a > b$, as we can pair up $(a,b)$ with $(b,a)$ for all $a \neq b$. One of these is an outcome where Amber wins, while the other is where Billy rolls a larger number than Amber. Thus, there are $\dfrac{n^2-n}{2}$ outcomes where Amber rolls a strictly larger number than Billy. Adding the two cases, there are $\dfrac{n^2-n}{2} + n = \dfrac{n^2 + n}{2}$ outcomes where Amber rolls at least as large as Billy. Thus, the probability Amber rolls larger than Billy i.e. wins is $$\dfrac{n(n-1)/2}{n(n+1)/2} = \dfrac{n-1}{n+1}$$ With $n = 10$, the answer is $\dfrac{9}{11}$.
hints: There are $n^2$ total outcomes for the two dice. Of those, how many outcomes have equal values? How many have Amber with a larger value?

title: Monty Hall I
statement: You  made it onto a game show! The host presents you with $n \geq 3$ doors. One door contains a prize, while the other $n-1$ doors are empty. The prize is uniformly random between the doors. You choose an initial door. Afterwards, the host opens a door (not the one you selected) which he knows has no prize behind it. You then are given the option to switch your door. Find the probability that you find the prize if you switch when $n = 8$.
solution: To win on the switch, you must have not picked the door with the prize on the original guess and then must pick the door with the prize behind it. On the original guess, there are $n$ doors for you to select from, so the probability that you don't select the door with the prize behind it initially is $\frac{n-1}{n}$, as $n-1$ of the $n$ doors have no prize behind them. After the host opens a door without a prize behind it, if you choose to switch, there are $n-2$ other doors that can be selected (all but your current choice and the one that the host opened). Since we already assume the prize is not in the door you selected nor the opened door, it must be in one of the other $n-2$ doors uniformly at random, so the probability you switch to the door with it is $\frac{1}{n-2}$. Multiplying these together, the probability that you win upon switching is $$\dfrac{n-1}{n} \cdot \dfrac{1}{n-2} = \dfrac{1}{n} \cdot \dfrac{n-1}{n-2} \geq \dfrac{1}{n}$$ Note that this implies that it is better to switch, no matter what $n$ is, as $1/n$ is the probability you win if you don't switch (you must have selected it initially). With the specified values, the answer is $7/48$.
hints: To win on the switch, you must have not picked the door with the prize on the original guess and then must pick the door with the prize behind it.

title: Consecutive Heads I
statement: A fair coin is flipped $5$ times. Find the probability of obtaining exactly $3$ heads consecutively.
solution: Since the coin is fair, we can just count sequences of coin flips, rather than working with the binomial distribution. In a problem like this, since $5$ is a small number of flips, it's best to enumerate the forms of the outcomes. The sequence of outcomes must be in the form $HHHT-, THHHT, or -THHH$, where $-$ can be either heads or tails. This implies that there are $2$ outcomes of the first and last form, while there is exactly $1$ outcome of the middle form. This is because $-$ has two options. Thus, there are $5$ total outcomes yielding exactly $3$ consecutive heads. There are $2^5 = 32$ total outcomes of the flipping sequence, as each flip has $2$ options, so the probability of obtaining exactly $3$ consecutive heads is $\dfrac{5}{32}$.
hints: The sequence of outcomes must be in the form $HHHT-, THHHT, or -THHH$.

title: Consecutive Heads II
statement: A fair coin is flipped $5$ times. Find the probability of obtaining at least $3$ heads consecutively.
solution: Since the coin is fair, we can just count sequences of coin flips, rather than working with the binomial distribution. To have at least $3$ consecutive heads consecutively, there can be exactly $3,4,$ or $5$ consecutive heads. In "Consecutive Heads I", we found that $5$ sequences had exactly $3$ consecutive heads. It is easy to see that the only sequence with $5$ consecutive heads is $HHHHH$. This is a single sequence. To have exactly $4$ consecutive heads, the sequence must either be $HHHHT$ or $THHHH$, which is $2$ possible outcomes. Adding all of these together, we obtain $8$ total outcomes out of $2^5 = 32$ total, so the answer is $8/32 = 1/4$.
hints: To have at least $3$ consecutive heads consecutively, there can be exactly $3,4,$ or $5$ consecutive heads. You already computed the case of exactly $3$ in "Consecutive Heads I".

title: Consecutive Heads III
statement: A fair coin is flipped $6$ times. Find the probability of obtaining exactly $3$ heads consecutively.
solution:
Since the coin is fair, we can just count sequences of coin flips, rather than working with the binomial distribution. In a problem like this, since $6$ is a small number of flips, it's best to enumerate the forms of the outcomes. To have exactly $3$ consecutive heads, the form of the sequence must be $HHHT--, THHHT-, -THHHT,$ or $--THHH$. Note that the first two are just reflections of the last two forms, so we can count the number of ways that fall into the first two forms, and then multiply by $2$ to account for the last two, as they will have equal numbers of satisfactory sequences. 

$$$$

For the first sequence, there are $2$ dashes, implying that there are $2^2 = 4$ sequences of this form. For the second sequence, there is one $-$, implying that there are $2$ sequences of this form. Thus, for the first two forms combined, there are $2^2 + 2 = 6$ outcomes of these forms. Thus, there are $2 \cdot 6 = 12$ total sequences with exactly $3$ consecutive heads after accounting for the forms that are reflections. Since the coin is flipped $6$ times, there are $2^6 = 64$ total sequences of coin flips, so the probability of exactly $3$ consecutive heads is $$\dfrac{12}{64} = \dfrac{3}{16}$$
hints: To have exactly $3$ consecutive heads, the form of the sequence must be $HHHT--, THHHT-, -THHHT,$ or $--THHH$, where $-$ can be either $H$ or $T$.

title: Room Divider
statement: There are $n$ people in a room, of which $1 \leq r \leq n$ are special. The people are divided up into $r$ distinct groups of sizes $n_1,\dots,n_r$, with each $n_i \geq 1$. Find the probability that each group consists of one special person when $n = 10, r = 3, n_1 = 2, n_2 = 3,$ and $n_3 = 5$.
solution:
We are looking to assign distinct people to distinct groups, so the multinomial coefficient is the best approach here. With no restrictions at all, there are $\binom{n}{n_1,\dots, n_r}$ ways to assign people to the groups with these respective sizes. To compute the probability that each group has exactly $1$ special person, we should fix one in each group. We know that there are $r!$ ways to arrange around the special people between the groups, as we are permuting the $r$ people to the $r$ groups. Now, there are $n-r$ people left to distribute to the groups, and group $i$ should have $n_i - 1$ more people assigned to it, as one person is already in the group. The total number of ways to do this is $\binom{n-r}{n_1-1,\dots, n_r -1}$. Thus, there are $r! \cdot \binom{n-r}{n_1-1,\dots, n_r -1}$ ways to do this in total, so as all arrangements are equally likely, the probability is $$\dfrac{r! \cdot \binom{n-r}{n_1-1,\dots, n_r -1}}{\binom{n}{n_1,\dots, n_r}} = \dfrac{n_1\dots n_r}{\binom{n}{r}}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $1/4$.

Suppose that all $n$ people are already assigned to their groups before anyone special has been selected. Now, we want to pick $r$ of the $n$ people to be special. There are $\binom{n}{r}$ ways to do this without restriction. However, with the restriction that there is exactly one person per group that is special, there are $n_i$ ways to pick the special person from group $i$, so there would be $n_1\dots n_r$ total ways to do this, as each group is independently. Thus, the probability of our event of interest is $$\dfrac{n_1\dots n_r}{\binom{n}{r}}$$
hints: How many ways are there to divide up the people with no restrictions? Fix one special person per group. How many people are left to divide. and how many should be assigned per group?

title: Maxima Range
statement: Suppose that $X_1,\dots, X_n \sim \unif{0}{a}$ for some $a > 0$. Define $M_n = \max(X_1,\dots, X_n)$. For $(b,c] \subseteq (0,a)$, compute $\prob{b < M_n \leq c}$ when $n = 4, a = 5,$ and $(b,c] = (2,4]$.
solution: Computing statements of the form $\prob{M_n \leq x}$ are easy. We can write $\prob{b < M_n \leq c} = \prob{M_n \leq c} - \prob{M_n \leq b}$, as $(0,b] \subseteq (0,c]$. Therefore, we want to compute $\prob{M_n \leq x}$ for any $0 < x < a$. We can write out $$\prob{M_n \leq x} = \prob{\max(X_1,\dots, X_n) \leq x} = \prob{X_1 \leq x,\dots, X_n\leq x} = \prob{X_1\leq x}\dots \prob{X_n \leq x} = (\prob{X_1} \leq x)^n$$ The event splits out, as if $M_n \leq x$, the maximum of all $n$ are at most $x$, so this means all of the $n$ random variables are at most $x$. The other two equalities are by the fact that the $X_i$ random variables are IID. Since $X_1 \sim \unif{0}{a}$, we can take ratios of lengths of intervals to compute probabilities. Namely, the total support is of length $a$, and the interval $(0,x]$ is of length $x$, so $\prob{X_1 \leq x} = \dfrac{x}{a}$. Therefore, $\prob{M_n \leq x} = \left(\dfrac{x}{a}\right)^n$. All that remains is plugging in these values into the expression from the start. Namely, $$\prob{b < M_n \leq c} = \left(\dfrac{c}{a}\right)^n - \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)^n$$ With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{4^4 - 2^4}{5^4} = \dfrac{48}{125}$.
hints: Computing statements of the form $\prob{M_n \leq x}$ are easy. We can write $\prob{b < M_n \leq c} = \prob{M_n \leq c} - \prob{M_n \leq b}$, as $(0,b] \subseteq (0,c]$.

title: Missing Subset
statement: Fix positive integers $k,r,$ and $n$. $r$ elements are drawn uniformly at random with replacement from $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$. Let $S \subseteq [n]$ with $|S| = k$. Compute the probability that none of the $r$ integers drawn are in $S$ when $n = 10, |S| = 4,$ and $r = 4$.
solution: For none of the integers drawn to be in $S$, all of the $r$ integers must be in $[n]\setminus S$, which has cardinality $n-k$. Since we draw uniformly at random, the probability this occurs per trial is $\dfrac{n-k}{n} = 1- \dfrac{k}{n}$. Therefore, by the independence of the draws, the probability this occurs for all $r$ trials is $\left(1 - \dfrac{k}{n}\right)^r$. With the specific values, the answer is $\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^4 = \dfrac{81}{625}$.
hints: All of the $r$ integers must be in $[n]\S$, which has cardinality $n-k$. What is the probability this occurs per element drawn?

title: Primary Ten
statement: A standard deck of cards is shuffled and dealt one one-by-one without replacement. Find the probability that no face cards come before the ten of spades.
solution: We only care about the orderings of the face cards and the $10$ of spades in this question, so the rest of the cards can be disregarded. As the deck is shufled completely at random, all orderings of these cards are equally likely, so all cards are equally likely to be in any spot relative to each other. In particular, of the $13$ cards we are considering (the $4 \cdot 3 = 12$ face cards and the $10$ of spades), we want the $10$ of spades to be first among them. This would ensure that no face cards come before the $10$ of spades. As this card is equally likely to be in any of the $13$ spots of the relative ordering, the probability is $1/13$.
hints: We only care about the orderings of the face cards and the $10$ of spades in this question, so the rest of the cards can be disregarded.

title: Some Rain I
statement: On Saturday, there is a probability $0 < p_1 < 1$ of rain. On Sunday, there a probability $0 < p_2 < 1$ of rain. Assuming that rain on the two days is independent, find the probability it does not rain this weekend when $p_1 = 0.4$ and $p_2 = 0.5$.
solution: Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be the events that it rains Saturday and Sunday, respectively. We are looking to compute $\prob{R_1^c \cap R_2^c}$, which is the event that there isn't rain on either day. Note that $R_1$ and $R_2$ are independent, so their complements are too. Thus, we can state that $$\prob{R_1^c \cap R_2^c} = \prob{R_1^c} \prob{R_2^c} = (1-\prob{R_1})(1-\prob{R_2}) = (1-p_1)(1-p_2)$$ With the specified values, the answer is $0.3$.
hints: Let $R_1$ and $R_2$ be the events that it rains Saturday and Sunday, respectively. We are looking to compute $\prob{R_1^c \cap R_2^c}$, which is the event that there isn't rain on either day. Note that $R_1$ and $R_2$ are independent.

title: Exponential Gamma Variance
statement: Suppose that $X \sim \gam{a}{b}$. Compute $\var{e^X}$ when $a = 4$ and $b = 1/4$. Round to the nearest thousandth.
solution: Whenever dealing with random variables in the form of $e^X$, where $X$ is some other random variable, the best approach is typically something with MGFs, as the definition of the MGF of $X$ is $M_X(\theta) = \ev{e^{\theta X}}$. Therefore, the first step is to use the definition of variance and note the form of the resulting expression. Doing this, we see that $$\var{e^X} = \ev{(e^X)^2} - (\ev{e^X})^2 = \ev{e^{2X}} - (\ev{e^X})^2 = M_X(2) - (M_X(1))^2$$ The terms are substituted in by noting that these are exactly the definition of the MGF with the values $1$ and $2$ in for $\theta$. The MGF of $X \sim \gam{a}{b}$ is $M_X(\theta) = (1-b\theta)^{-a}$. Plugging in the specific values of $\theta$ for each term in the above, we see that $$\var{e^X} = (1-2b)^{-a} - ((1-b)^{-a})^2 = (1-2b)^{-a} - (1-b)^{-2a}$$ Note that $b < 1/2$ for this expression to be valid, as the MGF of $X$ is only defined for $\theta < 1/b$, and we need a finite value for $M_X(2)$. With the specified values, the answer is $2^4 - \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^8 \approx 6.011$.
hints: Whenever dealing with random variables in the form of $e^X$, where $X$ is some other random variable, the best approach is typically something with MGFs, as the definition of the MGF of $X$ is $m(\theta) = \ev{e^{\theta X}}$. Use the definition of variance and note the form of the resulting expression.

title: Forehead
statement: Find the expected number of flips that need to be performed on a coin that has probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads per flip to obtain $k$ heads (not necessarily consecutively) when $k = 4$ and $p = 1/3$.
solution: This scenario here is exactly one that belongs to a named distribution. Since we are looking at the distribution of the $k$th success (in this scenario, heads) of some event in IID trials, the negative binomial distribution is most appropriate here. The parameters are $k$ for the number of successes that we want to observe and $p$ for the probability of success per trial. Therefore, if $N$ is the random variable that represents the number of flips we need to perform, $N \sim \negbinom{k}{p}$. This distribution is known to have mean $\ev{N} = \frac{k}{p}$. With the specific values, the answer is $12$.
hints: What distribution does this follow?

title: Car Stopper
statement: You are looking to drive to a friend's house. With no interruptions, this takes $m$ minutes to do. However, there are $n$ stoplights along the way labelled $1-n$. Stoplight $i$ stops you with probability $p_i$. Given that you are stopped by stoplight $i$, you are stopped for $L_i$ minutes. Find the expected amount of time it takes for you to reach your friends house when $m = 10, n = 4, p_i = 1/i,$ and $L_i = i$.
solution: The base amount of time that you take to reach your friend's house from your house is $m$. The stoplights add on additional time, so if $T_i$ is the amount of time that stoplight $i$ stops you for, $T =\displaystyle  m + \sum_{i=1}^n T_i$ gives the total amount of time it takes for you to reach your friend's house, as it is the base time plus the time spent at stoplights. We are looking to compute $\ev{T}$. By linearity of expectation, we have that $$\ev{T} = m + \sum_{i=1}^n \ev{T_i}$$ $\ev{T_i}$ is the expected amount of time that you are stopped at light $i$. Stoplight $i$ either stops you, in which you spend $L_i$ minutes at it with probability $p_i$, or you don't get stopped, which means you don't spend any time at the stoplight. Therefore, $\ev{T_i} = p_iL_i + 0(1-p_i) = p_iL_i$. Plugging this in, $$\ev{T} = m + \sum_{i=1}^n p_iL_i$$ With the specified values, the answer is $14$.
hints: The base amount of time that you take to reach your friend's house from your house is $m$. The stoplights add on additional time, so if $T_i$ is the amount of time that stoplight $i$ stops you for, $T =\displaystyle  m + \sum_{i=1}^n T_i$ gives the total amount of time it takes for you to reach your friend's house, as it is the base time plus the time spent at stoplights.
Linearity of Expectation.

title: Prior Die Sum II
statement: Jeffrey is rolling a pair of standard fair $6-$sided dice until he obtains a sum of either $2$ or $4$ on the upfaces. Find the probability Jeffrey rolls a sum of $4$.
solution: Since we are looking at the probability that an event occurs before some other event disjoint to it, the paradigm of "Prior Event I" is particularly appealing to solve this problem. Clearly, the events of rolling a sum of $2$ and a sum of $4$ are disjoint on a given trial. By writing out the PMF table of the sum of two dice, sums of $2$ and $4$ occur with respective probabilities $\dfrac{1}{36}$ and $\dfrac{3}{36} = \dfrac{1}{12}$. These sum to at most $1$, so the result of "Prior Event I" yields that the probability of obtaining a sum of $4$ before a sum of $2$ is $\dfrac{3/36}{1/36 + 3/36} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.
hints: Make this question fit the paradigm of "Prior Event I" with some appropriate events.

title: Come to Besiktas
statement: Ricardo Quaresma followed directions and went to Besiktas. When he arrived, he had a house waiting for him that was numbered $331455$. However, some people swarmed his house and knocked off $2$ of the numbers. Each pair of numbers is equally likely to have fallen. When he goes outside and sees the damage, as he is new to the area, he forgets what order they should go in, so he puts them back up uniformly at random in the two open slots in the address. Find the probability that Quaresma correctly obtains $331455$ as his address again.
solution: If $33$ or $55$ fell off of the address, no matter how he puts them back up, they will form the correct address. However, this is not true for any other pair. Thus, the best approach is to condition on whether or not the two numbers that fell off were the same or not. There are $\binom{6}{2} = 15$ pairs of numbers that can fall off his address, as we select $2$ from $6$. Of these $15$ pairs $2$ of these consist of the same values twice. Thus, the other $13$ consist of two distinct. values. Let $C$ be the event that Quaresma has the correct address after he puts the values up again, and let $S$ be the event that the two numbers that fell off were the same. By Law of Total Probability, we have that $$\prob{C} = \prob{C \mid S}\prob{S} + \prob{C \mid S^c}\prob{S^c}$$ We see that $\prob{S} = 2/15$ and $\prob{S^c} = 13/15$ by the discussion above and the fact that each pair of numbers is equally likely to fall off. If the two numbers are the same, he recreates the correct address, so $\prob{C \mid S} = 1$. Otherwise, if they are different, there are $2$ orders in which he can rearrange the numbers, of which $1$ is correct, so $\prob{C \mid S^c} = 1/2$. Plugging these in, $$\prob{C} = \dfrac{2}{15} \cdot 1 + \dfrac{13}{15} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{17}{30}$$
hints: If $33$ or $55$ fell off of the address, no matter how he puts them back up, they will form the correct address. However, this is not true for any other pair.
The best approach is to condition on whether or not the two numbers that fell off were the same or not.

title: Bold Element
statement: Erica intends to construct a subset $S$ of $[n] = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$. If she is unsure about including an element $x \in [n]$ in $S$, she will boldface $x$ and include it in $S$. For example, with $n = 4$, $\{ 1,2\},$ $\{ 1,\mathbf{3},4 \},$ and $\{ \mathbf{1},\mathbf{2},\mathbf{3},\mathbf{4} \}$ are valid examples of subsets $S$, while $\{ 1,2,\mathbf{2},4 \}$ is not. Find the total number of such sets $S$ that Erica can construct when $n = 5$.
solution: For every element in $[n]$, there are three options, include in $S$, exclude in $S$, or bold it and include in $S$. Every valid subset $S$ is formed by selecting one of the three options for each of the $n$ elements of $[n]$. Therefore, the number of subsets that can be formed is $3^n$, as there are $3$ options for each of $n$ elements. For $n = 5$, the answer is $3^5 = 243$.
hints: For every element in $[n]$, there are three options, include in $S$, exclude in $S$, or bold it and include in $S$.

title: Uniformly Decreasing Chain
statement:
Let $X_1,X_2,\dots \sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Define $N$ as the first index such that $X_N$ is not the minimum of the first $N$ random variables i.e. $N = \min\{n : X_n \neq \min(X_1,\dots, X_n)\}$. Compute $\ev{X_{N-1}}$, the expected value of the smallest random variable among the $N$. Report your answer to the nearest thousandth.

$$$$

Note: You may find it helpful to solve Uniformly Increasing Chain first.
solution:
The expected value is determined by the current smallest value. For example, if the current smallest value is close to $1$, then there will be a lot of room to decrease. However, if the current minimum observed is already quite small, then there is not much room to decrease. Therefore, let $m(x)$ represent the expected minimum given that the current minimum of the chain is $x$. Since the expectation here is dependent on the next draw, the approach is to condition on the next value observed. Let this next value be $X \sim \unif{0}{1}$. Using the Law of Total Expectation, we obtain $$m(x) = \int_0^1 m(x \mid X = t)f_X(t)dt$$ The notation $m(x \mid X = t)$ represents the conditional expectation of the minimum of the chain given that the next draw was $t$ and the current minimum is $x$. Since $X$ is uniform on $(0,1)$, $f_X(t) = 1$. To evaluate the interior, we need to break this up based on the value of $t$. If $t \geq x$, then we are no longer in a decreasing chain, which implies that $m(x \mid X = t) = x$. Otherwise, if $t < x$, so the new minimum is $t$. This would imply that $m(x \mid X = t) = m(t)$, as this represents the expected minimum when the (new) current minimum is $t$. Plugging in, we obtain $$m(x) = \int_0^1 m(x \mid X = t)dt = \int_0^x m(t)dt + \int_x^1 xdt = \int_0^x m(t)dt + x(1-x)$$ To determine the function $m(x)$, the approach is to convert this integral equation into a differential equation by taking the derivative on both sides. This yields $$m'(x) = m(x) + (1-2x) \iff m'(x) - m(x) = 1-2x$$ The initial condition for this differential equation is $m(0) = 0$, as if the current observed minimum is $0$, it is not possible to go any lower. This is a linear first-order differential equation, so the method of integrating factors is most appropriate here. The integrating factor here is $\mu(t) = e^{\int (-1)dx} = e^{-x}$, as the function in front of $m(x)$ is $g(x) = -1$. Multiplying this through and rewriting with the product rule, we obtain $$m'(x)e^{-x} - m(x)e^{-x} = (1-2x)e^{-x} \iff \dfrac{d}{dx}(m(x)e^{-x}) = (1-2x)e^{-x}$$ Now, integrating on both sides, we obtain $$m(x)e^{-x} = \int (1-2x)e^{-x}dx = (2x+1)e^{-x} + C \iff m(x) = (2x+1)  + Ce^x$$ Plugging in the initial condition of $m(0) = 0$, we can solve for $C$. Namely, this is $0 = 1 + C \iff C = -1$. Therefore, our particular solution is $m(x) = 1+2x-e^x$. $m(1)$ is the solution to this question, as when we start, there is no minimum value yet, so to ensure that the first value we select is always the minimum, we must take $1$ as the minimum before any values have been selected, as this is the maximum possible value that any of the $\unif{0}{1}$ random variables can assume. Therefore, the answer is $m(1) = 3-e$.

$$$$

If you have completed "Uniformly Increasing Chain", you have seen the answer to that was $M(1) = e-2$. Note that $3-e + e-2 = 1$, and this is not a coincidence! Note that if $X \sim \unif{0}{1}, 1-X \sim \unif{0}{1}$ as well. Therefore, the random variables here, which look to measure the minimum of the chain $X_1,X_2,\dots$, could be replaced with $1-X_1,1-X_2,\dots$, which are still $\unif{0}{1}$. The minimum of the chain $X_1,X_2,\dots$ would be the maximum of the chain $1-X_1,1-X_2,\dots$, as we would be subtracting the least amount possible. Since $X_i + (1-X_i) = 1$ for all $i$, we can conclude that this will also hold for the index $N$ from this question, which implies that the expected value of the maximum of the chain from "Uniformly Increasing Chain" and the minimum of the chain from this question should sum to $1$, which indeed holds true.
hints: The expected value is determined by the current smallest value. For example, if the current smallest value is close to $1$, then there will be a lot of room to decrease. However, if the current minimum observed is already quite small, then there is not much room to decrease. Therefore, let $m(x)$ represent the expected minimum given that the current minimum of the chain is $x$. Since the expectation here is dependent on the next draw, condition on the next value observed.

title: Transpositions
statement: Let $P = (p_1,\dots, p_n)$ be a uniformly random permutation of $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$. We say $(i,j)$ is a $\textit{transposition}$ if $p_i = j$ and $p_j = i$ for $i < j$. For example, if $n = 4$, then in $(1,2,4,3)$, $(3,4)$ is a transposition, as the fourth element is $3$ and the third element is $4$. Find the expected number of transpositions in $P$ when $n = 10$.
solution:
We are looking to compute the expected number of non-independent events that occur, utilizing the linearity of expectation is the best approach since it applies whether or not the events are independent.

$$$$

There must be an indicator for each possible pair of values $(i,j)$ with $i < j$. However, whenever we select two distinct values $a \neq b$, there is exactly one way to arrange them into a pair $(i,j)$, as $i = \min(a,b)$ and $j = \max(a,b)$. Therefore, we just need to count the number of ways to select a pair of distinct values from $[n]$, which is $\binom{n}{2}$. Label the pairs $1$ to $\binom{n}{2}$ arbitrarily, and let $I_k$ be the indicator that pair $k$ is a transposition. 

$$$$

Then, $T = I_1 + \dots + I_{\binom{n}{2}}$ gives the total number of transpositions in the permutation. Since the labels of these pairs were arbitrarily assigned, the random variables $I_1,\dots, I_{\binom{n}{2}}$ are exchangeable, and hence identically distributed. Since they are identically distributed, they also have the same mean. By linearity of expectation, we have $$\ev{T} = \binom{n}{2}\ev{I_1}.$$

$$$$

 $\ev{I_1}$ is the probability that pair $1$ is a transposition. Since the labels are arbitrary, suppose that pair $1$ is $(1,2)$. $(1,2)$ is a transposition exactly when $2$ is in the first spot of the permutation and $1$ is in the second spot. In other words, the first two elements of the permutation are $2$ and $1$. The probability that the first element is $2$ is $1/n$, as there are $n$ equally likely options for the first element of the permutation. After $2$ has been fixed in the first element, there are $n-1$ elements left, so the probability that the second element is $1$ is $1/n-1$. 

$$$$

Therefore, the probability that $(1,2)$ is a transposition is $\ev{I_1} = \dfrac{1}{n(n-1)}$. Plugging this back in, $$\ev{T} = \dfrac{1}{n(n-1)} \cdot \binom{n}{2} = \dfrac{1}{n(n-1)} \cdot \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$ This result is independent of $n$, so the answer is $1/2$.
hints: We are looking to compute the expected number of non-independent events that occur, so linearity of expectation is the best approach. There must be an indicator for each possible pair of values $(i,j)$ with $i < j$.

title: Differencing I
statement: Suppose that $X_1,X_2,\dots$ is a sequence of random variables with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. The sequence also has an auto-correlation function $\rho(i,j)$ i.e. $\rho(i,j) = \corr{X_i}{X_j}$ Define the new sequence of random variables $Y_i = X_{i+1} - X_i$ for $i \geq 2$. Compute $\ev{Y_j - Y_i}$ for $i = 10, j = 15, \mu = 4, \sigma^2 = 9,$ and $\rho(i,j) = \dfrac{1}{1 + |i-j|}$.
solution: The first appropriate step would be to substitute in the definitions of $Y_i$ and $Y_j$ in terms of the sequence of $X_k$ random variables. Namely, this is $\ev{Y_j - Y_i} = \ev{X_{j+1} - X_j + X_{i+1} - X_i}$. By linearity of expectation, the above is the same as $\ev{X_{j+1}} - \ev{X_j} + \ev{X_{i+1}} -\ev{X_i}$. However, all of the above random variables have the same mean $\mu$, so the above evaluates to $\mu - \mu + \mu - \mu = 0$. This is independent of $i$ and $j$, so the answer is $0$.
hints: Note that the $X_i$ random variables all have the same mean. Apply linearity of expectation.

title: Vote Count I
statement: Alice and Bob are running for presidency of a school club. It is known that Alice has $a$ votes and Bob has $b$ votes, where $a > b$. The votes are counted one-by-one, and a running tally is recorded. Find the probability that Alice is always strictly ahead in the vote count when $a = 40$ and $b = 20$.
solution:
Utilize the reflection principle in this question. For Alice to be strictly ahead of Bob throughout the counting of the votes, they are never able to tie. If the first vote is for Bob, Alice and Bob must tie at some point, as Alice has more votes than Bob, so they must equalize at some point. For any sequence of drawing where the first vote is for Alice and it reaches a tie, reflect the votes up until the first point of equalization. This means that all votes for Alice are flipped to be for Bob, and vice versa. An important note is that the reflected sequence is still one with $a$ votes for Alice and $b$ votes for Bob, respectively, as they have an equal amount of votes up until the point of equalization. This reflected sequence becomes one where the first vote is for Bob, as the first vote in the original sequence was for Alice. This reflected sequence could be any sequence that starts with a vote for Bob, as you're flipping all of the votes around. What this proves is that there is a one-to-one correspondence between the sequences where a tie is reached with the first vote being for Alice and sequences where the first vote is for Bob. 

$$$$

The probability that Alice always leads the vote is just $1 - \prob{\text{Alice and Bob tie at some point}}$. Any sequence that ties starts with a vote for either Alice or Bob. However, by the above, the number of sequences where the first vote is Alice and there is a tie is equal to the number of sequences where there is a tie and the first vote is for Bob. Thus, $\prob{\text{Alice and Bob tie at some point}} = 2\prob{\text{Alice and Bob tie at some point and the first vote is for Bob}}$. However, all sequences where Bob is the first vote tie at some point, so $\prob{\text{Alice and Bob tie at some point and the first vote is for Bob}} = \prob{\text{First vote is for Bob}}$. Since $b$ of the $a+b$ total votes are for Bob, the probability that the first vote is for Bob is $\dfrac{b}{a+b}$. Plugging this in, we obtain that the probability Alice always leads is $1 - 2 \cdot \dfrac{b}{a+b} = \dfrac{a-b}{a+b}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{1}{3}$.
hints: Utilize the reflection principle in this question. For Alice to be strictly ahead of Bob throughout the counting of the votes, they are never able to tie. If the first vote is for Bob, Alice and Bob must tie at some point, as Alice has more votes than Bob, so they must equalize at some point. For any sequence of drawing where the first vote is for Alice and it reaches a tie, reflect the votes up until the point of equalization.

title: Vote Count II
statement:
Alice and Bob are running for presidency of a school club. It is known that Alice has $a$ votes and Bob has $b$ votes, where $a > b$. The votes are counted one-by-one, and a running tally is recorded. Find the probability that Alice is never behind in the vote count when $a = 40$ and $b = 20$.

$$$$

Note: Solve Vote Count I before attempting this question.
solution:
The situation of this question is very similar to that of the first part, so we should try to use the result of the first part of the question. The difference between a sequence where Alice always has strictly more votes than Bob versus can tie would be $1$ vote. In other words, any sequence where Alice is never behind Bob can be converted into a sequence where Alice is always strictly ahead of Bob by appending a vote for Alice at the beginning of the sequence. Similarly, we can also convert a sequence where Alice is always ahead of Bob with $a+1$ votes for Alice and $b$ for Bob into a sequence where Alice is never behind Bob with $a$ and $b$ votes for each person, respectively, by eliminating the first vote for Alice. Note that we know the first two votes of any such sequence where Alice is strictly ahead are for Alice, as there would be a tie if the first was for Alice and the second was for Bob. Thus, this action is valid. This implies that the number of sequences where Alice is never behind Bob with $a$ and $b$ votes for each, respectively, is equal to the number of sequences where Alice is always ahead of Bob when they respectively have $a+1$ and $b$ votes. Note that this does not imply that the probabilities are equal, as the number of sequences of votes that can be drawn when there are $a+1$ and $b$ votes for the candidates is not equal to when there are $a$ and $b$ votes. In other words, the sample spaces of the two experiments are not the same. 

$$$$

By "Vote Count I", the probability of the latter event is already known to be $\dfrac{a+1-b}{a+b+1}$. Thus, as all sequences are equally likely to occur, the number of sequences that satisfy the latter event is just equal to the probability multiplied by the number of sequences. The total number of votes that are drawn out in the latter experiment is $a+b+1$. Since it only matters which candidate the vote is for, we can pick the locations of the $b$ votes for Bob in $\binom{a+b+1}{b}$ ways, as the order of selection is irrelevant, and the other $a+1$ spots belong to Alice. Thus, there are $\binom{a+b+1}{b}$ sequences total in the sample space of the latter experiment, so the number of sequences that satisfy our event of interest is $$\dfrac{a-b+1}{a+b+1}\binom{a+b+1}{b} = \dfrac{a-b+1}{a+b+1} \cdot \dfrac{(a+b+1)!}{b!(a+1)!} = \dfrac{a-b+1}{a+1}\cdot \dfrac{(a+b)!}{a!b!} = \dfrac{a-b+1}{a+1}\binom{a+b}{a}$$ The above is also equal to the number of sequences where Alice is never behind in the count when there are $a$ and $b$ votes, respectively, as we already established the number of sequences that satisfy the two events are equal. There are $\binom{a+b}{a}$ ways to draw out the votes with no restrictions when there are $a$ and $b$ votes the candidates, as we fix the location of the $a$ votes for Alice, which means that the other $b$ votes for Bob go in the remaining $b$ spots in the drawing sequence. Since each sequence is equally likely, the probability of Alice never being behind Bob is the ratio of the above, which is just $\dfrac{a-b+1}{a+1}$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{21}{41}$.
hints: Try to use the result of "Vote Count I" with an extra vote for Alice appended somewhere.

title: Multiballs I
statement: You have two urns in front of you, say $1$ and $2$. Urn $1$ has $m$ red and $n$ blue marbles inside, while urn $2$ has $n$ red and $m$ blue marbles inside. Assume that $m,n \geq 1$. You select one urn uniformly at random and select $2$ marbles uniformly at random without replacement. In your selection, you observe $1$ red and $1$ blue marble. Find the probability that you drew from urn $1$ when $m = 7$ and $n = 4$.
solution:
We are given information here about what appears in the sequence of draws, so using the definition of conditional probability/Bayes' Theorem here is most relevant. Let $U_1$ and $U_2$ be the events that we select from urns $1$ and $2$, respectively. Similarly, let $S$ be the event that we obtain a selection of $1$ red and $1$ blue marble among $2$ marbles drawn without replacement. We are looking to compute $\prob{U_1 \mid S} = \dfrac{\prob{U_1 \cap S}}{\prob{S}}$. If we know which urn we selected, then it's quite easy to determine the probability of obtaining the selection above, as we know the counts of the marbles in the urn. Therefore, we should condition on the selected urn. Namely, $\prob{S \cap U_1} = \prob{S \mid U_1}\prob{U_1}$. $\prob{U_1} = 1/2$, as you select the urn uniformly at random to start. Then, given you selected urn $1$, you must select $1$ red and $1$ blue marble. Since the marbles are selected uniformly at random, we can compute the number of ways to obtain such a selection, and then divide by the number of ways to draw $2$ marbles unrestricted.

$$$$

As there are $m+n$ marbles in the urn and we select $2$, there are $\binom{m+n}{2}$ ways to do this without restriction. There are $n$ ways to pick the one blue marble and  $m$ ways to pick one red marble from urn $1$. Thus, $\prob{S \mid U_1} = \dfrac{mn}{\binom{m+n}{2}}$. 

$$$$

We compute $\prob{S}$ in a similar way. As per the above, we condition on the urn that is being drawn from to obtain $\prob{S} = \prob{S \mid U_1}\prob{U_1} + \prob{S \mid U_2}\prob{U_2}$. The first term is exactly the numerator. We also know that $\prob{U_2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, as each urn is equally likely to be selected from at first. Then, given that we selected from urn $2$, we must find the probability of obtaining the desired selection. There are $\binom{m+n}{2}$ ways to pick the marbles without restriction once again. In this case, the roles of $m$ and $n$ are reversed, as the other bag has $n$ red and $m$ blue marbles. Therefore, $\prob{S \mid U_2} = \dfrac{nm}{\binom{m+n}{2}}$. Plugging all of this in, we obtain $$\prob{U_1 \mid S} = \dfrac{\dfrac{mn}{\binom{m+n}{2}}}{\dfrac{mn}{\binom{m+n}{2}} + \dfrac{mn}{\binom{m+n}{2}}} = \dfrac{mn}{mn + mn} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$ This answer makes intuitive sense, as the information that is given is symmetric between the two urns. In other words, drawing one red and one blue marble gives no information at all regarding which urn was selected, as the information says that we draw one marble of each color, and the urns are also symmetric in their counts of each type of marble. This result is independent of $m$ and $n$, so the answer is $1/2$.
hints: You are given information here about what appears in the sequence of draws, so using the definition of conditional probability here is most relevant. Let $U_1$ and $U_2$ be the events that we select from urns $1$ and $2$, respectively. Similarly, let $S$ be the event that we obtain a selection of $1$ red and $1$ blue marble among $2$ marbles drawn without replacement. We are looking to compute $\prob{U_1 \mid S}$.

title: Same Sequence I
statement: Alice and Bob both flip fair coins $n$ times. Find the probability that Alice and Bob obtain the same sequence when $n = 6$.
solution: As the coin is fair, all sequences are equally likely, so we can fix Alice's sequence arbitrarily. Of all of the sequences that Bob can flip, exactly $1$ of them is the one Alice has. There are $2^n$ equally likely sequences of flips that Bob can obtain, as each of the $n$ flips has the option to be either heads or tails. Therefore, the probability that Alice and Bob flip the same sequence is $\frac{1}{2^n} = 2^{-n}$. With $n = 6$, the answer is $\frac{1}{64}$.
hints: As the coin is fair, all sequences are equally likely, so we can fix Alice's sequence arbitrarily. How many of the sequences that Bob can flip are the one that Alice has.

title: Same Sequence III
statement: Alice and Bob flip coins with respective probabilities $0 < p < 1$ and $0 < q < 1$ of heads $n$ times each. Find the probability that Alice and Bob obtain the same sequence when $n = 4, p = 1/3,$ and $q = 1/4$.
solution: We can't employ the same approach as "Same Sequence I" because of the fact that the sequences are not equally likely now. To reduce the problem, consider the case of $n = 1$. In $1$ flip, Alice and Bob flip the same sequence if they either both obtain a head or both obtain a tail. Since their flips are independent, the probability they both obtain a head is $pq$, while the probability that they both obtain a tail is $(1-p)(1-q)$. As these two cases are disjoint, the probability that the both obtain the same sequence in $1$ flip is $pq + (1-p)(1-q)$. However, we can note that for Alice and Bob to obtain the same sequence of $n$ flips, each of the individual $n$ flips must be the same. Each flip is independent, so the probability of all $n$ flips being the same is just the same as the product of the probabilities each individual flip is the same. However, each individual flip is the same with probability $pq + (1-p)(1-q)$ by the above. Therefore, the probability that all $n$ flips are the same i.e. they have the same sequence is $(pq + (1-p)(1-q))^n$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{2401}{20736}$.
hints: Use an approach similar to "Same Sequence II" with a slight modification.

title: All Values Represented
statement: How many distinct $6-$sided dice with values in the set $[6] = \{1,2,\dots, 6\}$ are there such that the following property holds: When this die is rolled twice, there is positive probability that the sum of the upfaces is $k$ for each $2 \leq k \leq 12$. Two dice are considered indistinguishable if the number of faces that show value $i$ for $1 \leq i \leq 6$ is the same for all $i$ between the two dice, regardless of orientation. Assume that each of the $6$ sides appear with equal probability.
solution:
We must ensure that all values $2 \leq k \leq 12$ have positive probability of appearing. The easiest values to determine on the die to consider first are the extreme values, as they are the ones that have the fewest possible ways to obtain them. Namely, $2$ and $12$ must have positive probability of appearing, which is only possible through $2 = 1 + 1$ and $12 = 6  + 6$, meaning $1$ and $6$ must be on the die. Similarly, let's look at the next most extreme values of $3$ and $11$. As $3 = 1 + 2$ and $11 = 6 + 5$, these are only possible to obtain with positive probability when $2$ and $5$ are also on the die. Now, let's see which sums are possible to obtain with the values $1,2,5,$ and $6$ thus far, and we can figure out what to add from there.

$$$$

The possible sums with two dice with these $4$ values thus far are $$2 (1+1),3 (2+1),4 (2+2),6 (5+1),7 (5+2),8 (6+2),10 (5+5),11 (5+6), 12 (6+6)$$ Only $5$ an $9$ are not possible to obtain yet. We could obtain $9 = 6+3 = 5+4$, so either $3$ or $4$ must be on the die as well. Once either $3$ or $4$ is on the die, there are no restrictions what the last value is, as all of the possible sums are now represented. Therefore, we need to count the number of combinations where at least one of $3$ or $4$ is among the last two values. There are $2$ options for which of $3$ or $4$ goes on the die, and once that is settled, there are $6$ options for the last value on the die, as any value can be placed on it. This yields $2 \cdot 6 = 12$ ways to pick the final $2$ values of the dice. However, note that the option of putting $3$ and $4$ is counted twice in the above. It is counted in the case where we fix $3$ on the die and $4$ is the choice for the unrestricted spot, as well as when we fix $4$ and $3$ is in the unrestricted spot. Therefore, this outcome is double-counted, meaning that we must subtract $1$ to remove the double-counting of this outcome. This implies there are $12-1 = 11$ distinct dice that satisfy this condition.
hints: Sums of $2$ and $12$ must be possible, so how can those be obtained from two dice?
Ask the same question about $3$ and $11$, as those are also extreme values. What potential values are left?

title: Quadratic Solutions
statement: Suppose that $B,C\sim \unif{0}{1}$ IID. Compute the probability that $x^2 + 2\sqrt{B}x + C = 0$ has two real solutions.
solution:
When looking for the occurrence of real solutions in a quadratic equation, the first idea that should come to mind is the discriminant. In other words, if $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ is our quadratic equation, the roots are given by $\dfrac{-b\pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$, and the discriminant is the $\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}$ term. For there to be two real roots, the square root term must be positive, so $b^2 - 4ac > 0$. In this case, the coefficients are random: $a = 1, b = 2\sqrt{B},$ and $c = C$. The condition for the discriminant being larger than $0$ is given by $$(2\sqrt{B})^2 - 4(1)(C) > 0 \iff 4B - 4C > 0 \iff B > C$$
Therefore, the event that there are two real roots is exactly the event $\{B > C\}$. Thus, we must find $\prob{B > C}$. Since $B$ and $C$ are IID with some continuous distribution, the answer is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
hints: Consider the discriminant of the quadratic equation. What must be true about it for there to be $2$ real solutions.

title: Bertrand's Paradox I
statement: A random chord is formed by selecting two uniformly random points, say $X_1$ and $X_2$, on the circumference of the unit circle and connecting a line segment between them. Find the probability that the length of this chord is at least $\sqrt{3}$.
solution:
The key here is that we select $X_1$ and $X_2$ uniformly at random. Note that we can fix $X_1$ arbitrarily at $(1,0)$, as no matter where $X_1$ ends up, we can just rotate the circle about it's center until $X_1$ lands at $(1,0)$. This doesn't affect the length of the chord, so this is a legal movement. Therefore, fix $X_1$ at $(1,0)$, which removes a degree of randomness. Now, the angle $\theta$ between $X_2$ and $(1,0)$ is $\unif{0}{\pi}$. This is because of the fact that being $\theta$ radians away from $(1,0)$ means it can be $\theta$ radians CW or CCW, so there are two locations with equal density for $X_2$ to be such that it is $\theta$ radians away. The maximum distance away is $\theta = \pi$, as this is being located at $(-1,0)$. 

$$$$

We now need to find the distance of $X_2$ from $(1,0)$ if the angle between them is $\theta$. The coordinates of $X_2$ could be $(\cos\theta,\pm \sin\theta)$, as the angular difference can be above or below the $x-$axis. However, both of these are equidistant from $(1,0)$. In particular, the distance would be $$L = \sqrt{(\sin\theta-0)^2 + (1 - \cos\theta)^2} = \sqrt{\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta + 1 - 2\cos\theta} = \sqrt{2(1-\cos\theta)}$$ We are looking to compute $\prob{L \geq \sqrt{3}}$. As we know $L = \sqrt{2(1-\cos\theta)}$ and $\theta \sim \unif{0}{\pi}$, the best first step is to express this event in terms of $\theta$. Namely, we get $$\prob{L \geq \sqrt{3}} = \prob{\sqrt{2(1-\cos\theta)} \geq \sqrt{3}} = \prob{2(1-\cos\theta) \geq 3} = \prob{\cos\theta \leq -1/2} = \prob{\theta \geq 2\pi/3}$$ The last equality comes from the fact that the region in the support of $\theta$ such that $\cos\theta \leq -1/2$ is when $2\pi/3 \leq \theta \leq \pi$. As $\theta \sim \unif{0}{\pi}$, we can take ratios of lengths to compute probabilities. The total length of the support is $\pi$, while the region of our event of interest is of length $\pi/3$, so the answer is $\dfrac{1}{3}$.
hints: Since the two points are selected independently and uniformly at random from the circumference of the unit circle, all arrangements have the same joint density. Therefore, we can always rotate the circle such that one of the points is fixed at $(1,0)$ without changing the problem, as rotating the circle does not change the length of chord between the selected points.
The length of the chord is dependent on the angle $\theta$ that lies between them.

title: Best So Far!
statement: Suppose that $X_1,X_2,\dots, X_n$ are IID continuous random variables and $1 \leq k \leq n$. Define $M_r = \max\{X_1,\dots, X_r\}$. Find $\prob{X_k = M_n \mid X_k = M_k}$ when $k = 10$ and $n = 25$. In other words, given that $X_k$ is the largest random variable among the first $k$, find the probability it is the largest among all of the random variables.
solution: Since this is a conditional probability, the best thing to do is first use the definition of conditional probability, and then simplify from there. Namely, we have that $$\prob{X_k = M_n \mid X_k = M_k} = \dfrac{\prob{X_k = M_n, X_k = M_k}}{\prob{X_k = M_n}}$$ Note that if $X_k = M_n$, then $X_k$ is the maximum of all of the $n$ random variables. Therefore, it would also be the maximum of the first $k$, so the event $\{X_k = M_n\} \subseteq \{X_k = M_k\}$, meaning $\prob{X_k = M_n, X_k = M_k} = \prob{X_k = M_n}$. However, as $X_1,\dots, X_n$ are IID and continuous, all random variables are equally likely to be in any relative order with respect to the other random variables, so $\prob{X_k = M_n} = 1/n$, as this is one of $n$ equally likely spots for $X_k$ to be among all $n$ random variables. By the same logic $\prob{X_k = M_k} = 1/k$, as it is one of $k$ equally likely spots for $X_k$ be among the first $k$ random variables. Thus, $$\prob{X_k = M_n \mid X_k = M_k} = \dfrac{1/n}{1/k} = \dfrac{k}{n}$$ This result makes intuitive sense. The additional information obtained by moving from $k$ to $k+1$ is constant over time i.e. no spot gives "more information" than any other spot. This is because the difference is $1/n$ for each additional increase in $k$. Furthermore, when $k = n$, the answer is $1$, as we would expect. With the specified values, the answer is $2/5$.
hints: Since this is a conditional probability, the best thing to do is first use the definition of conditional probability, and then simplify from there.
Since these random variables are IID and continuous, all permutations of their orders are equally likely.

title: Subby Choice I
statement: A uniformly random subset $S$ of $[n] = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$ is selected. Find the expected sum of the elements in $S$ when $n = 15$.
solution:
Since the subset is selected uniformly at random, each element is equally likely to be in or not be in the subset. If it is in the subset, then we count it in the sum, whereas if it is not in the subset, we ignore it. This methodology seems reminiscent of indicators. Therefore, let $I_i = i$ if $i \in S$ and $0$ if not. In other words, this indicator counts for us a sum of $i$ if the element is in the subset and $0$ if not. We can write $T = I_1 + \dots + I_n$ as the sum of all elements in $S$, as each indicator adds $i$ if $i \in S$. By linearity of expectation, we have that $\ev{T} = \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n \ev{I_i}$. Since each element is equally likely to be inside or outside $S$, $\prob{I_i = i} = \prob{I_i = 0} = 1/2$. Therefore, $\ev{I_i} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot i + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0 = \dfrac{i}{2}$. Plugging this in, we get that $$\ev{T} = \sum_{i=1}^n \dfrac{i}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{4}$$ With $n = 15$, the answer is $60$.

One can also see the above answer by noting that the average size of a subset would be $n/2$, as, on average, half of the elements are in $S$ and half are not in $S$, and the average value of the elements of $[n]$ is $\frac{n+1}{2}$, so multiplying these together yields the answer above.
hints: Since the subset is selected uniformly at random, each element is equally likely to be in or not be in the subset. If it is in the subset, then we count it in the sum, whereas if it is not in the subset, we ignore it. This methodology seems reminiscent of indicators.

title: Include The Element!
statement: A uniformly random subset $S$ of $[n] = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$, with $1 \leq k \leq n$, is selected. Find the probability that $1 \in S$ when $n = 10$ and $k = 8$.
solution:
Since the subset is selected uniformly at random from all subsets of size $k$, we can compute the probability by taking the ratio of the number of subsets of size $k$ that satisfy the condition to the total number of subsets of size $k$. As we are selecting $k$ elements from $n$ in such a subset without replacement and order irrelevant, there are $\binom{n}{k}$ ways to do this. Now, to have $1$ inside our subset, fix $1$ as one of the elements. Now, there are $k-1$ more elements that must be selected from the remaining $n-1$ elements, which can be done in $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ ways. Therefore, the probability that $1 \in S$ is $$\dfrac{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}{\binom{n}{k}} = \dfrac{\frac{(n-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!}}{\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}} = \dfrac{k}{n}$$ This result makes a lot of intuitive sense. With $k = 0$, there is no subset being selected, so there is $0$ probability of $1$ being in the subset. With $k = n$, the entire set $[n]$ is being selected, so there is probability $1$ of $1$ being in the subset. Lastly, we see that each additional element that is included in the subset increases the probability by a constant amount of $1/n$ per increase in $k$ by $1$. This makes sense, as there is no reason to believe that one increase in $k$ should provide more/less incremental probability of $1$ being in the subset than any other increase in $k$.

One can also prove this via indicators. This is because the expectation of an indicator is the probability of the event that it indicates. Let $I_i$ be the indicator that $i \in S$. We know that $I_1 + \dots + I_n = k$, as there are $k$ total elements in $S$, so exactly $k$ of the indicators must take the value $1$. However, as the subset is selected uniformly at random, no element is more or less likely to be in $S$ than any other element, so $I_1,\dots, I_n$ are all identically distributed, and therefore have the same mean. This means $\ev{I_1 + \dots + I_n} = n\ev{I_1} = k$. However, $\ev{I_1}$ is the probability that $1 \in S$, just as desired. Therefore, we can conclude that the probability at hand is $k/n$ by dividing $n$ on both sides.
hints: Since the subset is selected uniformly at random from all subsets of size $k$, we can compute the probability by taking the ratio of the number of subsets of size $k$ that satisfy the condition to the total number of subsets of size $k$. How many total subsets of size $k$ are there? How many of those include $1$?

title: Different Intersection I
statement: Fix $0 \leq a,b \leq n$. Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of $[n]$ that are independently and uniformly at random selected from the collection of subsets of sizes $a$ and $b$, respectively. Find $\ev{|A\cap B|}$ when $a = 6, b = 8,$ and $n = 12$.
solution:
There is no clear way to proceed in this problem by deriving the PMF of $|A \cap B|$, so an alternative must be better. Note that the number of elements in $|A\cap B|$ is just the sum of indicators that represent whether or not each element $1 \leq i \leq n$ is in $A \cap B$. Therefore, the best approach is to use linearity of expectation on indicators. 

$$$$

In particular, let $I_i$ be the indicator that element $1 \leq i \leq n$ is in $A \cap B$. We set up the indicators this way so that we can count the expected number of elements in $A \cap B$. Therefore, we have that $|A\cap B| = I_1 + \dots + I_n$ gives the total number of elements in $A\cap B$. As the two subsets are selected uniformly at random from the subsets of those respective sizes, each element has the same probability of being included in $A$, and likewise with $B$. Therefore, the indicators are all exchangeable, and hence have the same mean. By linearity of expectation, we have $$\ev{|A \cap B|} = n\ev{I_1}$$ $\ev{I_1}$ is the probability that $1$ is in $A \cap B$. Since $A$ are $B$ are selected independently, we have that $\prob{1 \in A \cap B} = \prob{1 \in A}\prob{1 \in B}$. By the result of "Include The Element!", as $|A| = a$ and $|B| = b$, $\prob{1 \in A} = \dfrac{a}{n}$ and $\prob{1 \in B} = \dfrac{b}{n}$. Plugging these in, we get $$\ev{|A\cap B|} = n \cdot \dfrac{a}{n} \cdot \dfrac{b}{n} = \dfrac{ab}{n}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $4$.
hints: There is no clear way to proceed in this problem by deriving the PMF of $|A \cap B|$, so an alternative must be better. Note that the number of elements in $|A\cap B|$ is just the sum of indicators that represent whether or not each element $1 \leq i \leq n$ is in $A \cap B$. Therefore, use linearity of expectation on appropriately selected indicators.

title: Modular Pairs
statement: What is the minimum number of pairs of integers $(a,b)$ that are needed to guarantee that there exist two pairs $(a_1,b_1)$ and $(a_2,b_2)$ such that $a_1 \hspace{3pt} \text{mod} \hspace{3pt} n = a_2 \hspace{3pt} \text{mod} \hspace{3pt} n$ and $b_1 \hspace{3pt} \text{mod} \hspace{3pt} n = b_2 \hspace{3pt} \text{mod} \hspace{3pt} n$, where $n \geq 2$ is an integer? Solve this when $n = 7$.
solution: Note that there are $n$ options for the equivalence class that $a_1$ and $a_2$ both belong to. Similarly, there are $n$ options for the equivalence class that both $b_1$ and $b_2$ belong to. Therefore, by the multiplication principle, there are $n^2$ total ways to pick the pair of equivalence classes that the $a_i$s and the $b_i$s belong to. By the Pigeonhole Principle, if there are at least $n^2 + 1$ pairs, there must exist two pairs that satisfy the above, as there are only $n^2$ pigeonholes (pairs of equivalence classes). With less than $n^2 + 1$ pairs, it is possible that no two belong to the same pigeonhole, so $n^2 + 1$ is the absolute minimum. With the specified value here, the answer is $50$.
hints: How many choices are there for the equivalence class of the $a_i$? Similar for the $b_i$?

title: Conditional Values
statement: Suppose that $X$ is a discrete random variable with positive integer support. Fix a subset $B \subseteq \Z^+$. For any $i \in Z^+ \setminus B$, compute $\prob{X = i \mid X \notin B}$ when $X \sim \geom{1/2}, B = \{1,2,\dots, 10\}$, and $i = 12$.
solution:
Since we are looking to compute a conditional probability here, it's best to first apply the definition of conditional probability! Applying the definition and reducing yields $$\prob{X = i \mid X 
otin B} = \dfrac{\prob{X = i, X
