title: Tuple Birthdays
statement: There are $n$ people in a probability class. Each person is equally likely to be born on any day of the $365$ days in a year. Compute the expected number of groups of $2 \leq k \leq n$ people that have the same birthday when $n = 25$ and $k = 4$. Round to the nearest hundred-thousandth.
solution:
In this problem, we are looking to compute the expected number of $k-$subsets of people that have the same birthdays. Therefore, we should set up indicators that indicate whether each $k-$subset of people have the same birthday or not. There are $\binom{n}{k}$ such subsets of $k$ people. Label the $k-$subsets $1$ to $\binom{n}{k}$ arbitrarily, and let $I_{i}$ be the indicator of the event that $k-$subset $i$ all shares the same birthday. By the above discussion, $\displaystyle T = I_1 + \dots + I_{\binom{n}{k}}$ gives the total number of $k-$subsets of people sharing a birthday. Since the labels for the $k-$subsets are arbitrary, the random variables are all exchangeable, meaning they all have the same mean. By linearity of expectation, $$\ev{T} = \binom{n}{k}\ev{I_{1}}$$ 

$$$$

Now, $\ev{I_{1}}$ is just the probability that the people in the $k-$subset labeled $1$ all have the same birthday. Since the labels are arbitrary, suppose the people in this group are labelled $1$ to $k$. Since all days are equally likely, fix the birthday of person $1$ arbitrarily. There is a $1/365$ chance that each of the other $k-1$ people have the same birthday as person $1$, as there is $1$ day of the year that matches the birthday of person $1$. Since each person is independent, the probability all $k$ people share the same birthday is $\ev{I_1} = 365^{-(k-1)}$. Plugging this in above, $$\ev{T} = \dfrac{1}{365^{k-1}}\binom{n}{k}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 0.00026$.
hints: Define an indicator random variable that is equal to 1 if all of the people in a particular subset all have the same birthday. Then, use the linearity of expectation.

title: Ice Cream Orders
statement: An ice cream store sells cups and cones. A cup can hold small, medium, and large scoops, while a cone can only hold small and medium scoops. There are $8$ cup toppings and $12$ cone toppings. How many one-topping ice cream orders are there?
solution:
The size of the ice cream order allowed is dependent on whether a cone or cup is selected. Therefore, it's best to break up this problem into two cases: Cone and cup. These cases are disjoint (you can't have both a cone and cup) and exhaustive (every ice cream order uses either a cone or cup). 

$$$$

For the cup case, there are $3$ size options and $8$ toppings, meaning there are $3 \cdot 8 = 24$ ice cream options with a cup. For a cone, there are only $2$ sizes and $12$ toppings, so there are $2 \cdot 12 = 24$ ice cream options with a cone. Adding these together, we have $48$ total orders.
hints: The size of the ice cream order allowed is dependent on whether a cone or cup is selected. Therefore, it's best to break up this problem into two cases: Cone and cup.

title: NASCAR Results
statement: $100$ cars in NASCAR are racing. Each car is designated a distinct number $0-99$. Find the number of outcomes that have all $10$ cars of single-digit label finishing together (For example, cars $0-9$ finish in the top 10 or in places $52-61$). The answer is in the form $a!b!$ for some integers $a$ and $b$. Report $ab$.
solution:
To count the number of outcomes satisfying this, we must first select the $10$ spots for which all $10$ of the single-digit cars will reside in. Note that the spot of the first single-digit car locks in the spots for the other $9$ single-digit label cars. They can start as early as the first spot or as late as the $91$st spot, as that would be the last $10$ spots. Thus, there are $91$ ways to pick the $10$ spots of the single-digit cars. Then, once those spots are selected, there are $10!$ ways to arrange the $10$ single-digit label cars on those $10$ spots. Lastly, there are $90!$ ways to arrange the other $90$ cars on the remaining $90$ spots. Thus, by the multiplication principle, there are $91 \cdot 10! \cdot 90! = 10!91!$ outcomes that satisfy this condition. 

Alternatively, we could treat the $10$ single-digit cars as a "block", as they must finish together. The other $90$ cars still exist and are distinct. Thus, we have $91$ items we must order: the block and the other $90$ cars. There are $91!$ ways to arrange all of these items. Then, inside the block, the $10$ cars can finish in $10!$ different ways, as we are permuting the $10$ cars inside the block to the $10$ spots inside of it, so the number of satisfactory outcomes is $10!91!$.
hints: To count the number of outcomes satisfying this, first select the $10$ spots for which all $10$ of the single-digit cars will reside in. Note that the spot of the first single-digit car locks in the spots for the other $9$ single-digit label cars.

title: Modified Full House I
statement: How many $5-$card hands from a standard $52-$card deck consist of $2$ cards of one suit and $3$ cards of another suit?
solution:
The first thing we need to ask ourselves is: Does the ordering of suits matter? The answer is yes because we are selecting only $2$ of one, but $3$ of the other, so if we swap the two suits around, we do indeed get a different full house. Thus, we first have to permute $k=2$ suits from $n=4$ total suits in the deck, as which suit receives $3$ cards vs. $2$ cards matters. There are $P(4,2)$ ways to do this. 

$$$$

For the suit that has $3$ replicates in the hand, the order of the cards selected is irrelevant, so we want a subset of size $k = 3$ from a set of $n = 13$ cards of that suit, which can be selected in $\binom{13}{3}$ ways. Then, for the suit with $2$ replicates, by the same logic, there are $\binom{13}{2}$ ways to pick $2$ cards from the other suit. By the multiplication principle, the answer is $$\displaystyle P(4,2)\cdot \binom{13}{3} \cdot \binom{13}{2} = 267696$$
hints: The first thing we need to ask ourselves is: Does the ordering of suits matter?
The answer is yes because we are selecting only $2$ of one, but $3$ of the other, so if we swap the two suits around, we do indeed get a different full house.

title: Special Term
statement: Determine the coefficient of $x^{25}y^{50}$ when expanding $(2x-y)^{75}$. The answer can be written in the form $a \cdot 10^b$ in scientific notation. Report the answer of $a + b$, rounded to the nearest hundredth.
solution: We can write $(2x-y)^{75} = (2x+ (-y))^{75}$, so by applying the binomial theorem with $2x, -y,$ and $75$, we obtain $$(2x-y)^{75} = \sum_{k=0}^{75} \binom{75}{k}(2x)^k(-y)^{75 - k} = \sum_{k=0}^{75}\binom{75}{k}2^k(-1)^{75-k} x^ky^{75-k}$$ We get $x^{25}y^{50} = x^{25}y^{75-25}$ when $k = 25$. Plugging in $k =25$, we get the term $$\binom{75}{25}(2x)^{25}(-y)^{50} = 2^{25}\binom{75}{25}x^{25}y^{50}$$ Therefore, $\displaystyle 2^{25}\binom{75}{25} \approx 1.76 \cdot 10^{27}$ is the coefficient. The answer is $28.76$.
hints: We can write $(2x-y)^{75} = (2x+ (-y))^{75}$. Apply the binomial theorem.

title: Binomial Coefficient Difference
statement: Find an expression, potentially dependent on $n$, for $\displaystyle \sum_{0 \leq k \leq n, \hspace{2pt} k \hspace{2pt} \text{even}} \binom{n}{k} - \sum_{0 \leq k \leq n,\hspace{2pt} k \hspace{2pt} \text{odd}} \binom{n}{k}$. Evaluate this when $n = 20$.
solution: In this, we see a sum and difference of binomial coefficients, so we should instantly think to use the binomial theorem. We can condense the two sums into one because all that changes is the sign for even vs. odd. Doing this, $$\sum_{0 \leq k \leq n, \hspace{2pt} k \hspace{2pt} \text{even}} \binom{n}{k} - \sum_{0 \leq k \leq n,\hspace{2pt} k \hspace{2pt} \text{odd}} \binom{n}{k} = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}(-1)^k = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}(-1)^k1^{n-k} = (-1 + 1)^n = 0$$ We are able to condense the two sums into one by noting that all the terms with even $k$ are positive, while those with odd $k$ are negative. Lastly, we applied the binomial theorem with $x = -1$ and $y = 1$. Since this holds for all $n$, the answer is $0$.
hints: Can you somehow condense this difference into one sum?

title: Diego's Exam
statement: Diego is randomly answering questions on a multiple choice test with $10$ questions. Each question has $4$ answer choices, of which $1$ is correct. He selects uniformly at random for each question. Find the probability that Diego gets at least $2$ questions correct on this exam. Round to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
Since this an "at least" probability involving separate questions (his answers to previous questions don't influence his answers to future questions), the complementary rule is best to apply. 

$$$$

Let $A$ be the event that Diego correctly answers at least $2$ questions. $A^c$ is the event that he answers either $0$ or $1$ question correctly, as these outcomes ensure Diego did not answer at least $2$ questions correctly. Since we are looking at the number of correct answers in Diego's exam and we know each sequence of answers to the $10$ questions are equally likely, we should set up the sample space as all possible sequences of $10$ answers that Diego can submit. 

$$$$

Each answer has $4$ options, so there are $4^{10}$ possible ways to answer the exam. The events of obtaining exactly $0$ correct answers and exactly $1$ correct answer are disjoint events. Therefore, if we let $C_0$ and $C_1$ be the events that Diego gets $0$ and $1$ questions correct, respectively, $A^c = C_0 \cup C_1$. By finite disjoint additivity, $$\mathbb{P}[A^c] = \mathbb{P}[C_0] + \mathbb{P}[C_1]$$ $\mathbb{P}[C_0]$ is the probability he selects a wrong answer for all $10$ questions. There are $3$ wrong answers per question of the $4$ questions, so there are $|C_0| = 3^{10}$ ways he can answer every question wrong. Therefore, $\mathbb{P}[C_0] = 3^{10}/4^{10}$. $\mathbb{P}[C_1]$ is the probability that Diego gets exactly $1$ question right. There are $10$ ways to pick the answer he gets correct. For that question, there is only one right answer. For the other $9$ questions, there are $3$ ways to pick a wrong answer. By the multiplication rule, there are $|C_1| = 10 \cdot 1 \cdot 3^9 = 10 \cdot 3^9$ ways to get one answer correct. Therefore, $\mathbb{P}[C_1] = 10 \cdot 3^9 / 4^{10}$. Substituting back in, we have that $$\mathbb{P}[A^c] = \dfrac{3^{10} + 10 \cdot 3^9}{4^{10}} \iff \prob{A} = 1 - \prob{A^c} = 1 - \dfrac{3^{10} + 10 \cdot 3^9}{4^{10}}$$
hints: Since this an "at least" probability involving separate questions (his answers to previous questions don't influence his answers to future questions), the complementary rule is best to apply.

title: The Fixed One I
statement: Fix $n \geq 2$. A uniformly random permutation $f: [n] \rightarrow [n]$ is being formed, where $[n] = \{1,2,\dots,n\}$. We say that $1 \leq i \leq n$ is fixed if $f(i) = i$. When $n = 10$, find the probability that $1$ is fixed, but $2$ is not fixed.
solution:
Let's first convert this statement into the language of events. For each $1 \leq i \leq n$, let $F_i$ be the event that $i$ is a fixed point. We are looking to compute $\prob{F_1 \cap F_2^c}$, as we want $1$ fixed and $2$ not fixed. To compute a probability of this form, we can use the corollary of the differencing property above. We can write $$\prob{F_1 \cap F_2^c} + \prob{F_1 \cap F_2} = \prob{F_1} \iff \prob{F_1 \cap F_2^c} = \prob{F_1} - \prob{F_1 \cap F_2}$$ More simply, we consider all outcomes where $1$ is fixed, and then remove the outcomes where $2$ is also fixed. In this question, we know all permutations are equally likely, so we should consider the sample space to be all permutations of $[n]$. There are $n!$ total permutations without restrictions, as $[n]$ has size $n$. Now, we must compute $|F_1|$ and $|F_1 \cap F_2|$. For $|F_1|$, we first fix $1$, and then we permute the other $n-1$ elements in any order, as there are no other restrictions. Thus, there are $|F_1| = (n-1)!$ permutations for this case. For $|F_1 \cap F_2|$, we fix $1$ and $2$, and there we permute the other $n-2$ elements in any order. Thus, there are $|F_1 \cap F_2| = (n-2)!$ permutations for this case. By the equally likely model, $\prob{F_1} = \frac{(n-1)!}{n!} = \frac{1}{n}$ and $\prob{F_1 \cap F_2} = \frac{(n-2)!}{n!} = \frac{1}{n(n-1)}$. Substituting these into the differencing formula, $$\prob{F_1 \cap F_2^c} = \dfrac{1}{n} - \dfrac{1}{n(n-1)} = \frac{n-2}{n(n-1)}$$ With $n = 10$, the answer is $4/45$.

We can alternatively just directly compute this via combinatorics. There are $n(n-1)$ ways to assign $1$ and $2$ to $f(1)$ and $f(2)$, as they can't map to the same value. If $1$ is fixed, $f(1) = 1$ is the only option. If $2$ is not fixed, $f(2)$ can be any value besides $1$ and $2$. Thus, there are $n-2$ options for where $2$ maps to, meaning that the probability of the event is $$\dfrac{n-2}{n(n-1)}$$ With $n = 10$, the answer is $4/45$.
hints: For each $1 \leq i \leq n$, let $F_i$ be the event that $i$ is a fixed point. We are looking to compute $\prob{F_1 \cap F_2^c}$, as we want $1$ fixed and $2$ not fixed.

title: Powerball Winner I
statement: A lottery consists of $6$ values. The first $5$ values are distinct integers $1-69$, inclusive. The last value is the Powerball number, which is a value $1-26$, inclusive. The Powerball number can match one of the other $5$ values. One wins the lottery by matching all $6$ values. The order of the first $5$ values is irrelevant. All tickets are equally likely to be generated and can be generated multiple times. Find the probability that a ticket is one that wins the lottery. If $p$ is the probability, report the answer of $p \cdot 10^9$, rounded to the nearest thousandth.
solution: Since all outcomes are equally likely, the best approach to computing the probability is via counting. There are $26$ ways to pick the Powerball number. Additionally, there are $\binom{69}{5}$ ways to pick the other $5$ values, since the order of the other $5$ values are irrelevant. By the multiplication principle, there are $26 \cdot \binom{69}{5}$ Powerball tickets. Only one combination is winning, so the probability of winning is $$p = \dfrac{1}{26\binom{69}{5}} \approx 3.422 \cdot 10^{-9}$$ The answer to this question is $3.422$.
hints: Since all outcomes are equally likely, the best approach to computing the probability is via counting.

title: Powerball Winner II
statement: A lottery consists of $6$ values. The first $5$ values are distinct integers $1-69$, inclusive. The last value is the Powerball number, which is a value $1-26$, inclusive. The Powerball number can match one of the other $5$ values. One wins the lottery by matching all $6$ values. The order of the first $5$ values is irrelevant. All tickets are equally likely to be generated and can be generated multiple times. Suppose that you purchase $2$ lottery tickets once a week for the next $60$ years of your life. This means you purchase approximately $6240$ tickets. Find the probability you win the lottery at least once in the next $60$ years. If $q$ is the probability, report the answer of $q \cdot 10^5$, rounded to the nearest thousandth.
solution: Label the tickets $1-6240$, and let $T_i$ be the event that ticket $i$ is a winning ticket. Then we want $\mathbb{P}[T_1 \cup T_2 \dots \cup T_{6240}]$, the probability that at least one is a winning ticket. Since each ticket is generated randomly, we can assume each of these events are independent, so $$\prob{\bigcup_{i=1}^{6240} T_i} = 1 - \prob{\bigcap_{i=1}^{6240} T_i^c}$$ By the independence of the $T_i$ events, their complements must also be independent. Therefore, the above is $\prob{\bigcup_{i=1}^{6240} T_i} = 1 - \mathbb{P}[T_1^c]\dots \mathbb{P}[T_{6240}^c] = 1 - (1 - \mathbb{P}[T_1])\dots (1 - \mathbb{P}[T_{6240}])$. Since each of the tickets is randomly generated, they all have the same probability of being a winning ticket, which we found in "Powerball Winner I" to be about $3.422 \cdot 10^{-9}$. Thus, this probability is $$\prob{\bigcup_{i=1}^{6240} T_i} = 1 - (1 - 3.422 \cdot 10^{-9})^{6240} \approx 2.135 \cdot 10^{-5}$$ The answer to this question is $2.135$.
hints: Label the tickets $1-6240$, and let $T_i$ be the event that ticket $i$ is a winning ticket. Then we want $\mathbb{P}[T_1 \cup T_2 \dots \cup T_{6240}]$, the probability that at least one is a winning ticket.

title: Disease Prevalence I
statement: The prevalence of a disease within a population is $1\%$. A test for the disease is created. If the person has the disease, there is a $99\%$ chance they test positive. If they don't have the disease, there is still a false positive rate of $3\%$. Find the probability a person actually has the disease if they test positive.
solution:
In this question, we have two groups of people. Namely, they are infected and healthy individuals. Thus, one can have the disease by either obtaining a positive or negative test. This observation yields the natural choice of conditioning on whether the test is positive or negative.

\nl

Let $D$ denote an individual with the disease and $+$ denote an individual that tests positive. We have that $\mathbb{P}[D] = 0.01$, $\mathbb{P}[+ \mid D] = 0.99$, and $\mathbb{P}[+ \mid D^c] = 0.03$ from the question. We want $\mathbb{P}[D \mid +]$, the probability a person who receives a positive test has the disease. By the definition of conditional probability, this is $$\prob{D \mid +} = \dfrac{\mathbb{P}[D+]}{\mathbb{P}[+]}$$ By conditioning on whether or not the person has the disease, we have that $$\mathbb{P}[D \mid +] = \dfrac{\mathbb{P}[+ \mid D]\mathbb{P}[D]}{\mathbb{P}[+ \mid D]\mathbb{P}[D] + \mathbb{P}[+ \mid D^c]\mathbb{P}[D^c]}$$ Note that $\mathbb{P}[D^c] = 1 - \mathbb{P}[D] = 0.99$. Plugging all values in, we get that $$\mathbb{P}[D \mid +] = \dfrac{0.99 \cdot 0.01}{0.99 \cdot 0.01 + 0.03 \cdot 0.99} = \dfrac{1}{4}$$ This probability is very low. This is because the number of false positives arising in the general population outweighs the true positives themselves.
hints: In this question, we have two groups of people. Namely, they are infected and healthy individuals. Thus, one can have the disease by either obtaining a positive or negative test. This observation yields the natural choice of conditioning on whether the test is positive or negative.

title: Bertrand's Box
statement: Two boxes are in front of you. One box has a $\$100$ bill and a $\$1$ bill, while the other has $2$ $\$100$ bills. You pick a box at random and then pick a bill from it at random without replacement. It is an $\$100$ bill. Find the probability you select a second $\$100$ on the next draw.
solution:
Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ denote the boxes with $1$ and $2$ $\$100$ bills, respectively, and let $E$ be the event that you select an $\$100$ bill on your first draw. The probability of selecting two $\$100$ bills is dependent on what box you chose from. Therefore, the idea is to condition on the box of choice.

$$$$

If you are to select a second $\$100$ bill, then you must be in box $2$, as you select without replacement. Given that you are in box $2$, you must select a $\$100$ bill, whereas it's not possible if you are in box $1$, so we want to compute $$\mathbb{P}[B_2 \mid E] = \dfrac{\mathbb{P}[B_2E]}{\mathbb{P}[E]}$$ The numerator is just $\mathbb{P}[B_2E] = \mathbb{P}[E \mid B_2]\mathbb{P}[B_2]$. For the denominator, we condition on what box we are in. The denominator becomes $\mathbb{P}[E] = \mathbb{P}[E \mid B_1]\mathbb{P}[B_1] + \mathbb{P}[E \mid B_2]\mathbb{P}[B_2]$. We know $\mathbb{P}[B_1] = \mathbb{P}[B_2] = \dfrac{1}{2}$ because we choose at random. If we are in Box 1, it is equally likely whether or not you get an $\$100$ bill on the first draw, so $\mathbb{P}[E \mid B_1] = \dfrac{1}{2}$. If we are in Box 2, you are guaranteed an $\$100$ bill, so $\mathbb{P}[E \mid B_2] = 1$. Plugging this in, we get $\mathbb{P}[B_2 \mid E] = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} \cdot 1}{\frac{1}{2} \cdot 1 + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ after reduction. Note that there are $3$ $\$100$ bills between the two boxes, of which two of them belong to box $2$. Thus, it should make intuitive sense that if you draw a $\$100$ bill out, there is a probability $2/3$ that it was drawn from box $2$.
hints: Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ denote the boxes with $1$ and $2$ $\$100$ bills, respectively, and let $E$ be the event that you select an $\$100$ bill on your first draw. The probability of selecting two $\$100$ bills is dependent on what box you chose from. Therefore, the idea is to condition on the box of choice.

title: Multisocks
statement: Suppose you have $k \geq 1$ drawers with $r \geq 1$ distinct colors of socks. In drawer $i$, there are $n_{ij}$ socks of color $j$, where $1 \leq i \leq k$ and $1 \leq j \leq r$. One drawer is selected uniformly at random, and a sock from that drawer is selected uniformly at random. The sock is of color $1 \leq j \leq r$. Find the probability that you selected from drawer $i$. Solve this when $k = 3, r = 3, i = 2, j = 2$ and $n_{ij} = i+j$
solution:
The probability that you drawer a sock of color $j$ from a drawer depends on which drawer you selected from, as they each have different proportions of each color of sock. Therefore, the idea is to condition on the drawer number that was selected. Let $D_i$ be the event that drawer $i$ was selected, and let $S_j$ be the event that a sock of color $j$ was selected. We want to compute $\prob{D_i \mid S_j}$, as we know a sock of color $j$ was selected. To do this, we first use the conditional probability formula $$\prob{D_i \mid S_j} = \dfrac{\prob{D_i \cap S_j}}{\prob{S_j}}$$

On the numerator, we switch the direction of the conditional to obtain $\prob{D_i \cap S_j}  = \prob{S_j \mid D_i}\prob{D_i}$. Since the drawer is selected uniformly at random from the $k$ drawers, $\prob{D_i} = 1/k$ for each $i$. Given that drawer $i$ was selected, there are $n_{ij}$ total socks of color $j$ in drawer $i$, and there are a total of $\sum_{j=1}^r n_{ij}$ socks in drawer $i$, as we sum over the amounts of socks of each type. Therefore, we obtain $$\prob{S_j \mid D_i} = \dfrac{n_{ij}}{\sum_{j=1}^r n_{ij}}$$ On the numerator, we play the same game, but we condition on the drawer of selection. This yields $$\prob{S_j} = \sum_{i=1}^k \prob{S_j \mid D_i}\prob{D_i} = \dfrac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k \dfrac{n_{ij}}{\sum_{j=1}^r n_{ij}}$$ Plugging all of these in, $$\prob{D_i \mid S_j} = \dfrac{\frac{n_{ij}}{\sum_{i=1}^r n_{ij}}}{\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{n_{ij}}{\sum_{j=1}^r n_{ij}}}$$ In other words, the probability is the proportion of socks of type $j$ in drawer $i$ divided by the sum of the proportions among all drawers. With the specified values, the answer is $1/3$.
hints: The probability that you drawer a sock of color $j$ from a drawer depends on which drawer you selected from, as they each have different proportions of each color of sock. Therefore, the idea is to condition on the drawer number that was selected. Let $D_i$ be the event that drawer $i$ was selected, and let $S_j$ be the event that a sock of color $j$ was selected. We want to compute $\prob{D_i \mid S_j}$, as we know a sock of color $j$ was selected.

title: Sample Space Reduction
statement: Let $B$ be a non-empty set with $|B| = n$, and let $A \subseteq B$ with $|A| = k$, where $0 \leq k \leq n$. A uniformly random element of $B$ is selected. For any $b \in B\setminus A$, compute the probability $b$ is selected given that the chosen element is not in $A$. Solve this when $n = 10$ and $k = 4$.
solution:
For notation, let $x$ be the element selected from $B$. We are given that $x 
otin A$, and we want to compute the probability $x = b$. In other words, we must compute $$\prob{x = b \mid x 
otin A} = \dfrac{\prob{x = b, x 
otin A}}{\prob{x 
otin A}}$$ Since $x 
otin A$ by definition, $\prob{x = b, x 
otin A} = \prob{x = b} = 1/n$ by the uniformity of the selected element from $B$. Now, since the selected element is uniformly at random and $|A| = k$, the probability that $x \in A$ is $k/n$, as it contains $k$ of the $n$ equally likely elements. Thus, $\prob{x 
otin A} = 1 - k/n$. Plugging these in yields $$\prob{x = b \mid x 
otin A} = \dfrac{1/n}{1-k/n} = \dfrac{1}{n-k}$$ This result makes a lot of intuitive sense: If we know that the selected element is not in $A$, we remove $k$ possibilities from being selected, and then there are now $n-k$ equally likely elements remaining that can be selected. This means that the conditional probability of selecting any of these elements is just $ rac{1}{n-k}$. With the specified values, the answer is $1/6$.

title: Discrete-Time Memorylessness
statement: Suppose $X \sim \text{Geom}(p)$. For positive integers $r$ and $s$, compute $\mathbb{P}[X > r + s \mid X > r]$. Report the answer when $p = 1/3, r = 5,$ and $s = 3$.
solution:
To compute this probability, it would know how to compute unconditional probabilities of the form $\prob{X > x}$, where $x$ is an integer. The event $\{X \leq x\}$ means that the first heads appears in the first $x$ flips. In other words, there is at least one head in the first $x$ flips. However, as this is an "at least one" statement, it's typically easier to consider the complement. In particular, the complement would be the event $\{X > x\}$ i.e. it takes more than $x$ flips to see the first heads. This would mean that all of the first $x$ flips are tails. The probability that all of the first $x$ flips are tails is $(1-p)^x$, as each flip is independent. Therefore, $\prob{X > x} = (1-p)^x$. By complementation, we have $$\prob{X \leq x} = 1 - \prob{X > x} = 1 - (1-p)^x$$

$$$$

In this question, there is a conditional probability. Thus, the best first step is to use the definition of conditional probability. Namely, $$\prob{X > r+s \mid X > r} = \dfrac{\prob{X > r+s, X> r}}{\prob{X > r}}$$ If $X > r+s$, then $X > r$ automatically, as $r+s$ is larger than $r$. Thus, $\{X > r+s\} \subseteq \{X > r\}$, so $\prob{X > r+s,X>r} = \prob{X > r+s} = (1-p)^{r+s}$. The denominator, by letting $x = r$, is $\prob{X > r} = (1-p)^r$. Plugging these in, we get $$\prob{X > r+s \mid X > r} = \dfrac{(1-p)^{r+s}}{(1-p)^r} = (1-p)^s = \prob{X > s}$$

$$$$

What does this result intuitively mean and why does it make sense? This statement essentially says: Given that all of the first $r$ flips are tails, the probability that all of the first $r+s$ flips are tails is equal to the probability that $s$ flips are tails. This makes intuitive sense, as if the first $r$ flips are all tails, $s$ additional flips need to be tails for the first $r+s$ flips to be tails. Thus, the probability all $r+s$ flips are tails is just the probability that the other $s$ flips are all tails. 

$$$$

One could imagine this physically by the following: Imagine your friend flips a coin $r$ times and reports to you that all of them were tails. You then perform $s$ flips on the same coin. The probability that all $r+s$ flips are tails is equal to the probability that you flip $s$ tails. This is the start of your flipping sequence, so the number of flips needed until you obtain a heads is $X \sim \text{Geom}(p)$, so the probability that all of the flips you perform are tails is $\prob{X > s}$. With the specified values, the answer is $8/27$.
hints: To compute this probability, it would know how to compute unconditional probabilities of the form $\prob{X > x}$, where $x$ is an integer. Use the interpretation of the Geometric distribution.

title: Most Likely Poisson
statement: Suppose that $k > 0$ is a fixed integer. Find the value of $\lambda$ that maximizes $\mathbb{P}[X = k]$. Solve when $k = 4$.
solution: The objective of this problem is to maximize $f(\lambda) = \mathbb{P}[X = k] = \dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!}e^{-\lambda}$ with respect to $\lambda$, as $k$ is fixed. Since the $k!$ is a constant, we can just consider maximizing $g(\lambda) = \lambda^k e^{-\lambda}$. Taking the derivative with respect to $\lambda$ and applying product rule, we get that the derivative is $$g'(\lambda) = k\lambda^{k-1}e^{-\lambda} - \lambda^{k}e^{-\lambda} = \lambda^{k-1}e^{-\lambda}(k - \lambda)$$ We set the derivative equal to $0$ to find our critical points. These critical values are $\lambda = k, 0$. However, as the parameter of the Poisson distribution is positive, $\lambda = k$ must be the valid critical point. To verify that $k$ actually maximizes the probability, one can confirm that for $0 < \lambda < k$, the derivative is positive, while for $\lambda > k$, it is negative. With the specified value, the answer is $\lambda = 4$.
hints: The objective of this problem is to maximize $f(\lambda) = \mathbb{P}[X = k] = \dfrac{\lambda^k}{k!}e^{-\lambda}$ with respect to $\lambda$, as $k$ is fixed. What tools do you know for finding maximal/minimal values?

title: Lucky Lottery
statement: A lottery has an urn consisting of $70$ balls labeled distinct numbers $1-70$. $6$ balls are drawn at random for a lottery, and your lottery ticket also has $6$ distinct random numbers $1-70$ on it. You win the lottery if either $5$ or $6$ of your numbers match those drawn (in any order). Find the probability of winning the lottery. If the probability you find is $p$, report $p \cdot 10^6$, rounded to the nearest hundredth.
solution:
Let $N$ be the amount of numbers on the lottery card matching those drawn. We can regard the two groups in this question as numbers matching and numbers not matching those on the lottery card, and $N$ counts the amount of numbers that match. Thus, $N$ must be Hypergeometric, as the numbers are all distinct i.e. selected without replacement.

$$$$

There are $N = 6$ values matching those on your card, $M = 70 - 6 = 64$ values not matching those on your card, and $n = 6$ values selected. Thus $N \sim \text{Hypergeom}(6,64,6)$. To win, you must have at least $5$ numbers match, so the event of winning is the event $\{N \geq 5\} = \{N = 5\}\cup \{N = 6\}$. Since these events are disjoint, $\prob{N \geq 5} = \mathbb{P}[N = 5] + \mathbb{P}[N = 6]$. By substituting in $N = 6, M = 64, n = 6$, and $k = 5,6$, we obtain 

    $$\mathbb{P}[N = 5] = \dfrac{\displaystyle \binom{6}{5}\binom{64}{1}}{\displaystyle \binom{70}{6}} = \dfrac{384}{\displaystyle \binom{70}{6}} \hspace{3pt} \text{and} \hspace{3pt} \mathbb{P}[N = 6] = \dfrac{\displaystyle \binom{6}{6}\binom{64}{0}}{\displaystyle\binom{70}{6}} = \dfrac{1}{\displaystyle \binom{70}{6}}$$
Adding these together, the probability of a jackpot is $$\prob{N \geq 5} = \dfrac{385}{\displaystyle \binom{70}{6}} \approx 2.94 \cdot 10^{-6}$$ The answer is $2.94$.
hints: Let $N$ be the amount of numbers on the lottery card matching those drawn. We can regard the two groups in this question as numbers matching and numbers not matching those on the lottery card, and $N$ counts the amount of numbers that match.
$N$ must be Hypergeometric, as the numbers are all distinct i.e. selected without replacement.

title: Flight Duration I
statement: The length of a flight (in hours) is Exponentially distributed with parameter $1/4$. Find the probability that the flight lasts more than $5$ hours. Round to the nearest thousandth.
solution: First, we must frame this problem probabilistically. Let $T$ be the length of the flight (in hours). As per the question, $T \sim \text{Exp}\left(1/4\right)$. The question is asking us to compute $\mathbb{P}[T > 5]$, as this is the event where the length of the flight is more than $5$ hours. The CDF enables us to compute probabilities in the form $\prob{T \leq x}$. Thus, the idea is to complement the CDF in this question. Doing this, $$\mathbb{P}[T > 5] = 1 - \mathbb{P}[T \leq 5] = 1 - (1 - e^{-\frac{1}{4} \cdot 5}) = e^{-\frac{5}{4}}$$ The probability statement is evaluated with $\lambda = 1/4$ and $x = 5$.
hints: First, we must frame this problem probabilistically. Let $T$ be the length of the flight (in hours). As per the question, $T \sim \text{Exp}\left(1/4\right)$. The question is asking us to compute $\mathbb{P}[T > 5]$, as this is the event where the length of the flight is more than $5$ hours.

title: Flight Duration II
statement: The length of a flight (in hours) is Exponentially distributed with parameter $1/4$. Find the flight time that $75\%$ of flights are shorter than. Round to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
Using the same notation from "Flight Duration I," we know $T \sim \text{Exp}\left(1/4\right)$ and $F(t) = \left(1 - e^{-t/4}\right)I_{(0,\infty)}(t)$ from the previous example. We now want to find a time $t$ so that $\mathbb{P}[T \leq t] = F(t) = 0.75$. For such a time $t$, the probability that any given flight is shorter than $t$ in duration is $75\%$, so this is the quantity we want to compute. Therefore, our goal is to solve for $t$ in the equation $1 - e^{-\frac{t}{4}}  = 3/4$. 

$$$$

Subtracting $1$ and multiplying by $-1$ on both sides yields $e^{-\frac{t}{4}} = 1/4$. Taking the natural log of both sides yields $-\dfrac{t}{4} = \ln\left(1/4\right) = -\ln(4)$, meaning $t = 4\ln(4) \approx 5.545$.
hints: We want to find a time $t$ so that $\mathbb{P}[T \leq t] = F(t) = 0.75$.

title: Continuous-Time Memorylessness
statement: Let $X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$ and $s,t \geq 0$ be fixed real numbers. Compute $\mathbb{P}[X > s + t \mid X > t]$. Report the answer when $\lambda = 1, t = 3,$ and $s = 2$ to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
For any $x > 0$, $$\mathbb{P}[X > x] = 1 - \mathbb{P}[X \leq x] = 1 - (1-e^{-\lambda x}) = e^{-\lambda x}$$ The first proper step is to apply the definition of conditional probability to the two events. This yields $$\mathbb{P}[X > s + t \mid X > t] = \dfrac{\prob{X > s+t,X > t}}{\prob{X > t}} = \dfrac{\mathbb{P}[X > s + t]}{\mathbb{P}[X > t]}$$ The numerator event is the intersection of the events $\{X > s+t\}$ and $\{X> t\}$. However, since $s \geq 0$, we have that if $X > s+t$, then $X > t$, so $\{X > s+t$\} a subset of $\{X > t\}$, so the intersection is just $\{X > s+t\}$, justifying the simplification on the numerator. Substituting $x$ as both $s+t$ and $t$ into the expression fro the beginning, $\mathbb{P}[X > s+t] = e^{-\lambda (s+t)}$ and $\mathbb{P}[X > t] = e^{-\lambda t}$. Therefore, $$\mathbb{P}[X > s+t \mid X > t] = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda (s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda t}} = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda s} \cdot e^{-\lambda t}}{e^{-\lambda t}} = e^{-\lambda s} = \prob{X > s}$$ The result of this question is the exact same as in the case of the Geometric distribution, but now for any real $s$ and $t$: $\mathbb{P}[X > s+t \mid X > t] = \mathbb{P}[X > s]$.

$$$$

This result makes intuitive sense by thinking about the meaning of the Exponential distribution. The memorylessness property here says that given you have waited at least $t$ time units for the first occurrence event, the probability you must wait at least $t+s$ time units for the first occurrence of the event is just the probability you must wait $s$ time units (as if it was from the beginning). Imagine the following scenario: You are watching for a certain type of bird, and you wait $t$ units of time for the bird to appear, and it still doesn't. After $t$ units of time, your friend comes in to substitute for you in watching for the bird. The probability that the total time spent watching the bird is at least $t+s$ is therefore just the probability your friend spends at least $s$ units of time watching for the bird. Since the bird hasn't appeared yet, it's as if your friend had started watching from the beginning again, as the state is the exact same. In rough terms, the memorylessness property says: The amount of time that you have already waited for an event to occur does not give any information about how much longer you must wait for an event to occur. With the specified values, the answer is $e^{-2}$.
hints: Complement the CDF and use the definition of conditional probability.

title: Flight Duration III
statement: The length of a flight (in hours) is Exponentially distributed with parameter $1/4$. To the nearest thousandth, find the probability that the flight lasts more than $5$ hours given that it lasts more than $4$ hours.
solution: Using the same notation as the previous parts, $T \sim \exponential{1/4}$ and $F(t) = \left(1 - e^{-t/4}\right)I_{(0,\infty)}(t)$. We want to compute $\mathbb{P}[T > 5 \mid T > 4] = \mathbb{P}[T > 4 + 1 \mid T > 4]$, as we are now given that the flight lasts more than $4$ hours. We write the probability statement in this the form to mimic that of the memorylessness property, as $t = 4$ in this case. By applying the memorylessness of the Exponential distribution and substituting the CDF, $$\mathbb{P}[T > 4 + 1 \mid T > 4] = \mathbb{P}[T > 1] = 1 - \prob{T \leq 1} = e^{-1/4}$$
hints: Write out the probability statement that you want to compute and apply the memorylessness property of Exponential distributions.

title: Normal Moments I
statement: Suppose that $Z \sim N(0,1)$. Find $\ev{X^n}$, where $n$ is a positive odd integer. Report the answer when $n = 5$.
solution:
When computing $\ev{Z^k}$ for a general $k$, computing the $k$th derivative through the MGF or LOTUS explicitly is annoying. However, from the Taylor expansion of the MGF, one can read off the $k$th moment from the coefficient of $\theta^k$. Therefore, the best approach is to consider the Taylor series of the MGF. By taking $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma^2 = 1$ in the MGF of the Normal distribution, the MGF of $Z$ is given by $M(\theta) = e^{\frac{1}{2}\theta^2}$. Luckily, we do know the Taylor series of $e^x$, so we can conclude that $$M(\theta) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{\left(\frac{1}{2}\theta^2\right)^k}{k!} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^k k !}\theta^{2k}$$ Note that there are only even powers of $\theta$ in the Taylor expansion. This means that the coefficient of all odd powers of $\theta$ are $0$, which also means that $\ev{Z^n} = 0$ when $n$ is odd. Therefore, the answer is $0$.

$$$$

One can also see this result from writing out the LOTUS integral. We have that $$\ev{Z^n} = \int_{\R} x^n \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{x^2}{2}}~dx$$ When $n$ is odd, $x^n$ is an odd function. The PDF of the standard Normal distribution is an even function, so their product must be odd. Since their product is odd, we integrate over the entire real line, and MGF exists (implying the integral is finite), we can conclude that the integral must be $0$.
hints: Write out the LOTUS integral or use the MGF of the standard Normal distribution.

title: Carousel Box I
statement: A box has $1$ red and $1$ blue ball. $3$ people named $1,2,$ and $3$, draw from the box one-at-a-time with replacement in that order. A round will be considered as the process of people $1,2,$ and $3$ drawing consecutively. Let $X$ be the number of the person who selects the first red ball and $Y$ be the round in which the first red ball is drawn. For each valid value of $x$ and $y$, compute $\prob{X = x, Y = y}$. Evaluate this when $x = 1$ and $y = 2$.
solution:
This question is essentially asking us to determine the joint PMF of $X$ and $Y$. Let's first find the joint support. The support of $X$ is $\{1,2,3\}$, as $X$ is just the player number. Now, the support of $Y$ is just $\mathbb{Z}^+$, as any player can win on any round, which are indexed by the positive integers. There is no interaction between the round the player wins on and who is allowed to win, so, the joint support is $S = \{1,2,3\} \times \Z^+$. Thus, for each $x \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $y \in \mathbb{Z}^+$, we need to find $\mathbb{P}[X = x, Y = y]$. 

$$$$

The event $\{X = x, Y = y\}$ means that player $x$ must win in round $y$. For this to occur, there can't be a winner in the first $y-1$ rounds, and the people before person $x$ on the $y$th round also can't win. There would be $3(y-1)$ flips that occur in the first $y-1$ rounds, and $x-1$ flips that occur before person $x$ on the $y$th round. Therefore, for this event to occur, the first $3(y-1) + x-1$ draws of the game must all be blue, and then person $x$ must end it with a red. Since each draw is independent, as we draw with replacement, for any $(x,y) \in S$, the probability is given by $$\prob{X = x, Y = y} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3(y-1) + (x-1)} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3(y-1) + x}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $1/16$.
hints: The support of $X$ is $\{1,2,3\}$, as $X$ is just the player number. Now, the support of $Y$ is just $\mathbb{Z}^+$, as any player can win on any round, which are indexed by the positive integers. There is no interaction between the round the player wins on and who is allowed to win, so, the joint support is $S = \{1,2,3\} \times \Z^+$.
Consider interpreting the event $\{X = x\} \cap \{Y = y\}$ in context of the game.

title: Carousel Box II
statement: A box has $1$ red and $1$ blue ball. $3$ people named $1,2,$ and $3$, draw from the box one-at-a-time with replacement in that order. A round will be considered as the process of people $1,2,$ and $3$ drawing consecutively. Just as in the previous part, the person who draws the first red ball is the winner. Compute the probability that player $2$ wins on an even round.
solution: Using the notation of the previous part, if player 2 wins, then $X = 2$ by definition. If the round won is even, then $Y = 2k$ for some positive integer $k$. Thus, we want to compute $\mathbb{P}[X = 2, Y = 2k]$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. To evaluate this, we can use the joint PMF from the previous part. For a fixed $k$, $$\mathbb{P}[X = 2, Y = 2k] = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2 + 3(2k-1)} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6k-1}$$ Since $k$ can be any positive integer for $Y$ to be even, we sum over all positive integers $k$ to evaluate the probability. This is done because the events are disjoint for varying $k$. Namely, this is $$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \mathbb{P}[X = 2,Y = 2k] = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6k-1} = 2 \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{2^6}\right)^k = 2 \cdot \dfrac{1/64}{1-1/64} = \dfrac{2}{63}$$ In the last sum, we brought the $6$ inside to the ratio and then use the geometric series formula.
hints: Using the notation of the previous part, if player 2 wins, then $X = 2$ by definition. If the round won is even, then $Y = 2k$ for some positive integer $k$. Thus, we want to compute $\mathbb{P}[X = 2, Y = 2k]$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$.
Find the probability in the first hint for fixed $k$ and sum over all positive integers $k$.

title: MrBeast's Coin Challenge
statement: You’re pulling up to a MrBeast challenge 🎬, and he hits you with this setup: First, he spins a wheel that randomly picks some probability $X \sim \unif{0}{1}$. Afterwards, you have to flip a coin with probability $x$ of heads per flip $n$ times, where $n$ is fixed. Let $Y$ be the number of heads that you obtain from your $n$ flips.  As a function of $n$ and/or $y$, for any $0 \leq y \leq n$, compute $\prob{Y = y}$. Evaluate this when $n = 9$.
solution: This question is really asking us to find the unconditional distribution of $Y$. We must first find the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$. The conditional distribution tells us that for all $y = 0,1,\dots, n$, $$\mathbb{P}[Y = y \mid X = x] = p(y \mid x) = \binom{n}{y}x^y(1-x)^{n-y}$$ We also have that $f_X(x) = I_{(0,1)}(x)$. By the above work, the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ is $$g(x,y) = p(y \mid x)f_X(x) = \binom{n}{y}x^y(1-x)^{n-y}I_{(0,1)}(x)$$ To find the unconditional distribution of $Y$, we must remove $X$ from the joint distribution. As $X$ is a continuous random variable, we integrate it out. Note that $Y$ is a discrete random variable, so our result of this integral will be a PMF. Therefore, $$\mathbb{P}[Y = y] = \int_0^1 g(x,y)~dx = \int_0^1 \binom{n}{y}x^y(1-x)^{n-y}~dx$$ Writing $\displaystyle \binom{n}{y} = \dfrac{n!}{y!(n-y)!}$ and adding and subtracting $1$ from each exponent, we have that the integral becomes $$\prob{Y = y} = \int_0^1 \dfrac{n!}{y!(n-y)!}x^{\textcolor{red}{(y+1)}-1}(1-x)^{\textcolor{blue}{(n-y+1)}-1}~dx$$ The form of the above integrand suggests that we should transform it into that of a $\bet{\textcolor{red}{y+1}}{\textcolor{blue}{n-y+1}}$ distribution. Note that $y! = \Gamma(y+1)$, $(n-y)! = \Gamma(n-y+1)$, and $n! = \Gamma(n+1)$, which is why we subtracted and added $1$ to each exponent. Writing this in, $$\prob{Y = y} = \int_0^1 \dfrac{\Gamma(n+1)}{\Gamma(y+1)\Gamma(n-y+1)}x^{(y+1)-1}(1-x)^{(n-y+1)-1}~dx$$ This looks similar to a Beta integral with our desired parameters. However, the normalizing constant is slightly off. The sum of the two parameters of our desired distribution is $n+2$, but the numerator is only $\Gamma(n+1)$. Thus, we must multiply and divide by $n+1$, as we can apply the reduction property $\Gamma(a+1) = a\Gamma(a)$ with $a = n+1$ to get our desired PDF. Our desired integral is therefore $$\prob{Y = y} = \dfrac{1}{n+1}\int_0^1\dfrac{\Gamma(n+2)}{\Gamma(y+1)\Gamma(n-y+1)}x^{(y+1)-1}(1-x)^{(n-y+1)-1}~dx = \dfrac{1}{n+1}$$ The last integral was that of a PDF, so it evaluates to $1$. The unconditional PMF of $Y$ is given by $\mathbb{P}[Y = y] = 1/(n+1)$ for $y = 0,1,\dots, n$. In other words, $Y \sim \text{DiscreteUnif}\{0,1,\dots,n\}$. With the specified values, the answer is $1/10$.
hints: This question is really asking us to find the unconditional distribution of $Y$. We must first find the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$. Afterwards, find the marginal by removing $X$ from the joint. How do you do this?

title: Heads Before Tails
statement: A coin with probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads is flipped repetitively until $r \geq 1$ heads appear. Find the expected number of tails that appear when $r = 10$ and $p = 1/3$.
solution: As we are waiting for the $r$th occurrence of some events that are independent per trial, we should apply the Negative Binomial distribution. As there is probability $p$ per trial of landing heads and we want $r$ heads, the number of trials needed is $N \sim \negbinom{r}{p}$. From the known properties of the Negative Binomial distribution $\ev{N} = r/p$. Of these flips, $r$ of them must be heads, so the average number of tails is just the average number of total flips minus the number of heads. Thus, the answer is $$\dfrac{r}{p} - r = r \cdot \dfrac{1-p}{p}$$ This answer passes the intuition check, as $p = 1$ implies that there are no tails, which makes sense, as every flip is a heads. Similarly, if $p = 1/2$, there should intuitively be an equal amount of heads and tails that appear, in which our formula does indeed imply there are $r$ heads and $r$ tails on average. With our specified values, the answer is $20$.
hints: Can you find the total number of flips that it takes on average to obtain $r$ heads? How many of those flips are heads?

title: Limited Hitter I
statement: A standard fair $n-$sided die is rolled infinitely. The cumulative sum of all observed rolls is recorded after each roll. For each integer $k \geq 1$, let $f(n,k)$ be the probability that the cumulative sum is ever exactly $k$. For a fixed $k$, compute $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} f(n,k)$. Report the answer when $k = 6$.
solution: As $n \rightarrow \infty$, the number of sides on the die tends to $\infty$. The probability of ever being exactly $k$ must be extremely small as the number of sides grows arbitrarily large. Therefore, it becomes extremely improbable that the sum ever is exactly $k$, as you are extremely likely to exceed $k$ in your first roll! With this intuition in mind, we can conclude that the limit is $0$ for all $k$.
hints: As $n \rightarrow \infty$, the number of sides on the die tends to $\infty$. The probability of ever being exactly $k$ must be extremely small as the number of sides grows arbitrarily large.

title: Both Show
statement: A coin with probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads is repeatedly flipped until both a heads and tails appear (not necessarily consecutively). Find the expected number of flips that are performed when $p = 1/3$.
solution: Since the two sides are not necessarily equally likely, the expected number of additional flips is dependent on what appears on the first flip. Therefore, the best approach is to condition on the first flip. Let $N$ be the total number of flips performed to see both heads and tails. Similarly, let $H$ and $T$ be the events of the first flip being head and tail, respectively. By the Law of Total Expectation, $$\ev{N} = \ev{N \mid H}\prob{H} + \ev{N \mid T}\prob{T}$$ As per the question, $\prob{H} = p$ and $\prob{T} = 1-p$. If a heads is observed at the first flip, we need to observe a tail. The number of additional flips that need to be performed follows a $\geom{1-p}$ distribution, as there is probability $1-p$ of each flip being tail. The expected number of additional flips needed would be $1/(1-p)$, so $\ev{N \mid H} = 1 + \frac{1}{1-p}$ The $1$ comes from performing $1$ flip to obtain the initial heads. Similarly, if a tail is observed on the first flip, a head must be seen afterwards. The expected number of additional flips needed in this case is $1/p$, so $\ev{N \mid T} = 1 + \frac{1}{p}$. Plugging all of these values in yields $$\ev{T} = p \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{1-p}\right) + (1-p)\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{1-p}\right) = 1 + \dfrac{p^2 + (1-p)^2}{p(1-p)} =  \dfrac{1-p(1-p)}{p(1-p)}$$ This expression makes intuitive sense, as it satisfies some properties we would expect. The expected value is minimized at $p = 1/2$, which is reasonable given that the flips are "most random" at $p = 1/2$. Similarly, the expected values grow to $\infty$ as $p \rightarrow 0$ and $p \rightarrow 1$. With $p = 1/3$, the answer is $7/2$.
hints: Since the two sides are not necessarily equally likely, the expected number of additional flips is dependent on what appears on the first flip. Use Law of Total Expectation to condition on what happens in the first flip.
What are the distributions of the number of additional flips needed?

title: Absolute Brownian Conditions
statement: Let $W_t$ be a Brownian Motion. For $0 \leq s \leq t$, compute $\ev{W_s \mid |W_t|}$. Report the answer when $s = 1, t = 3,$ and $|W_t| = 6$.
solution: $|W_t|$ provides us the magnitude, but not direction, of the Brownian Motion. If we knew the direction of the Brownian Motion, we can compute this fairly easily. The idea is to condition on $W_t > 0$ or $W_t \leq 0$ so that we know the direction and magnitude. Applying the Law of Total Expectation, $$\ev{W_s \mid |W_t|} = \ev{W_s \mid |W_t|, W_t > 0}\prob{W_t > 0} + \ev{W_s \mid |W_t|, W_t \leq 0}\prob{W_t \leq 0}$$ Since $W_t \sim N(0,t)$, the two probability terms are $0$, as the Normal distribution is symmetric about it's mean. The two conditional expectation terms are now Brownian Bridges on $[0,t]$ that have the same length and opposite direction. The two terms are $\frac{s}{t}|W_t|$ and $-\frac{s}{t}|W_t|$, respectively. Plugging these in, $$\ev{W_s \mid |W_t|} = \dfrac{s}{t}|W_t| \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{s}{t}|W_t| \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 0$$ This holds for any values of $s,t,$ and $|W_t|$! Intuitively, this makes sense because the Brownian Motion has a density at time $t$ symmetry about $0$, and we only know the magnitude, but not the direction, of the Brownian Motion. Therefore, on average, the process is at $0$ at all times.
hints: $|W_t|$ provides us the magnitude, but not direction, of the Brownian Motion. If we knew the direction of the Brownian Motion, we can compute this fairly easily. The idea is to condition on $W_t > 0$ or $W_t < 0$ so that we know the direction and magnitude.

title: Coin Flipper I
statement: Mike flips a fair coin infinitely. He starts off with $\$1$. If he receives a heads, he doubles his current balance. If he receives a tails, he loses his entire balance. What is the probability that Mike eventually loses all of his money?
solution: For Mike to lose his money, he must obtain a tails at some point. This type of problem is best handled through the Borel-Cantelli Lemma. We actually obtain something stronger from it: We can obtain the probability that infinitely many tails occur. Define the events $T_1,T_2,\dots$, where $T_i$ is the event that the $i$th flip is a tails. The events are independent because each flip is independent. In addition, $\prob{T_i} = 1/2$ for all $i$, as the coin is fair. Therefore, by the 2nd Borel-Cantelli Lemma, $$\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \prob{T_i} = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{2} = \infty \implies \prob{T_i \hspace{3pt} \text{i.o.}} = 1$$
hints: For Mike to lose his money, he must obtain a tails at some point. What lemma talks about events occurring at some point?

title: Coin Flipper II
statement: Mike flips a fair coin $n$ times. He starts off with $\$1$. If he receives a heads, he doubles his current balance. If he receives a tails, he loses his entire balance. What is Mike's expected balance at the end? Report the answer when $n = 10$.
solution: If Mike obtains a tails at any point in the $n$ flips, he has $\$0$. Otherwise, if Mike obtains all heads, he has $\$2^n$, as he doubles his money each time. The probability he obtains all heads is $1/2^n$ by independence of the flips. Thus, the probability he obtains at least one tail is $1 - 1/2^n$. By the definition of expected value, Mike's expected balance is $$\dfrac{1}{2^n} \cdot 2^n + \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2^n}\right) \cdot 0 = 1$$ This is very counter-intuitive, as for any finite $n$, his expected payout is $\$1$, but as $n \rightarrow \infty$, his payout is $\$0$ with probability $1$. This discrepancy arises from deeper measure-theoretic details about the probability space we are working in. In particular, the Dominated Convergence Theorem doesn't apply here. The answer to this question is $\$1$, regardless of $n$.
hints: If Mike obtains a tails at any point in the $n$ flips, he has $\$0$. Otherwise, how much money does he have?

title: Proportional Bets I
statement: George starts with $\$1$. George repeatedly plays a game where he has probability $0 < p < 1$ of winning, independently between rounds. If George wins, he receives $\$r$. If George loses, his current balance is multiplied by $0 < q < 1$. If George plays infinitely, what does his expected balance converge to? Report the answer when $p = 1/3, q = 1/2,$ and $r = 3$.
solution: George's wealth after the $(n+1)$st round is dependent on his wealth at the $n$th round. Therefore, the idea is to condition on George's wealth at the $n$th round and derive a recurrence relation to determine his wealth at the $(n+1)$st round. By the Law of Total Expectation, $$\ev{X_{n+1}} = \ev{\ev{X_{n+1} \mid X_n}} = p \cdot (\ev{X_n} + r) + (1-p)(q\ev{X_n})$$ The interior was evaluated by conditioning on George winning or losing. If he wins, he obtains $\$r$ extra, which is the first term. Similarly, his balance is multiplied by $q$ if he loses. If we define $E_i = \ev{X_i}$, we now have a first-order non-homogenous recurrence relation. Suppose that the limit of this relation exists, and call it $L$. Since $L = \displaystyle \lim_{i \rightarrow \infty} E_i = \lim_{i \rightarrow \infty} E_{i-1}$, taking the limit on both sides of the recurrence yields $$L = p(L+r) + (1-p)(qL) \iff L(1-p)(1-q) = pr \iff L = \dfrac{pr}{(1-p)(1-q)}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $\$3$.
hints: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be George's wealth after $n$ rounds. To make the notation easier, define $E_i = \ev{X_i}$. Derive a recurrence relation for $E_n$, and then find the limit.

title: Rank and Suit Diff
statement: Two cards are drawn without replacement uniformly at random from a standard deck. Find the probability that the cards differ in both rank and suit.
solution: Since there are the same number of ranks and suits among all different ranks/suits, fix the first card arbitrarily. There are now $51$ cards in the deck remaining. Of these cards, there are $12$ cards from each of the three suits that aren't the one drawn on the first trial that differ in rank as well. Therefore, there are $12 \cdot 3 = 36$ valid cards that can be selected for the second card, so the answer is $36/51 = 12/17$.
hints: Since there are the same number of ranks and suits among all different ranks/suits, fix the first card arbitrarily. How many valid cards remain?

title: Dart Covariance
statement: Maddie is throwing darts at a very realistic dartboard that is infinitely tall and wide. Let $(0,0)$ be the exact center of the bullseye. Let $X$ and $Y$ represent the horizontal and vertical distance that Maddie's dart lands from the bullseye, respectively. This means that Maddie's shot is a random point $(X,Y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$. Assume that $X,Y \sim N(0,1)$ IID. Let $R$ be the (Euclidean) distance from the origin that the dart lands. Compute $\cov{X}{R^2}$.
solution: Since $R$ is the distance from the origin, it can be written in terms of $X$ and $Y$. Namely, $R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$, so $R^2 = X^2 + Y^2$. We now have a covariance solely in terms of $X$ and $Y$. Substituting in and applying bilinearity, $$\cov{X}{R^2} = \cov{X}{X^2 + Y^2} = \cov{X}{X^2} + \cov{X}{Y^2}$$ Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, the second covariance is $0$. To compute the first covariance, we can expand it out with the common formula to obtain $$\cov{X}{X^2} = \ev{X^3} - \ev{X}\ev{X^2}$$ Recall that all odd moments of the standard Normal distribution are $0$, so the above term also vanishes. Therefore, $\cov{X}{R^2} = 0$.
hints: Since $R$ is the distance from the origin, it can be written in terms of $X$ and $Y$. Substitute that into the covariance and use bilinearity.

title: Correlated Indicators
statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be events with $0 < \prob{A}, \prob{B} < 1$. Define $I_A$ and $I_B$ to be the indicator random variables of $A$ and $B$, respectively. Suppose $\corr{I_A}{I_B} = \rho$. If possible, find $\corr{I_{A^c}}{I_{B^c}}$ when $\rho = 0.3$. If not, answer $-2$.
solution: Let's first understand how the indicator of an event and it's complement are related. $I_A = 1$ exactly when $A$ occurs, which means $I_{A^c} = 0$. Similarly, $I_A = 0$ exactly when $A$ doesn't occur i.e. $A^c$ occurs, so $I_{A^c} = 1$. We can encapsulate this relationship by saying $I_{A^c} = 1 - I_A$. The same idea holds for $B$. Therefore, $$\corr{I_{A^c}}{I_{B^c}} = \corr{1 - I_A}{1 - I_B}$$ This is a linear transformation of the original indicators. From the properties of correlation, for any real constants $a,b,c,$ and $d$, with $a,c \neq 0$, $\corr{aX+b}{cY+d} = \text{sign}(ac)\corr{X}{Y}$, as the magnitude of the correlation is unchanged. In this case, $a = c = -1$, while $b = d = 1$. Therefore, $\text{sign}(ac) = \text{sign}(1) = 1$, meaning $\corr{I_A}{I_B} = \corr{I_{A^c}}{I_{B^c}}$. With the specified values, the answer is $0.3$.
hints: $I_A = 1$ exactly when $I_{A^c} = 0$, and vice versa. Therefore, for any event $E$, $I_E = 1 - I_{E^c}$. What do you know about correlation and linear transformations?

title: Dying Population
statement: Consider a population that originally consists of $N$ individuals. Each individual dies independently of one another, and the time of the last death has no bearing on when the next death occurs. When there are exactly $i$ individuals in the population, the rate of death of each individual in the population is $\mu_i$. Find the expected amount of time until the population goes extinct when $N = 4$ and $\mu_i = \frac{1}{5-i}$.
solution: The death rate is constant given the amount of people in the population, so it's best to break up the problem into distinct time intervals based on the population: Time spent with $N$ individuals, $N-1$ individuals, and so on. Let $T_i$ be the amount of time spent with exactly $i$ individuals in the population. The total lifetime of the population is given by $T = T_N + T_{N-1} + \dots + T_1$. The sum stops at $1$ because $T_1$ is the amount of time spent until the last individual dies, in which extinction is reached. The random variables are not exchangeable, as they don't have the same death rates. Applying linearity of expectation, $$\ev{T} = \sum_{i=1}^N \ev{T_i}$$ $\mathbb{E}[T_i]$ is the expected time spent with exactly $i$ individuals. Each individual dies independently of each other and with respect to when the last individual died. Thus, the rate of death when there are exactly $i$ individuals must be $i\mu_i$, as each individual dies at a rate $\mu_i$ and there are $i$ independent individuals in the population. Since the rate of death is $i\mu_i$ per unit time, the expected amount of time spent with exactly $i$ individuals is $\ev{T_i} = \frac{1}{i\mu_i}$. Substituting in, $$\ev{T} = \sum_{i=1}^N = \dfrac{1}{i\mu_i}$$ With the specified values, $\ev{T} = 77/12$.
hints: The death rate is constant given the amount of people in the population, so it's best to break up the problem into distinct time intervals based on the population: Time spent with $N$ individuals, $N-1$ individuals, and so on. Let $T_i$ be the amount of time spent with exactly $i$ individuals in the population. Use linearity of expectation somehow.

title: Linearly Normal I
statement: Suppose $X,Y \sim N(0,1)$ IID. For any constants $a,b > 0$, compute $\ev{aX + bY \mid X+Y}$. Report your answer when $a = 2, b = 4,$ and $X+Y = 2$.
solution: Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, we obtain some symmetry that simplifies the problem. In particular, as $X$ and $Y$ are IID and the given information is symmetric in $X$ and $Y$, $\ev{X \mid X+Y} = \ev{Y \mid X+Y}$. By the linearity of conditional expectation and known information, $$\ev{X \mid X+Y} + \ev{Y \mid X+Y} = \ev{X+Y \mid X+Y} = X+Y$$ By the equality above, $$\ev{X \mid X +Y } = \ev{Y \mid X+Y} = \dfrac{X+Y}{2}$$ This intuitively makes sense, as each should contribute equally to the sum $X+Y$ on average since they are IID. With this information in hand, we can apply linearity of conditional expectation to our original problem and obtain $$\ev{aX + bY \mid X+Y} = a\ev{X \mid X+Y} + b\ev{Y \mid X+Y} = (X+Y) \cdot \dfrac{a+b}{2}$$ Plugging in the specified values, the answer is $6$.
hints: Apply linearity of conditional expectation. Since $X$ and $Y$ are IID, what can be said about the conditional expectation term?

title: Zeta Zonk I
statement: We say that $X$ follows a Zeta$(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $$\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$$ Here, $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. For positive integers $k$, define $D_k$ to be the event that $p_k$ divides $X$. Find $\prob{D_k}$ when $k = 4$ and $s = 3$.
solution: For $p_k \mid X$, $X$ must be an integer multiple of $p_k$. In other words, $X = np_k$ for some positive integer $k$. The events $\{X = np_k\}$ are disjoint for varying $n$, so we can say $$\prob{D_k} = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \prob{X = np_k} = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \dfrac{(np_k)^{-s}}{\zeta(s)} = \dfrac{1}{p_k^s \cdot \zeta(s)} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n^s} = \dfrac{1}{p_k^s}$$ The last term was evaluated by the definition of $\zeta(s)$. With the specified values, $p_4 = 7$, so the answer is $1/343$.
hints: For $p_k \mid X$, $X$ must be an integer multiple of $p_k$. In other words, $X = np_k$ for some positive integer $k$. The events $\{X = np_k\}$ are disjoint for varying $n$.

title: Zeta Zonk II
statement:
We say that $X$ follows a Zeta$(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $$\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$$ Here, $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. For positive integers $k$, define $D_k$ to be the event that $p_k$ divides $X$. Evaluate $\displaystyle \prod_{i=1}^{\infty} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{p_i^s}\right)$ when $s = 4$. Round to the nearest thousandth.

$$$$

Note: It may be helpful to complete Zeta Zonk I first.
solution:
The term $1 - 1/p_i^s$ looks like the complement of what was found in "Zeta Zonk I". In particular, this is $\displaystyle \prod_{i=1}^{\infty} \prob{D_i^c}$. For independent events, the probability of the intersection is the product of the probabilities. Thus, a natural question to ask is if $$\displaystyle \prod_{i=1}^{\infty} \prob{D_i^c} = \prob{\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty}D_i^c}$$ In other words, we must determine if the events $D_1,D_2,\dots$ are independent. 

\nl

To establish independence, we must verify that for any arbitrary $n_1 \neq n_2 \neq \dots \neq n_r$, the probability of the intersection is the product of the probabilities. Fix some arbitrary $n_1 \neq n_2 \neq \dots \neq n_r$. Since the primes are clearly relatively prime to one another, $$\displaystyle \mathbb{P}\left[\bigcap_{i=1}^r D_{n_i}\right] = \mathbb{P}[X\text{ is divisible by }p_{n_1},\dots, p_{n_r}] = \dfrac{1}{(p_{n_1}p_{n_2}\dots p_{n_r})^s}$$ Separating out the previous expression, this equals  $\mathbb{P}[D_{n_1}]\dots \mathbb{P}[D_{n_r}]$, which establishes independence.

\nl

Since we have independence, we can now confirm the expression in question is equal to $\displaystyle \prob{\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty}D_i^c}$. The event $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty}D_i^c$ says that $X$ is divisible by no positive primes. The only integer in the support for which this is possible is $1$, so this probability just evaluates to $\prob{X = 1} = 1/\zeta(s)$. With $s = 4$, $\zeta(s) = \pi^4/90$, so the answer is $90/\pi^4 \approx 0.924$.
hints: The term $1 - 1/p_i^s$ looks like the complement of what was found in "Zeta Zonk I".

title: Zeta Zonk III
statement:
We say that $X$ follows a Zeta$(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $$\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$$ Here, $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Let $S$ be the event that $X$ is square-free (i.e. every perfect square that isn't $1$ does not divide $X$). Find $\mathbb{P}[S]$ when $s = 2$, rounded to the nearest thousandth.

$$$$

Note: Complete Zeta Zonk I and Zeta Zonk II before attempting this question.
solution: We want the probability that $X$ is square-free. This means that no square divides $X$. However, the square of a positive integer has the same factors as the integer it is a square of. Since every positive integer has a unique prime factorization, we can just write this as the event that $X$ is not divisible by $p_k^2$ for any prime $p_k$. The probability that $p_k^2 \mid X$ is just $1/(p_k^{2})^s = 1/p_k^{2s}$ by the same exact methodology of the previous parts. We showed previously the $D_k$ events are independent, so this also carries over to the squares. By independence, the probability $X$ is square-free is $$\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{p_i^{2s}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\zeta(2s)}$$ With $s = 2$, the answer is $90/\pi^4$.
hints: We want the probability that $X$ is square-free. This means that no square divides $X$. However, the square of a positive integer has the same factors as the integer it is a square of. Since every positive integer has a unique prime factorization, we can just write this as the event that $X$ is not divisible by $p_k^2$ for any prime $p_k$.

title: Zeta Zonk IV
statement:
We say that $X$ follows a Zeta$(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $$\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$$ Here, $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Suppose that $X,Y \sim \text{Zeta}(s)$ IID. Compute the probability $X$ and $Y$ are relatively prime when $s = 2$. Round your answer to the nearest thousandth.

$$$$

Note: Complete Zeta Zonk I - III before attempting this question.
solution:
For $X$ and $Y$ to be relatively prime, they must share no common prime divisor. From the previous parts, we know that $$\prob{p_k \mid X} = \prob{p_k \mid Y} = \dfrac{1}{p_k^s}$$ Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent, the events $\{p_k \mid X\}$ and $\{p_k \mid Y\}$ are independent. Therefore, the probability that $p_k$ divides both $X$ and $Y$ is $1/p_k^{2s}$. For each prime $p_k$, we want the probability that $p_k$ does not divide both $X$ and $Y$, so this is $1 - 1/p_k^{2s}$ by complementation.

$$$$

The events above are independent for varying $k$ from "Zeta Zonk II". Therefore, the probability that $X$ and $Y$ are relatively prime i.e. no prime divides both of them is $$\prod_{k=1}^{\infty} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{p_k^{2s}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\zeta(2s)}$$ This last product was evaluated by the result of "Zeta Zonk II". With the specified values, the answer is $90/\pi^4$.
hints: For $X$ and $Y$ to be relatively prime, they must share no common prime divisor. How can you use the previous parts to help?

title: Zeta Zonk V
statement:
We say that $X$ follows a Zeta$(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $$\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$$ Here, $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Suppose that $X \sim \text{Zeta}(s)$. For any positive integers $n$ and $k$, compute $\prob{X = kn \mid \{n \mid X\}}$. Compute this when $s = 2, n = 3,$ and $k = 2$. Return your answer to the nearest thousandth.

$$$$

Note: Complete Zeta Zonk I - IV before attempting this question.
solution: As this is a conditional probability statement, it's best to expand out the definition of conditional probability. $$\prob{X = kn \mid \{n \mid X\}} = \dfrac{\prob{X = kn, n \mid X}}{\prob{n \mid X}} = \dfrac{\prob{X = kn}}{\prob{n \mid X}}$$ From the previous parts, $\prob{n \mid X} = 1/n^s$. By applying the PMF of the Zeta$(s)$ distribution, $$\prob{X = kn} = \dfrac{1}{(kn)^s\zeta(s)} = \dfrac{1}{k^s \zeta(s)} \cdot \dfrac{1}{n^s}$$ Plugging these in and cancelling reveals $$\prob{X = kn \mid \{n \mid X\}} = \dfrac{1}{k^s\zeta(s)}$$ Thus, the conditional PMF of $X$ on multiples of $n$ given that $n \mid X$ is Zeta$(s)$ distributed. This makes intuitive sense, as this is exactly the PMF of $nX$. With the specified values, the answer is $\frac{1}{4\zeta(2)} = \frac{3}{2\pi^2}$.
hints: Apply the definition of conditional probability and reduce.

title: Zeta Zonk VI
statement:
We say that $X$ follows a Zeta$(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $$\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$$ Here, $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Suppose that $X,Y \sim \text{Zeta}(s)$ IID. Define $G$ to be the greatest common divisor (GCD) of $X$ and $Y$. For any positive integer $m$, compute $\prob{G = m}$. Evaluate when $s = 2$ and $m = 3$. Round your answer to the nearest thousandth.

$$$$

Note: Solve Zeta Zonk I - V before attempting this question.
solution:
For $X$ and $Y$ to have GCD $m$, $m$ must divide both $X$ and $Y$ and $X/m$ must be relatively prime to $Y/m$. If we knew that $m \mid X$ and $m \mid Y$, we can apply the result of "Zeta Zonk V" to know that the conditional distributions of $X$ and $Y$ given they are multiples of $m$ are still Zeta$(s)$ IID. Therefore, $$\prob{G = m} = \prob{\text{gcd}(X/m,Y/m) = 1 \mid \{m \mid X\} \cap \{m \mid Y\}}\prob{m \mid X}\prob{m \mid Y}$$ The last two terms are both $m^{-s}$ by our previous work. By the discussion above, the conditional distributions of $X/m$ and $Y/m$ given $m \mid X$ and $m \mid Y$ are Zeta$(s)$ IID. Therefore, the first term is just asking the probability that two IID Zeta$(s)$ distributions are relatively prime. By the result of "Zeta Zonk IV", the answer is $\dfrac{1}{\zeta(2s)}$. Plugging these in, $$\prob{G = m} = \dfrac{1}{m^{2s}\zeta(2s)}$$, and further plugging in for $s = 2$ and $m = 3$ yields,
$$\prob{G = m} = \dfrac{1}{3^{4}\zeta(4)} \approx 0.011$$
hints: For $X$ and $Y$ to have GCD $m$, $m$ must divide both $X$ and $Y$ and $X/m$ must be relatively prime to $Y/m$.

title: Zeta Zonk VII
statement:
We say that $X$ follows a Zeta$(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $$\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$$ Here, $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Let $N$ be the event that $X$ is $n-$free (i.e. every integer that is the $n$th power of some other integer that isn't $1$ does not divide $X$). Find $\mathbb{P}[N]$ when $s = 3/2$ and $n = 4$. Return your answer to the nearest thousandth.

$$$$

Note: Complete Zeta Zonk I - VI before attempting this question.
solution: We want the probability that $X$ is $n-$free. This means that no $n$th power divides $X$. However, the $n$th power of a positive integer has the same factors as the integer it is the $n$th power of. Since every positive integer has a unique prime factorization, we can just write this as the event that $X$ is not divisible by $p_k^n$ for any prime $p_k$. The probability that $p_k^n \mid X$ is just $1/(p_k^{n})^s = 1/p_k^{ns}$ by the same exact methodology of the previous parts. We showed previously the $D_k$ events are independent, so this also carries over to the $n$th powers. By independence, the probability $X$ is $n-$free is $$\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{p_i^{ns}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\zeta(ns)}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $945/\pi^6$.
