title: Zeta Zonk VIII
statement:
We say that $X$ follows a Zeta$(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $$\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$$ Here, $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Suppose that $X_1,\dots, X_n \sim \text{Zeta}(s)$ IID. Compute the probability that $X_1,\dots, X_n$ are coprime (i.e. the only positive integer dividing all of them is $1$) when $n = 3$ $s = 2$. Report your answer rounded to the nearest thousandth.

$$$$

Note: Complete Zeta Zonk I - VII before attempting this question.
solution:
For $X_1,\dots, X_n$ to be relatively prime, they must share no common prime divisor. From the previous parts, we know that $$\prob{p_k \mid X_1} = \dots = \prob{p_k \mid X_n} = \dfrac{1}{p_k^s}$$ Since $X_1,\dots, X_n$ are independent, the events $\{p_k \mid X_1\},\dots, \{p_k \mid X_n\}$ are independent. Therefore, the probability that $p_k$ divides $X_i$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$ is $1/p_k^{ns}$. For each prime $p_k$, we want the probability that $p_k$ does not divide all of the $X_i$, so this is $1 - 1/p_k^{ns}$ by complementation.

$$$$

The events above are independent for varying $k$ from "Zeta Zonk II". Therefore, the probability that $X_1,\dots, X_n$ are coprime i.e. no prime divides all of them is $$\prod_{k=1}^{\infty} \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{p_k^{ns}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\zeta(ns)}$$ This last product was evaluated by the result of "Zeta Zonk II". With the specified values, the answer is $945/\pi^6$.
hints: For $X_1,\dots, X_n$ to be relatively prime, they must share no common prime divisor. How can you use the previous parts to help?

title: Zeta Zonk IX
statement:
We say that $X$ follows a Zeta$(s)$ distribution if it has support on the positive integers with PMF $$\mathbb{P}[X=k] = \dfrac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)}$$ Here, $\zeta(s) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-s}$, and we require $s > 1$. Let $p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < \dots$ be all the prime integers. Suppose that $X,Y \sim \text{Zeta}(s)$ IID. Define $G$ to be the greatest common divisor (GCD) of $X_1,\dots, X_n$. For any positive integer $m$, compute $\prob{G = m}$. Evaluate when $s = 2, n = 3,$ and $m = 3$. Round your answer to the nearest thousandth.

$$$$

Note: Complete Zeta Zonk I - VIII before attempting this question.
solution: For $X_1,\dots, X_n$ to have GCD $m$, $m$ must divide all of $X_1,\dots, X_n$ and $X_1/m,\dots, X_n/m$ must be coprime. If we knew that $m \mid X_1,\dots,m \mid X_n$, we can apply the result of "Zeta Zonk V" to know that the conditional distributions of $X_1,\dots, X_n$ given they are multiples of $m$ are still Zeta$(s)$ IID. Therefore, $$\prob{G = m} = \prob{\text{gcd}(X_1/m,\dots, X_n/m) = 1 \mid \{m \mid X_1\} \cap \dots \cap \{m \mid X_n\}}\prob{m \mid X_1}\dots\prob{m \mid X_n}$$ The $n$ terms out back are all $m^{-s}$ by our previous work. By the discussion above, the conditional distributions of $X_1/m,\dots, X_n/m$ given $m \mid X_i$ for all $1 \leq i\leq n$ are Zeta$(s)$ IID. Therefore, the first term is just asking the probability that $n$ IID Zeta$(s)$ distributions are coprime. By the result of "Zeta Zonk VIII", the answer is $\dfrac{1}{\zeta(ns)}$. Plugging these in, $$\prob{G = m} = \dfrac{1}{m^{ns}\zeta(ns)}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{35}{27\pi^6}$.
hints: For $X_1,\dots, X_n$ to have GCD $m$, $m$ must divide all of $X_1,\dots, X_n$ and $X_1/m,\dots, X_n/m$ must be coprime.

title: Void Suits
statement: A casino deals deals you $13$ cards from a standard deck of $52$ cards. We say that a hand is void of a suit if it has no cards from that suit. Compute the probability that you are void in at least one suit. Round your answer the nearest thousandth.
solution:
Let's first frame this problem with events. First, arbitrarily label the suits $1-4$. This can be done because all suits have the same number of cards. For $k = 1,2,3,4$, let $A_k$ be the event that you are void in suit $k$. More simply stated, $A_k$ is the event that your hand has no card from suit $k$. The event
of being void in at least one suit is now $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup A_4$. We choose unions since it is an "at least" problem. Note that the events $A_1,\dots, A_4$ depend on one another: For example, the hand is void of three suits, it can't be void of the last suit. Therefore, complementation doesn't work. Instead, we apply the inclusion-exclusion formula. The probability of being void in a suit shouldn't depend on what the suit or suits we're void in, so the second special case of the inclusion-exclusion formula holds. 

$$$$

To compute the probabilities, consider the interpretation of each event. For example, for $A_1$ to occur, no cards from suit $1$ can be selected. Thus, $13$ cards must be selected from the other $52-13 = 39$ cards that are not of suit $1$, which can be done in $\binom{39}{13}$ ways. There are $\binom{52}{13}$ ways to pick $13$ cards with no restrictions. Similarly, for $A_1 \cap A_2$ to occur, the $13$ cards must come from the other $26$ cards that are of suits $3$ or $4$. Applying this logic yields 
$$\mathbb{P}[A_1] = \frac {{39\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}}, \quad \mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2] = \frac {{26\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}},$$
$$\mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3] = \frac {{13\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}},\quad \text{and} \quad \mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3\cap A_4]=0$$

$$$$

We can now apply the inclusion-exclusion formula directly.
$$\prob{\bigcup_{k=1}^4 A_k} = \binom{4}{1}\mathbb{P}[A_1] - \binom{4}{2} \mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2] +
\binom{4}{3} \mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2 \cap A_3] - \binom{4}{4} \mathbb{P}[A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3 \cap A_4]$$
$$=4\cdot \frac {{39\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}} - 6\cdot 
\frac {{26\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}} + 4\cdot \frac {{13\choose 13}}{{52\choose 13}} \approx 0.051$$
hints:
Let's first frame this problem with events. First, arbitrarily label the suits $1-4$. This can be done because all suits have the same number of cards. For $k = 1,2,3,4$, let $A_k$ be the event that you are void in suit $k$. More simply stated, $A_k$ is the event that your hand has no card from suit $k$. The event
of being void in at least one suit is now $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup A_4$. We choose unions since it is an "at least" problem. Note that the events $A_1,\dots, A_4$ depend on one another.

title: Big Up Chip
statement: A box has $n$ chips labeled with distinct numbers $1$ to $n$. You draw two chips at random without replacement and record their values. Find the probability that the larger of the two values is exactly $1 \leq k \leq n-1$ larger than the smaller of the two values. Evaluate this when $n = 10$ and $k = 4$.
solution: Since each pair of values is equally likely to be selected, we can compute the probability by counting. There are $\binom{n}{2}$ ways to pick two distinct chips. To have a difference of exactly $k$ between the chips, the chip values must be in the form $(i,i+k)$ for some value $i$. The possible values of $i$ are $1 \leq i \leq n-k$ to ensure that both bounds are within $\{1,2,\dots, n\}$. Therefore, the probability of selecting two chips with difference exactly $k$ is $$\dfrac{n-k}{\binom{n}{2}} = \dfrac{2(n-k)}{n(n-1)}$$With the specified values, the answer is $2/15$.
hints: To have a difference of exactly $k$ between the chips, the chip values must be in the form $(i,i+k)$ for some value $i$.

title: All and None
statement: Let $S$ be a set of $2^n$ elements. Suppose that $A_1,\dots, A_n$ are subsets of $S$ selected independently and uniformly at random from all $2^{2^n}$ subsets of $S$. Define $p(n)$ to be the probability that $\displaystyle \bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i = S$ and $\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^n A_i = \emptyset$. If it exists, determine $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} p(n)$ to the nearest thousandth. If this limit does not exist, report the answer $-1$.
solution:
To evaluate the limit, we should evaluate $p(n)$ for fixed $n$ first. For each $s \in S$, we want it to be in at least one of the sets $A_1,\dots, A_n$, but not all of them. Since the subset is selected uniformly at random, there is probability $1/2$ for each $s \in S$ of it being in $A_i$ or not in $A_i$ for all $i$.

$$$$

To compute the probability above for a singular $s \in S$, we should consider the complement, as we are looking at an "at least one" probability. The complement of being in at least one but not all is $s$ belongs to either none or all of $A_1,\dots, A_n$. By independence of the selected sets, the probability $s$ belongs to none of the $A_i$ sets is $1/2^n$. Similarly, the probability $s$ beongs to all of the $A_i$ sets is $1/2^n$. Thus, with probability $1 - (1/2^n + 1/2^n) = 1 - 1/2^{n-1}$, $s$ belongs to at least one and not all of $A_1,\dots, A_n$. Note that there are $2^n$ total elements in $S$. The decision of which of the $A_i$ sets a fixed $s$ belongs to is independent between elements. Therefore, the probability that this condition holds for all of the elements is given by $$p(n) = \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2^{n-1}}\right)^{2^n}$$ This limit looks similar to that of the definition of $e$. To evaluate this limit, we can apply the following lemma: If $\{a_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ and $\{b_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ are two sequences of real numbers such that $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_n = 0$ and $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} a_nb_n = c$, then $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\left(1 + a_n\right)^{b_n} = e^c$. This can be proved using the tools of an introductory calculus course. In this case, $a_n = -1/2^{n-1}$ and $b_n = 2^n$. These sequences satisfy the conditions, and $a_nb_n = -2$ for all $n$, meaning the limit is also $-2$. Therefore, $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} p(n) = e^{-2}$.

Since the subset is selected uniformly at random, there is probability $1/2$ for each $s \in S$ of it being in $A_i$ or not in $A_i$ for all $i$.

title: One Then Two
statement: Two fair standard $n-$sided dice are rolled until at least one $1$ appears. Upon stopping, find the probability that both dice show $1$ when $n = 8$.
solution: Since the dice are fair, we can convert this into a counting problem. The number of outcomes where both dice show $1$ is clearly $1$. To count the number of outcomes where at least one die shows the value $1$, we can apply complementation. This works because we are looking to count an "at least one" event. The complement of having at least one $1$ appear is having no $1$s appear. There are $n^2$ total outcomes without restrictions. If neither die is a $1$, then there are $n-1$ outcomes per die, so there are $(n-1)^2$ total outcomes without a $1$. Thus, $n^2 - (n-1)^2 = 2n-1$ outcomes have at least one $1$. Therefore, the probability is $\dfrac{1}{2n-1}$. With $n = 8$, the answer is $1/15$.
hints: How many outcomes have at least one $1$ appearing? How many have both ones appearing?

title: Nearest Diagonal I
statement: A point is selected uniformly at random from the unit square. Find the expected distance of the point to the $y = x$ line to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
Let $D$ be the distance to the $y=x$ line. We don't know the PDF of $D$ directly, which makes direct integration not possible. Instead, we can consider the tail integral formula $\ev{X} = \ctailsum{X}$. This is the best way because we don't know the PDF nor any direct symmetry in this scenario.

$$$$

In this scenario, we are looking at the perpendicular distance from the points to the diagonal. Thus, the maximum possible distance to the $y=x$ line occurs at $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$, which are both $1/\sqrt{2}$ distance away from the $y=x$ line, as the nearest point is $(1/2,1/2)$. To find the distance of a point $(x,y)$ from the line $ax + by + c = 0$, we can use the distance formula $$d(ax+by+c=0, (x,y)) = \dfrac{|ax + by + c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$$ In this case, $y = x$ can be written as $x-y = 0$, so the distance of a point $(x,y)$ to the line is given by $|x-y|/\sqrt{2}$. We can now express $D = |X-Y|/\sqrt{2}$. Using this, $$\{D \geq d\} = \left\{\dfrac{|X-Y|}{\sqrt{2}} \geq d\right\} = \{|X-Y| \geq d\sqrt{2}\}$$ Drawing this region out in the plane, we get two disjoint right triangles whose side lengths are $1-d\sqrt{2}$. Since $X$ and $Y$ are uniform, we can take a ratio of areas to compute probabilities. The area of the full support is $1$, while the area of the two triangles is given by $2 \cdot 1/2 (1-d\sqrt{2})^2 = (1-d\sqrt{2})^2$. Thus, $\prob{D \geq d} = (1-d\sqrt{2})^2$. Plugging this into the continuous tail integral formula yields $$\ev{D} = \int_0^{1/\sqrt{2}} (1-x\sqrt{2})^2~dx = \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}$$
hints: Let $D$ be the distance to the $y=x$ line. Consider the continuous tail expectation formula $\ev{X} = \ctailsum{X}$. What does the event $\{D \geq d\}$ look like, and what are the bounds on it?

title: Convolution Convergence I
statement: Let $X$ be a random variable with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Fix $0 < \lambda < 1$, and define the sequence of random variables as follows, where $'$ denotes an independent copy of the random variable: $Y_1 = \lambda X + (1-\lambda)X'$ and $Y_{n+1} = \lambda Y_n + (1-\lambda) Y_n'$. If it exists, compute $\displaystyle \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \ev{Y_n}$ when $\lambda = 1/3, \mu = 4,$ and $\sigma^2 = 9$. If the limit does not exist, enter $-100$.
solution: Since we know how to express $Y_n$ in terms of $Y_{n-1}$, we should relate the two expected values. By linearity of expectation, $$\ev{Y_n} = \ev{\lambda Y_{n-1} + (1-\lambda) Y_{n-1}'} = \lambda \ev{Y_{n-1}} + (1-\lambda)\ev{Y_{n-1}'} = \ev{Y_{n-1}}$$ The expected values combine because $Y_{n-1}$ and $Y_{n-1}'$ are IID. Therefore, $\ev{Y_n} = \ev{Y_1}$ for all $n$, and we know $$\ev{Y_1} = \ev{\lambda X + (1-\lambda) X'} = \lambda \ev{X} + (1-\lambda)\ev{X'} = \ev{X} = \mu$$ Therefore, the answer is $\mu$, as all terms in the sequence are $\mu$. The answer for the specified values given here is $4$.
hints: Can you find $\ev{Y_n}$ for general $n$ by linearity of expectation? You can express $Y_n$ in terms of $Y_{n-1}$.

title: Variable Gambler
statement: You got to Vegas successfully. They call you the variable gambler. You play a slot machine such that you win with probability $1/2$ your first turn. After the first turn, you win with probability $1/2$ if you lost the previous turn and with probability $0 < p < 1/2$ if you won the previous turn. Let $p_n$ be the probability that you win on the $n$th turn. Evaluate $p_4$ when $p = 1/3$.
solution:
The probability that you win on your current turn is dependent on whether you won or lost in the previous turn. Therefore, the best approach is to condition on whether you won or lost on the previous turn. If you won on the previous turn, which occurs with probability $p_{n-1}$, then you win with probability $p$ on this turn. Otherwise, if you lost on the previous turn, which occurs with probability $1-p_{n-1}$, you win on this turn with probability $1/2$. Applying the Law of Total Probability, we get $$p_n = pp_{n-1} + (1-p_{n-1})\cdot 1/2 \iff p_n = (p - 1/2)p_{n-1} + 1/2$$ To solve this recurrence, the best method is by differencing, as it has a constant of $1/2$ out back. This allows us to eliminate the constant. Since we will get to a term with $p_1$ in it, it helps to define $p_1 = 1/2$, which is consistent with the information in the question. We will derive a recurrence for $r_n = p_n - p_{n-1}$. Namely, $$p_n - p_{n-1} = \left[(p - 1/2)p_{n-1} + 1/2\right] - \left[(p - 1/2)p_{n-2} + 1/2\right] = (p-1/2)(p_{n-1} - p_{n-2})$$ This is now a fairly easy recurrence to solve. Namely, we get that $$p_n - p_{n-1} = (p-1/2)(p_{n-1} - p_{n-2}) = (p-1/2)^2(p_{n-2} - p_{n-3}) = \dots = (p-1/2)^{n-2}(p_{2} - p_{1})$$ Recall that $p_1 = 1/2$ from the above. We can use the recurrence to obtain $p_2 = 1/2 \cdot p + 1/2 \cdot 1/2 = (2p+1)/4$, so $p_2 - p_1 = (2p-1)/4$. We now have a simple recurrence to solve, since the term out back is summable. Namely,
\begin{align*}
    p_n &= p_{n-1} + \dfrac{2p-1}{4} \cdot \left(p - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-2}\\
    &= p_{n-2} +  \dfrac{2p-1}{4} \cdot\left[ \left(p - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-3} + \left(p - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-2}\right]\\
    &= \dots \\
    &= p_1 + \dfrac{2p-1}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{n-2} \left(p - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{k}\\
    &= \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{2p-1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{1-(p-1/2)^{n-1}}{1-(p-1/2)}\\
    &=\dfrac{1-(p-1/2)^n}{3-2p}
\end{align*}

$$$$

The geometric series formula was used with common ratio $p - 1/2$. With the specified values, the answer is $\dfrac{185}{432}$.
hints: The probability that you win on your current turn is dependent on whether you won or lost the previous turn. Condition on whether you won or lost on the previous turn.

title: Arc Up I
statement: Two points are selected uniformly at random from the circumference of a semi-circle of radius $1$, including the diameter at the bottom. Find the probability that exactly one point lies on the diameter to the nearest thousandth.
solution: The length of the diameter is $2$, while the length of the circular portion is $\pi$. Thus, the total length is $2 + \pi$. By the uniformity of the selection, the probability that any given point lands on the diameter is $\frac{2}{2 + \pi}$, while the probability it lands on the circular portion is $\frac{\pi}{2+\pi}$. There are $2$ ways to arrange the points between the portions (first one diameter and second circular, or vice-versa). By independence of the points, the probability of exactly one point in each region is $$2 \cdot \dfrac{2}{2 + \pi} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2 + \pi} = \dfrac{4\pi}{(2+\pi)^2} \approx 0.475$$
hints: What is the total length of the perimeter of the circle, including the diameter?

title: Lotto I
statement: Let $N > 0$ be fixed. $2N$ people play the lottery each week. Each of the people are assigned a uniformly random integer in $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$, independently of other people. One of the $N$ integers is selected uniformly at random to be the winning value. Let $W_N$ be the random variable that counts the number of people that win the lottery in a given week. Compute $\displaystyle \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \prob{W_N \leq 3}$ to the nearest thousandth.
solution: For a fixed $N$, $W_N$ counts the number of successes in $2N$ independent trials (people). The success probability is $1/N$, as one of the $N$ values is the correct one. Therefore, $W_N \sim \binomial{2N}{1/N}$. Note that as $N \rightarrow \infty$, the success probability is tending to $0$. Since we have a limit of Binomial random variables that have trials tending to $\infty$ and success probabilities tending to $0$, we should consider the Poisson limit theorem. The means of the Binomial distributions converge to $2$. Therefore, by the Poisson limit theorem, $\displaystyle \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \prob{W_N \leq 3} = \prob{X \leq 3}$, where $X \sim \poisson{2}$. Using the PMF of $X$, $$\prob{X \leq 3} = \prob{X = 0} + \prob{X = 1} + \prob{X = 2} + \prob{X = 3} = \dfrac{19}{3e^2}$$
hints: For a fixed $N$, what is the distribution of $W_N$? Can you use some limit theorem here?

title: Lotto II
statement: Let $N > 0$ be fixed. $2N$ people play the lottery each week. Each of the people are assigned a uniformly random integer in $\{1,2,\dots,N\}$, independently of other people. One of the $N$ integers is selected uniformly at random to be the winning value. Given that you, one of the participants, has a winning ticket, find the expected number of winning tickets when $N = 10$.
solution: For a fixed $N$, $W_N$ counts the number of successes in $2N$ independent trials (people). The success probability is $1/N$, as one of the $N$ values is the correct one. However, we are given the information that you won. Therefore, the total number of people that won, is $1 + X$, where $X \sim \binom{2N-1}{1/N}$, as we already know that you won, so there are $2N-1$ people that remain. By linearity of expectation, the expected number of people that win is $$\ev{1+X} = 1 + \ev{X} = 1 + (2N-1) \cdot \dfrac{1}{N} = 3 - \dfrac{1}{N}$$ With $N = 10$, the answer is $2.9$.
hints: We are looking to count the number of winners among the $2N$. Among the other $2N-1$ people, what is the distribution of the number of winners?

title: Die Duo I
statement: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. Both dice are fair in the sense that each side appears with probability $1/6$. While your die is a standard fair $6-$sided die, your friend's die has the values $111666$ on the sides. Both of you roll the die one time. Find the probability that you roll a strictly higher value than your friend.
solution: To roll strictly higher than your friend, they must obtain a $1$ on their die, as it's not possible for your to obtain a strictly larger value than $6$. Your friend rolls $1$ with probability $1/2$. Given your friend rolls a $1$, you must obtain some value strictly larger than $1$. This occurs with probability $5/6$ on your die, as all outcomes but $1$ are strictly better than your friend's roll. Therefore, the answer is $5/6 \cdot 1/2 = 5/12$.
hints: Is it possible to roll strictly higher if your friend obtains a $6$?

title: Container Circle I
statement: $n$ points are independently selected uniformly at random from the interior of the unit circle. Find the expected area of the largest circle centered at the origin that contains no points when $n = 4$ to the nearest thousandth.
solution: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the circle. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and radius are related. The largest circle that doesn't contain any points would have a radius equal to the minimum distance of any points from the origin. Thus, the area of this circle is $A = \pi R^2$, where $R = \min\{R_1,\dots, R_n\}$ and $R_1,\dots, R_n$ are the IID distances of the selected points from the origin. The maximum possible area of the circle is $\pi$, as that would be the entire region itself. Therefore, we integrate on $(0,\pi)$ and obtain $$\ev{A} = \int_0^{\pi} \prob{A \geq x}~dx = \int_0^{\pi} \prob{\pi R^2 \geq x}~dx = \int_0^{\pi} \prob{R \geq \sqrt{\dfrac{x}{\pi}}}~dx$$ The event $\left\{R \geq \sqrt{\frac{x}{\pi}}\right\}$ means that no point lies within a distance of $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ of the origin. Since the points are selected uniformly at random, we can take ratios of areas to compute probabilities. The area of the region more than $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ from the origin is $\pi\left(1 - (\sqrt{x/\pi})^2\right)$, as the collection of points whose distance is at most $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ from the origin is a circle of radius $\sqrt{x/\pi}$. We used the complement to compute the area. The total area of the region is $\pi$, so the probability of any given point being a distance more than $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ away from the origin is $1 - x/\pi$ by dividing. Since there are $n$ independently selected points that all must satisfy this condition to ensure the minimum distance is at least $\sqrt{x/\pi}$, $$\prob{A \geq x}  = \prob{R \geq \sqrt{\dfrac{x}{\pi}}} = \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{\pi}\right)^n$$ Plugging this into the integral with the $u-$substitution $u = x/\pi$, we get $$\ev{A} = \int_0^{\pi} \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{\pi}\right)^n~dx = \pi \int_0^1 (1-u)^n ~du = \dfrac{\pi}{n+1}$$ With $n = 4$, the answer is $\pi/5$.
hints: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the circle. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and radius are related. The largest circle that doesn't contain any points would have a radius equal to the minimum distance of any points from the origin.

title: Container Circle II
statement: $n$ points are independently selected uniformly at random from the interior of the unit circle. Find the expected area of the smallest circle centered at the origin that contains all $n$ points when $n = 4$ to the nearest thousandth.
solution: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the circle. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and radius are related. The smallest circle that contains all the points would have a radius equal to the maximum distance of any points from the origin. Thus, the area of this circle is $A = \pi R^2$, where $R = \max\{R_1,\dots, R_n\}$ and $R_1,\dots, R_n$ are the IID distances of the selected points from the origin. The maximum possible area of the circle is $\pi$, as that would be the entire region itself. Therefore, we integrate on $(0,\pi)$ and obtain $$\ev{A} = \int_0^{\pi} \prob{A \geq x}~dx = \int_0^{\pi} \prob{\pi R^2 \geq x}~dx = \int_0^{\pi} \prob{R \geq \sqrt{\dfrac{x}{\pi}}}~dx$$ Since $R$ is now defined as a maximum, it's better to consider events of the form $\{R < x\}$, as we can apply the "all points satisfy this condition" argument from the previous example. By complementation, $$\prob{R \geq \sqrt{\dfrac{x}{\pi}}} = 1 - \prob{R < \sqrt{\dfrac{x}{\pi}}}$$ The event $\left\{R < \sqrt{\frac{x}{\pi}}\right\}$ means that all of the points lie within a distance of $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ of the origin. Since the points are selected uniformly at random, we can take ratios of areas to compute probabilities. The area of the region within $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ from the origin is $\pi \cdot (\sqrt{x/\pi})^2 = x$, as the collection of points whose distance is at most $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ from the origin is a circle of radius $\sqrt{x/\pi}$. The total area of the region is $\pi$, so the probability of any given point being a distance at most $\sqrt{x/\pi}$ away from the origin is $x/\pi$ by dividing. Since there are $n$ independently selected points that all must satisfy this condition to ensure the maximum distance is at most $\sqrt{x/\pi}$, $$\prob{A \geq x} = \prob{R \geq \sqrt{\dfrac{x}{\pi}}} =  1 - \prob{R \geq \sqrt{\dfrac{x}{\pi}}} = 1 - \left(\dfrac{x}{\pi}\right)^n$$ Plugging this into the integral, we get $$\ev{A} = \int_0^{\pi} 1 - \left(\dfrac{x}{\pi}\right)^n~dx = \pi - \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_0^{\pi} x^n~dx = \dfrac{n\pi}{n+1}$$ With $n = 4$, the answer is $\dfrac{4\pi}{5}$.
hints: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the circle. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and radius are related. The largest circle that doesn't contain any points would have a radius equal to the minimum distance of any points from the origin.

title: Container Square I
statement: $n$ points are independently selected uniformly at random from the interior of the square centered at the origin with vertices at $(\pm 1,\pm 1)$. Find the expected area of the largest square centered at the origin that contains no points when $n = 9$.
solution: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the square. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and side length are related. The largest square that doesn't contain any points would have a side length equal to the minimum distance (either vertically or horizontally) of any points from the origin. Thus, the area of this square is $A = (2S)^2$, where $S$ is the closest point to the origin either horizontally or vertically. Note that $S$ will only take values in $(0,1)$, as the square only extends $1$ unit in each direction. The maximum possible area of the square is $4$, as that would be the entire region itself. Therefore, we integrate on $(0,4)$ and obtain $$\ev{A} = \int_0^{4} \prob{A \geq x}~dx = \int_0^{4} \prob{4S^2 \geq x}~dx = \int_0^{4} \prob{S \geq \sqrt{x}/2}~dx$$ The event $\left\{S \geq \sqrt{x}/2\right\}$ means that no point lies within a distance of $\sqrt{x}/2$  of the origin horizontally nor vertically. Since the points are selected uniformly at random, we can take ratios of areas to compute probabilities. The forbidden region of the points is the square with side length $\sqrt{x}$, as the square extends in both directions. The area of the region more than $\sqrt{x}/2$ from the origin horizontally and vertically is $4 - x$, as the total area of the square is $4$ and the area of the square with side lengths $\sqrt{x}$ is $x$. We used the complement to compute the area. The probability of any given point being a distance more than $\sqrt{x}/2$ away from the origin in all directions is $1 - x/4$ by dividing. Since there are $n$ independently selected points that all must satisfy this condition to ensure the minimum distance is at least $\sqrt{x}/2$, $$\prob{A \geq x}  = \prob{S \geq \sqrt{x}/2} = \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{4}\right)^n$$ Plugging this into the integral with the $u-$substitution $u = x/4$, we get $$\ev{A} = \int_0^{4} \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{4}\right)^n~dx = 4 \int_0^1 (1-u)^n ~du = \dfrac{4}{n+1}$$ With $n = 4$, the answer is $2/5$.
hints: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the square. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and side length are related. The largest square that doesn't contain any points would have a side length equal to the minimum distance (either vertically or horizontally) of any points from the origin.

title: Container Square II
statement: $n$ points are independently selected uniformly at random from the interior of the square centered at the origin with vertices at $(\pm 1,\pm 1)$. Find the expected area of the smallest square centered at the origin that contains all $n$ points when $n = 9$.
solution: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the square. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and side length are related. The smallest square that contains all $n$ points would have a side length equal to the maximum distance (either vertically or horizontally) of any points from the origin. Thus, the area of this square is $A = (2S)^2$, where $S$ is the furthest point to the origin either horizontally or vertically. Note that $S$ will only take values in $(0,1)$, as the square only extends $1$ unit in each direction. The maximum possible area of the square is $4$, as that would be the entire region itself. Therefore, we integrate on $(0,4)$ and obtain $$\ev{A} = \int_0^{4} \prob{A \geq x}~dx = \int_0^{4} \prob{4S^2 \geq x}~dx = \int_0^{4} \prob{S \geq \sqrt{x}/2}~dx$$ Since $S$ is now defined as a maximum, it's better to consider events of the form $\{S < x\}$, as we can apply the "all points satisfy this condition" argument from the previous example. By complementation, $$\prob{S \geq \sqrt{x}/2} = 1 - \prob{S < \sqrt{x}/2}$$ Since the points are selected uniformly at random, we can take ratios of areas to compute probabilities. The event $\{S < \sqrt{x}/2\}$ means that all $n$ points lie within a distance of $\sqrt{x}/2$ vertically and horizontally of the origin. In other words, they lie within the square of side length $\sqrt{x}$ centered at the origin, as the square extends in both directions. The area of the region at most $\sqrt{x}/2$ from the origin horizontally and vertically is $x$. The total area of the square is $4$. The probability of any given point being within a distance of $\sqrt{x}/2$ from the origin in all directions is $x/4$ by dividing. Since there are $n$ independently selected points that all must satisfy this condition to ensure the maximum distance is at most $\sqrt{x}/2$, $$\prob{A \geq x}  = 1 - \prob{A < x}  = 1 - \prob{S \leq \sqrt{x}/2}\prob{S \geq \sqrt{x}/2} = 1 - \left(\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^n$$ Plugging this into the integral, we get $$\ev{A} = \int_0^{4} 1-\left(\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^n~dx = 4  - \dfrac{1}{4^n}\int_0^4 x^n ~dx = \dfrac{4n}{n+1}$$ With $n = 9$, the answer is $18/5$.
hints: Each of the points is selected uniformly at random from the square. Finding the expected distance from the origin isn't a difficult task and can be computed using the tail integral formula for expected value. This approach also works here, as the area and side length are related. The smallest square that contains all $n$ points would have a side length equal to the maximum distance (either vertically or horizontally) of any points from the origin.

title: Mean Point
statement: $n$ independent points $P_i = (X_i,Y_i)$ are selected uniformly at random from the boundary of the unit circle. Define $\overline{X} = \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ and $\overline{Y} = \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$. Compute $\cov{\overline{X}}{\overline{Y}}$ when $n = 10$.
solution:
The first important question is: How can we model $X_i$ and $Y_i$ with relation to the selected point. We know that a random point on the circumference can be modelled as $U \sim \unif{0}{2\pi}$, a uniformly random angle. The cosine of this angle would be the $x-$coordinate, while the sine is the $y-$coordinate. In other words, we select $U_1,\dots, U_n \sim \unif{0}{2\pi}$, and define two random variables $X_i = \cos{U_i}$ and $Y_i = \sin(U_i)$ for each $1 \leq i \leq n$. Since $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$ are defined as sums of random variables, bilinearity of covariance is the best approach here. $$\cov{\overline{X}}{\overline{Y}} = \cov{\dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i}{\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n Y_j} = \dfrac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \cov{X_i}{Y_j}$$ For $i \neq j$, $X_i$ and $Y_j$ concern different points, which are independent. Therefore, all terms when $i \neq j$ evaluate to $0$ in the sum. This sum reduces to $\dfrac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \cov{X_i}{Y_i}$. This problem now reduces to computing $\cov{X_i}{Y_i} = \cov{\cos{U_i}}{\sin(U_i)}$.

$$$$

Since there is no immediately clear way of computing this with some trick, using the classic expansion of covariance is the best approach. By expanding the definition and substituting, $$\cov{X_i}{Y_i} = \ev{\cos(U_i)\sin(U_i)} - \ev{\cos(U_i)}\ev{\sin(U_i)}$$ We know the PDF of $U \sim \unif{0}{2\pi}$, so these are easy to calculate. Firstly, $$\mathbb{E}[\sin(U_i)] = \displaystyle \int_0^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{2\pi} \cdot \sin(u) ~du = 0$$ This can also be seen by noting we are integrating a sine curve over a full period. For the first term, $$\mathbb{E}[\sin(U_i)\cos(U_i)] = \displaystyle \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} \sin(u)\cos(u)~du =  0$$ Alternatively, one can note that cosine and sine are orthogonal functions in the context of Fourier analysis, so the integral is $0$. Since both terms vanish, $\cov{X_i}{Y_i} = 0$ for each $1 \leq i \leq n$, meaning the answer to this question is also $0$.
hints: How can we model $X_i$ and $Y_i$ with relation to the point? What is $\cov{X_i}{Y_i}$?

title: Non-Transitive Dice I
statement: Let $A,B,$ and $C$ be three fair $6-$sided dice. $A$ has the three values $2,6,$ and $7$ on two sides each. $B$ has the three values $1,5,$ and $9$ on two sides each. $C$ has the three values $3,4,$ and $8$ on two sides each. Find the probability $A$ shows a strictly higher value than $B$.
solution: If we knew the value that $B$ showed, it would be easy to compute this probability. Therefore, the idea is to condition on the value of $B$ and find the number of outcomes for $A$ in each case where the condition is satisfied. Let $H$ be the event that $A$ shows a larger value. By Law of Total Probability, $$\mathbb{P}[H] = \mathbb{P}[H \mid 1]\mathbb{P}[1] + \mathbb{P}[H \mid 2]\mathbb{P}[5] + \mathbb{P}[H \mid 9]\mathbb{P}[9]$$ Since both dice are fair, $\mathbb{P}[1] = \mathbb{P}[5] = \mathbb{P}[9] = 1/3$. If there $1$ is rolled, all values on $A$ are larger, so $\mathbb{P}[H \mid 1] = 1$. If $5$ is rolled, $6$ and $7$ are larger, so $\mathbb{P}[H \mid 5] = 2/3$. If a $9$ is rolled, none of the values are larger, so $\mathbb{P}[H \mid 9] = 0$. Plugging these in, the answer is $\prob{H} = 5/9$.
hints: If we knew the value that $B$ showed, it would be easy to compute this probability. Therefore, the idea is to condition on the value of $B$ and find the number of outcomes for $A$ in each case where the condition is satisfied.

title: Game Off I
statement: Suppose $0 < p < 1$. Alice and Bob play game. The game consists of $3$ points. For the first point of each game, Alice has probability $p$ of winning, while Bob has probability $1-p$ of winning. For the other two points of the game, the winner of the previous round has probability $p$ of winning, while the loser has probability $1-p$ of winning. A winner is declared when someone wins two consecutive points. If neither player wins two consecutive points, the entire game replayed under the same rules until a winner is declared. Find the probability that Bob wins when $p = 1/3$.
solution:
This game is repeatedly played until a winner is declared. This implies that a recursive approach is best, as Bob's probability of winning the game is dependent on what happens during the first round. Let $b$ be Bob's probability of winning the game. For Bob to immediately win on the first round of the game, he must obtain two consecutive wins. This means the three points of the game must have either gone $BB$ or $ABB$, where $A$ and $B$ are points for Alice and Bob, respectively. The first case ($BB$) has probability $p(1-p)$, as Bob wins the first game with probability $1-p$, and since he won the first game, he wins the second game with probability $p$. The second case ($ABB$) occurs with probability $p^2(1-p)$ by similar logic. Adding these together, the probability that Bob wins immediately on the first round is $p(1-p) + p^2(1-p) = p(1-p^2)$. 

$$$$

The other way that Bob can win is by a tie. If there is a tie, the entire game restarts, and there is probability $b$ that he wins. For a tie to occur, the results must be in the form $ABA$ or $BAB$, as neither player can win twice consecutively. The probability of these two cases, by identical logic to the above, are $p(1-p)^2$ and $(1-p)^3$. The sum of these is $(1-p)^2$. By the Law of Total Probability and solving for $b$, $$b = p(1-p^2) + (1-p)^2b \iff b = \dfrac{p(1-p^2)}{1-(1-p)^2} = \dfrac{p(1-p^2)}{p(2-p)} = \dfrac{1-p^2}{2-p}$$ The recurrence arises from the fact that with probability $p(1-p^2)$, Bob immediately wins, while with probability $(1-p)^2$, there is a rematch, so the game "probabilistically restarts" and is identical to where it was at the start. Note that $p \neq 0$ because we cancelled a $p$ from the numerator and denominator. With $p = 1/3$, the answer is $8/15$.
hints: This game is repeatedly played until a winner is declared. This implies that a recursive approach is best, as Bob's probability of winning the game is dependent on what happens during the first round. Let $b$ be Bob's probability of winning the game. Derive a recurrence for $b$.

title: Game Off II
statement: Suppose $0 < p < 1$. Alice and Bob play game. The game consists of $3$ points. For the first point of each game, Alice has probability $p$ of winning, while Bob has probability $1-p$ of winning. For the other two points of the game, the winner of the previous round has probability $p$ of winning, while the loser has probability $1-p$ of winning. A winner is declared when someone wins two consecutive points. If neither player wins two consecutive points, the entire game replayed under the same rules until a winner is declared. If Alice wins the game, Bob pays her $\$1$. Assuming the game is fair, how much should Alice pay Bob if he wins when $p = 2/3$?
solution: From "Game Off I", we know the probability that Bob wins the game is $\frac{1-p^2}{2-p}$. By complementation, Alice wins the game with probability $1-  \frac{1-p^2}{2-p} = \frac{p^2 - p + 1}{2-p}$. Our goal is to find the value $k$ such that the expected profit/loss from the game is $\$0$ for both players. We will compute the expected value from Bob's perspective. He wins with probability $\frac{1-p^2}{2-p}$, in which he receives $\$k$. Otherwise, he loses with probability $\frac{p^2 - p + 1}{2-p}$, in which he pays $\$1$. By applying the definition of expected value directly, $$\dfrac{1-p^2}{2-p} \cdot k +  \dfrac{p^2 - p + 1}{2-p} \cdot (-1) = 0 \iff k = \dfrac{p^2 - p + 1}{1-p^2}$$ With $p = 2/3$, the answer is $\$1.40$.
hints: From "Game Off I", we know the probability that Bob wins the game is $\frac{1-p^2}{2-p}$. What is the probability Alice wins? Calculate the expected value directly.

title: Game Off III
statement: Alice and Bob play game. The game consists of $3$ points. For the first point of each game, Alice has probability $p$ of winning, while Bob has probability $1-p$ of winning. For the other two points of the game, the winner of the previous round has probability $p$ of winning, while the loser has probability $1-p$ of winning. A winner is declared when someone wins two consecutive points. If neither player wins two consecutive points, the entire game replayed under the same rules until a winner is declared. When $p = 0$, what is the probability that Bob wins the game?
solution: When $p = 0$, the person who lost the previous game wins the next game. In this case, Bob wins the first game guaranteed. Therefore, the sequence $BAB$ for points will always occur, meaning that the game never ends. This implies the probability Bob wins i.e. ever gets two consecutive points is $0$, as the game will just always restart back to the initial state.
hints: Run through the situation of one game in your head and see what happens

title: Love Island Lighting I
statement:
The Love Island villa has a very complex lighting system. For the swimming pool light to be on, a particular light in the bedroom and a particular light in the hallway must be on. There are $4$ identical switches in each of the bedroom and kitchen. As they are identical, it's not possible to determine which are on/off nor what they control. 

$$$$

The villa is cleaned every Monday morning, and all the switches in the bedroom are set to be on or off. All the switches are on with probability $0 < p < 1$. In the kitchen, each individual switch is set to be on or off with probability $1/2$, independently of all other switches. A new islander enters the villa after it's cleaned and selects one switch uniformly at random from both the kitchen and bedroom and flicks them in the opposite direction. Given that the light is on afterwards, find the probability that the new islander switched the swimming pool light in the bedroom. Evaluate this probability when $p = 1/3$.
solution:
There are a ton of moving parts in this question, so let's break it down into events. Let $O$ be the event that the swimming pool light is on, while $B$ is the event that the islander switched the swimming pool light in the bedroom. Our goal is to compute $\prob{B \mid O} = \frac{\prob{B \cap O}}{\prob{O}}$. 

$$$$

For the numerator, $\prob{B \cap O}$ is the probability that the bedroom light for the swimming pool is switched and the pool light is on at the end. It's helpful to compute this probability given that we flipped the bedroom light for the swimming pool. By the product rule of probability, $\prob{B \cap O} = \prob{O \mid B}\prob{B}$. Only one of the four switches in the bedroom controls the swimming pool, so $\prob{B} = 1/4$. 


$$$$

As for $\prob{O \mid B}$, if the swimming pool light is to be on at the end and we know we flipped the bedroom pool light, two things must have been true: The bedroom lights were initially off (occurs with probability $1-p$), and the kitchen pool light must be on. Note that this occurs with probability $1/2$: If the kitchen pool light is initially on (probability $1/2$), then you can swap any other switch (probability $3/4$). If the kitchen pool light is initially off (probability $1/2$), you must flip that one on (probability $1/4$). Adding these two cases together yields the answer of $1/2$. By multiplying all of the above quantities, $\prob{B \cap O} = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot (1-p) = \frac{1-p}{8}$. As for the denominator, we condition on $B$ and use our work from the numerator. This yields $$\prob{O} = \prob{O \mid B}\prob{B} + \prob{O \mid B^c}\prob{B^c}$$ The first term is exactly the numerator. As for the second term, $\prob{B^c} = 3/4$ by complementation. For the pool light to be on given the pool switch in the bedroom wasn't touched, all lights must have initially been on in the bedroom (probability $p$) and the pool light from kitchen must be on (probability $1/2$ by previous work). Thus, $$\prob{O} = \dfrac{1-p}{8} + p \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{2p+1}{8}$$ Plugging these into the conditional probability formula yields $$\prob{B \mid O} = \dfrac{1-p}{1+2p}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $2/5$.
hints: There are a ton of moving parts in this question, so let's break it down into events. Let $O$ be the event that the swimming pool light is on, while $B$ is the event that the islander switched the swimming pool light in the bedroom. Our goal is to compute $\prob{B \mid O} = \frac{\prob{B \cap O}}{\prob{O}}$. For the numerator, $\prob{B \cap O}$ is the probability that the bedroom light for the swimming pool is switched and the pool light is on at the end. It's helpful to compute this probability given that we flipped the bedroom light for the swimming pool.

title: Low Variance Measure
statement: We have two rods of lengths $a$ and $b$. However, we only have a noisy measure of each rod. The independent random observed lengths $A$ and $B$ of the two rods are such that $\ev{A} = a, \ev{B} = b,$ and $\var{A} = \var{B} = \sigma^2$. You measure the rods in the following way: Take $U = A+B$ and $V = A-B$, and define $\hat{a} = \frac{U+V}{2}$. When $a = 12, b = 710$ and $\sigma^2 = 16$, report $\var{\hat{a}}$.
solution: We can first check that $\hat{a}$ is an unbiased estimate for $a$ i.e. that $\ev{\hat{a}} = a$. By linearity of expectation, $$\ev{\hat{a}} = \ev{\dfrac{U+V}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\ev{U} + \dfrac{1}{2}\ev{V} = \dfrac{1}{2}\ev{A+B} + \dfrac{1}{2}\ev{A-B} = \ev{A} = a$$ Now, we use the properties of variance to see that $$\var{\hat{a}} = \var{\dfrac{U+V}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4}\var{U+V} = \dfrac{\var{U} + \var{V} + 2\cov{U}{V}}{4}$$ Since $U = A+B$, where $A$ and $B$ are independent, we should apply the properties of variance/covariance to compute the terms. We can use the linearity of variance on independent random variables to conclude $\var{U} = \var{A} + \var{B} = 2\sigma^2$. Similarly, $\var{V} = \var{A} + \var{B} = 2\sigma^2$. Lastly, $$\cov{U}{V} = \cov{A+B}{A-B} = \var{A} - \var{B} = 0$$ Therefore, $\var{\hat{a}} = \sigma^2$ after plugging in all of the quantities above. This shows that measuring together doesn't improve the accuracy/reduce variance of the measurement of each individual rod. Alternatively, by substituting in the definitions of $U$ and $V$ into the original term, one can see that $$\var{\hat{a}} = \var{\dfrac{(A+B) + (A-B)}{2}} = \var{A} = \sigma^2$$ With the specified values, the answer is $16$.
hints: We can first check that $\hat{a}$ is an unbiased estimate for $a$ i.e. that $\ev{\hat{a}} = a$. Use the properties of variance and covariance here, as $U$ and $V$ are defined as sums.

title: Mixed Coin
statement: Alice and Bob each have a coin. Alice's coin has probability $0 < p < 1/2$ of showing heads, while Bob's coin has probability $2p$ of showing heads. Let $A$ and $B$ be the indicator random variables of Alice and Bob having their respective coins show heads when flipped once. Find the value of $\lambda$ that minimizes the variance of $T_{\lambda} = \lambda A + \dfrac{1-\lambda}{2}B$ when $p = 1/3$.
solution: As we are looking to minimize a quantity, the approach is to find the variance of $T_{\lambda}$ as a function of $\lambda$ and take the derivative with respect to $\lambda$. By the variance of a sum formula, the fact that $A$ and $B$ are independent, and $\var{X} = p(1-p)$, when $X \sim \bern{p}$, $$f(\lambda) = \var{T_{\lambda}} = \var{\lambda A} + \var{\dfrac{1-\lambda}{2}B} = \lambda^2p(1-p) + \dfrac{(1-\lambda)^2}{4}2p(1-2p) = \dfrac{p}{2}\left[2\lambda^2 - 2p\lambda^2 + (1-\lambda)^2(1-2p)\right]$$ Now that we have a function representing $\var{T_{\lambda}}$, we just need to minimize it in $\lambda$. Taking the derivative and setting it equal to $0$, we get $$\dfrac{d}{d\lambda}(f(\lambda)) = -p + 2p^2 + 3\lambda p - 4\lambda p^2 = 0 \iff p = \dfrac{1-2p}{3-4p}$$ With the specified values, the optimal value of $\lambda$ is $1/5$.
hints: Find the variance of $T_{\lambda}$ as a function of $\lambda$ and take a derivative.

title: Summed Dice I
statement: Suppose you have two $6-$sided fair dice. You can assign numbers to the sides in any way you please. Is it possible to assign values to the sides such that the sums $\{1,2,\dots, 12\}$ each appear with probability $1/12$? If so, report $1$. If not, report $0$.
solution: The key here is to imagine being in the ranges $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ and $\{7,8,9,10,11,12\}$ with equal probability. This should be true because these sets are of the same size. Note that each value in the other set is $6$ larger than some value in the first set. Thus, one of the dice should take the values $0$ and $6$ with probability $1/2$ each. This die would be $000666$. Obtaining $0$ puts you in the first set, while obtaining $6$ appears in the second set. Once the set is selected, we can select uniformly at random from it. In other words, the other die can just be a standard fair die with sides $123456$. Since we have found an example that works, the answer is $1$.
hints: Imagine being in the ranges $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ and $\{7,8,9,10,11,12\}$ with equal probability. How can this be achieved?

title: Gamma Coding I
statement:
Gamma coding is a method to encode positive integers as strings of $0$ and $1$ (called bits) such that no encoding is a prefix of any other encoding. To encode an integer $x \geq 1$, you perform three steps: $\hspace{3pt}$ 1) Define $N = \floor{\log_2(x)}$ $\hspace{3pt}$ 2) Write out $N$ bits that are $0$ $\hspace{3pt}$ 3) Write out $x$ in binary form, which is an $(N+1)-$bit string.

$$$$

For example, $7 = 111$ becomes $00111$ in Gamma code, while $21 = 10101$ becomes $000010101$. We can combine Gamma codes into strings, and read off the components left to right. For example, $000110100011000100110011110101$ decodes to $$\textcolor{red}{0001101}\textcolor{blue}{0001100}\textcolor{orange}{010}\textcolor{green}{011}\textcolor{pink}{00111}1\textcolor{gray}{010}\textcolor{yellow}{1} = \textcolor{red}{13},\textcolor{blue}{12},\textcolor{orange}{2},\textcolor{green}{3},\textcolor{pink}{7},1,\textcolor{gray}{2},\textcolor{yellow}{1}$$ We note the pattern by seeing the number of zeroes that lead (which is $N$), and then consider the next $N+1$ digits to be our number in binary. Each of these individual component numbers are called codewords. We create an infinite string of $0$ and $1$ bits, where each spot is $1$ with probability $0 < p < 1$. Let $F$ be the length of the first codeword in our string. In the above example, $F$ would be $7$. Find $\ev{F}$ when $p = 1/3$.
solution: The length of the codeword is dependent on the number of leading zeroes it has. Therefore, we want to first find the distribution of the number of zeroes that lead the string. Let $Z$ be the number of leading zeroes the string has. As $Z$ counts the number of zeroes that occur before the first $1$, we should think about the Geometric distribution. However, $Z$ isn't exactly Geometric, as it counts the number of zeroes that come strictly before the first $1$. If the first $1$ occurs on the $n$th trial, $n-1$ zeroes come before it, so $Z = O - 1$, where $O \sim \geom{p}$ counts the location of the first $1$ in the string. The total length of the first codeword is $L = 2Z + 1$, as the first codeword consists of $Z$ zeroes and $Z+1$ digits that come after. By linearity of expected value, $$\ev{L} = \ev{2Z+1} = 2\ev{Z} + 1 = 2(\ev{O} - 1) + 1 = \dfrac{2}{p}-1$$ With $p = 1/3$, the answer is $5$.
hints: The length of the codeword is dependent on the number of leading zeroes it has. What is the distribution of the number of leading zeroes the string has? In terms of that quantity, what is the length of the codeword?

title: Music Enjoyer
statement: A certain music store sells records and album covers. The proportion of people that buy records and album covers is $p_1$ and $p_2$, respectively, while a proportion $p_3$ buy both. Given a person has purchase a record, find the probability they buy an album cover. Evaluate this when $p_i = 1 - 0.2i$, $i = 1,2,3$.
solution: This is a conditional probability, as you are given information about the purchase. Let $R$ and $C$ be the events that records and album covers are sold. We are looking for $\prob{C \mid R}$ here, as we know the customer bought a record. By the definition of conditional probability and substituting in our known facts from the question, $$\prob{C \mid R} = \dfrac{\prob{C \cap R}}{\prob{R}} = \dfrac{p_3}{p_1}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $1/2$.
hints: This is a conditional probability, as you are given information about the purchase. Let $R$ and $C$ be the events that records and album covers are sold. We are looking for $\prob{C \mid R}$ here, as we know they bought a record. Use the definition and the given quantities.

title: Product Of 5
statement: $5$ standard fair $6-$sided dice are rolled. Find the probability that the product of their upfaces is $144$.
solution:
As we are taking a product of values here, a natural idea to consider is the prime factorization. This allows us to determine what factors should be present among the dice. We can write $144 = 2^4 \cdot 3^2$, so we need $4$ factors of $2$ and two factors of $3$. In particular, the dice can never show $5$, as $5$ does not divide $144$. Any dice that show $1$ do not change the product, so the idea is to condition on the number of $1$s that appear, as this influences what must appear in the remaining dice.

$$$$

If no ones appear, then there are two general forms that lead to a product of $180$: $22236$ and $42233$. We obtain these by considering the powers of $2$ and $3$ that need to appear. As the dice are fair, we can just count all the permutations. As we know the total number of dice and we are assigning labels with a fixed amount per group, the multinomial coefficient is best. The two cases respectively have $\binom{5}{3,1,1} = 20$ and $\binom{5}{2,2,1} = 30$ permutations, so there are $50$ outcomes corresponding to this case.

$$$$

If $1$ one appears, there are three forms that suffice: $14433, 16622,$ and $16243$. We obtained these by conditioning on the number of $6$s that appear. These forms respectively have $\binom{5}{2,2,1} = 30, \binom{5}{2,2,1} = 30,$ and $5! = 120$ ways of appearing, so there are $180$ outcomes for this case.

$$$$

If $2$ ones appear, there is only one form that suffices: $11466$. There are $\binom{5}{2,2,1} = 30$ permutations of these values onto the dice. 

$$$$

By the above, there are $50 + 180 + 30 = 260$ permutations total that lead to a product of $144$. With no restrictions, there are $6^5 = 7776$ total outcomes of $5$ dice, so the probability of a product of $144$ is $260/7776 = 65/1944$.
hints: Consider the prime factorization of $144$. What terms need to be present?

title: Selection Inside
statement: Suppose that $(c,d) \subseteq (a,b) \subseteq \R$ are fixed intervals. Alice selects a uniformly random real number from $(a,b)$, while Bob selects a uniformly random real number from $(c,d)$. Find the probability that Bob selects a larger number than Alice when $a = 0, b = 10, c = 4,$ and $d = 8$.
solution:
The probability that Bob wins is dependent on what Alice selects. Bob's interval divides up Alice's interval into three regions: $(a,c),(c,d),$ and $(d,b)$. Thus, the idea is to condition on which interval Alice's value belongs to.

$$$$

As Alice and Bob select uniformly random values, we can just consider lengths of intervals to compute probabilities. If Alice's value is less than $c$, which occurs with probability $\frac{c-a}{b-a}$, Bob always selects a strictly larger value, so his conditional probability is $1$ in this case. If Alice selects a value in $(c,d)$, which occurs with probability $\frac{d-c}{b-a}$, conditional on this, the value selected is $\unif{c}{d}$ as well and independent of Bob. Thus, as these would be IID, they are exchangeable, so Bob selects a strictly larger value with probability $1/2$ in this case. Lastly, if Alice selects a value larger than $d$, Bob never has the larger value, so his conditional probability is $0$ here. By the Law of Total Probability, Bob selects the larger value with probability $$\dfrac{c-a}{b-a} + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{d-c}{b-a}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $3/5$.
hints: The probability that Bob wins is dependent on what Alice selects. Bob's interval divides up Alice's interval into three regions: $(a,c),(c,d),$ and $(d,b)$. Condition on which interval Alice's value belongs to.

title: Removed Portion
statement: Suppose you have $n$ red and $n$ blue cards. Each of the $n$ cards of each color have distinct labels $1$ to $n$. $1 \leq k \leq n$ blue cards are removed uniformly at random, and then one card is selected uniformly at random from the remaining $2n-k$ cards. Given that the value is $1$, find the probability the card is blue. Report the answer when $n = 10$ and $k = 4$.
solution: First, let's frame this problem probabilistically. Let $1$ be the event that the card's value is $1$ and $B$ be the event that the card is blue. We are looking to compute $\prob{B \mid 1}$. Applying the conditional probability formula, $$\prob{B \mid 1} = \dfrac{\prob{B \cap 1}}{\prob{1}}$$ In the number, for the blue $1$ to be selected, it can't be one of the $k$ cards removed initially before selection. As a uniformly random subset of $k$ cards from the $n$ were removed, the probability that the blue $1$ was not removed is $1 - k/n$. Given that the blue $1$ was not removed, the probability it is selected is $1/(2n-k)$, as there are $2n-k$ cards left in the deck. Therefore, $$\prob{B \cap 1} = \dfrac{1}{2n-k} \cdot \left(1 - \dfrac{k}{n}\right)$$ For the denominator, there are two ways to obtain the card with value $1$: Blue and red. By conditioning on the color, $$\prob{1} = \prob{B \cap 1} + \prob{B^c \cap 1}$$ The first term is the one in the numerator. The second term is the probability that the red $1$ is selected from the remaining deck, which is also $\frac{1}{2n-k}$. Plugging all of these in, the answer is $$\prob{B \mid 1} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2n-k} \cdot \left(1 -\frac{k}{n}\right)}{\frac{1}{2n-k} \cdot \left(1 -\frac{k}{n}\right) + \frac{1}{2n-k}} = \dfrac{n-k}{2n-k}$$ This probability statement is actually very intuitive: There are $n-k$ blue sides remaining out of $2n-k$ total, so the probability that the observed side was blue is exactly the above! As a sanity check, we can see that if $k = n$, the probability is $0$, which checks out: All blue cards would be removed. Similarly, if $k = 0$, then the probability is $1/2$, which also checks out: No blue cards are removed, so the $1$ is equally likely to be either color. With the specified values, the answer is $3/8$.
hints: Let $1$ be the event that the card's value is $1$ and $B$ be the event that the card is blue. We are looking to compute $\prob{B \mid 1}$. Use the conditional probability formula. For a blue $1$ to be selected, it can't be removed when taking away $k$ cards from the $2n$.

title: Transposition Trier I
statement: You start with the tuple $\hat{0} = (0,0,\dots,0) \in \R^n$. Every turn, you select one of the $n$ elements uniformly at random. If the element you select is $i$, you replace it with $1-i$ in the tuple. Find the expected number of turns until you obtain $\hat{0}$ again when $n = 10$.
solution:
Since the next state is dependent only on the current state, a Markov chain is best here. We will create a Markov Chain on the $2^n$ possible tuples themselves, as this will allow us to more clearly see the relationship between the states. There are $2^n$ tuples because each element can either be $0$ or $1$ at each time. 

$$$$

The transition matrix $P$ on $\{0,1\}^n = \{(a_1,\dots, a_n) : a_i = 0,1\}$ is given by $$P\left[(a_1,\dots, a_n), (b_1,\dots, b_n)\right] = \begin{cases}
1/n & \text{if} \hspace{3pt} \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n |a_i - b_i| = 1\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}$$

This transition matrix encapsulates the fact that only one element can differ by $1$ at each step (either a single $0$ turns to $1$, or vice versa). There are exactly $n$ such states that can be reached from any other state in $1$ step, as there are $n$ choices of which element to flip. Note that both the rows and columns of $P$ sum to $1$: If $(a_1,\dots, a_n)$ is your target state, there are exactly $n$ other states such that if an element is flipped, you obtain $(a_1,\dots, a_n)$. These $n$ states are the same ones that can be reached from $(a_1,\dots, a_n)$. As the rows and columns both sum to $1$, $P$ is doubly stochastic. 

$$$$

Doubly stochastic matrices have a special property: Their stationary distributions $\pi$ are discrete uniform over the state space. This is useful because we are able to compute expected return times from the stationary distribution. Namely, if $\pi = [\pi_i]_{i = 1}^r$ is the stationary distribution of a Markov Chain with $r$ states and $\tau_i$ is the random variable representing the first return to state $i$, $\ev{\tau_i} = 1/\pi_i$. In this case, $r = 2^n$, as there are $2^n$ possible states of this Markov Chain, so $\pi_{(a_1,\dots, a_n)} = 2^{-n}$ for all tuples $(a_1,\dots, a_n) \in \{0,1\}^n$. Using the above machinery, we can conclude that $$\ev{\tau_{(0,0,\dots, 0)}} = \dfrac{1}{\pi_{(0,0,\dots, 0)}} = 2^n$$ With $n = 10$, the answer is $1024$.
hints: Can you model this as a Markov Chain on the $2^n$ tuples? Is there some nice property about this Markov Chain?

title: Transposition Trier II
statement:
You start with the tuple $\hat{0} = (0,0,\dots,0) \in \R^n$. Every turn, you select one of the $n$ elements uniformly at random. If the element you select is $i$, you replace it with $1-i$ in the tuple. Find the expected number of turns until you reach the state $(0,0,\dots, 1)$, where there are $n-1$ zeroes in the above. Report the answer when $n = 10$.

$$$$

Note: It is helpful to solve Transposition Trier I before attempting this question
solution:
In "Transposition Trier I", we can break up the return of the chain to $\hat{0}$ into two steps: Flipping a $0$ to a $1$, and then flipping that $1$ back to $0$. Since the elements are selected uniformly at random and are all the same "distance" (in terms of amount of $1$s that need to be flipped) from $0$, the expected time to return to $(0,0,\dots 0)$ from any state with exactly one $1$ in it must be the same. This amount is known to be $2^n$ by the previous part of this question.

$$$$

On the first turn, no matter what element is flipped, there will be exactly one $1$ in the resulting tuple. As $2^n$ total turns are needed on average to return to $\hat{0}$ and the first turn always moves to a state with exactly one $1$ in it, on average, $2^n - 1$ turns are needed to get from $(0,0,\dots, 1)$ to $(0,0,\dots,0)$. 

$$$$

We now claim that $2^d - 1$ is also the expected number of steps needed to $(0,0,\dots, 1)$ from $(0,0,\dots,0)$. Imagine relabeling all the states such that $(0,0,\dots,1)$ is now $(0,0,\dots, 0)$. One possible way to do this is by the relabelling $(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1}, a_n) \mapsto (a_1,\dots, a_{n-1}, 1- a_n)$. You could imagine this as relabelling the vertices of the $n-$dimensional unit cube by reflecting it about the $n$th axis. Under this relabelling, $(0,0,\dots, 0)$ is now $(0,0,\dots 1)$, so the problems of reaching $(0,0,\dots, 1)$ from $(0,0,\dots,0)$ under the new cube and reaching $(0,0,\dots,0)$ from $(0,0,\dots,1)$ on the new cube are the exact same, so they must have the same expected time. With $n = 10$, the answer is $1023$.
hints: Can you relate this to "Transposition Trier I" somehow? Use symmetry of the cube and the movements.

title: Updated First Round
statement: A gambler starts with $\$k$ in a casino, where $k$ is a positive integer. The gambler bets $\$1$ per round in a fair game until they either have $\$m$, where $m \geq k$, or $\$0$. Given that the gambler ends with $\$m$, find the probability that they won the first round when $k = 10$ and $m = 20$. If necessary, round to the nearest thousandth.
solution: We need to update the probability that the gambler wins the first round with the information that they quit upon winning $\$m$. This is a classic conditional probability scenario, so we should apply the definition here. Let $W$ be the event that the gambler wins the first bet and $M$ be the event that the gambler cashes out with $\$m$. We are looking to compute $\prob{W \mid M}$. As per the definition, $$\prob{W \mid M} = \dfrac{\prob{W \cap M}}{\prob{M}}$$ We know how to compute the bottom probability from the known formulas for gambler's ruin to be $\prob{M} = k/m$. As for the numerator, we reverse the direction of the conditional to obtain $\prob{W \cap M} = \prob{M \mid W}\prob{W}$. With no information, the gambler wins each round with probability $1/2$, so $\prob{W} = 1/2$. Given that the gambler won the first round, they have $\$(k+1)$, so the probability they leave with $\$m$ is $\prob{M \mid W} = \frac{k+1}{m}$. Substituting these in yields $$\prob{W \mid M} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{k+1}{m}}{\frac{k}{m}} = \dfrac{k+1}{2k}$$ Interestingly, this is independent of $m$. With the specified values, the answer is $11/20$.
hints: We need to update the probability that the gambler wins the first round with the information that they quit upon winning $\$m$. This is a classic conditional probability scenario, so we should apply the definition here. Let $W$ be the event that the gambler wins the first bet and $M$ be the event that the gambler cashes out with $\$m$. We are looking to compute $\prob{W \mid M}$.

title: Autocorrelation of BM
statement: Fix $0 \leq s < t$, and let $W_t$ be a Brownian Motion. Compute $\corr{W_s}{W_t}$ when $s = 2$ and $t = 8$.
solution: To simplify the notation, suppose that $0 \leq s \leq t$, so that $\min(s,t) = s$ and $\max(s,t) = t$. This is a valid choice since one of the two will always be the min, while the other is the max. Our goal is to compute $$\corr{W_s}{W_t} = \dfrac{\cov{W_s}{W_t}}{\sqrt{\var{W_s}\var{W_t}}}$$ Since $W_s \sim N(0,s)$ and $W_s \sim N(0,t)$, we have that $\var{W_s} = s$ and $\var{W_t} = t$. All that remains is to compute $\cov{W_s}{W_t}$. To do this, we want to use the independent increments property, as this works well in conjunction with the bilinearity of covariance. Writing $W_t = (W_t - W_s) + W_s$, we have that $W_t - W_s$ is independent of $W_s$, meaning $$\cov{W_s}{W_t} = \cov{W_s}{W_s + (W_t - W_s)} = \cov{W_s}{W_s} + \cov{W_s}{W_t - W_s} = \var{W_s} + 0 = s$$ Substituting this in, $$\corr{W_s}{W_t} = \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{st}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{s}{t}}$$ This function satisfies some properties we would intuitively expect: If $s = t$, the autocorrelation is $1$, and with $s$ fixed and $t \rightarrow \infty$, the autocorrelation tends to $0$. This second property makes sense because as time grows large, the present grows less and less indicative of the long future, so the correlation should tend to $0$. With the specified values, the answer is $1/2$.
hints: To simplify the notation, suppose that $0 \leq s \leq t$, so that $\min(s,t) = s$ and $\max(s,t) = t$. This is a valid choice since one of the two will always be the min, while the other is the max.
What do you know about the distributions of $W_s$ and $W_t$?
Use the independent increments property.

title: Brownian Martingale I
statement: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Find the constant $c$ such that $X_t = W_t^3 - ctW_t$ is a martingale. If there is no such constant, answer $-1$.
solution: $X_t$ is defined in terms of a function of $W_t$, so it's best to use Ito's lemma to determine when $X_t$ is a martingale. Namely, $X_t = f(t,W_t)$, where $f(t,w) = w^3 - ctw$. By Ito's lemma, $$df(t,W_t) = dX_t = f_t(t,W_t)dt + f_w(t,W_t)dW_t + \dfrac{1}{2}f_{ww}(t,W_t)dt$$ $X_t$ is a martingale exactly when there is no drift term i.e. the coefficient of $dt$ is $0$. This happens exactly when $f_t(t,w) + \dfrac{1}{2}f_{ww}(t,w) = 0$. By taking partial derivatives, $f_t(t,w) = -cw$, while $f_{ww}(t,w) = 6w$, so $$-cw + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 6w = 0 \iff c = 3$$
hints: $X_t$ is defined in terms of a function of $W_t$, so it's best to use Ito's lemma to determine when $X_t$ is a martingale.

title: Ito Variance I
statement: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Evaluate $\displaystyle \var{\int_0^t W_s~ds}$ when $t = 3$.
solution: The goal here is to convert this into an Ito integral i.e. integrating against $dW_s$, as we will be able to apply Ito's isometry. To do this, we can integrate by parts with $u = W_s$ and $dv = ds$. By taking derivatives, $du = dW_s$ and $v = s$, so $$\int_0^t W_s~ds = sW_s\Big|_0^t - \int_0^t s~dW_s = tW_t - \int_0^t s~dW_s = t \int_0^t dW_s -\int_0^t s~dW_s = \int_0^t (t-s)~dW_s$$ By Ito's isometry, as $f(s) = t-s$ is a square-integrable deterministic function, $\displaystyle \int_0^t f(s)~dW_s$ is mean $0$ and has variance $\displaystyle \int_0^t |f(s)|^2~ds$. Plugging this in with $f(s) = t-s$, we have that $$\var{\int_0^t W_s~ds} = \int_0^t (t-s)^2~ds = \int_0^t s^2~ds = \dfrac{t^3}{3}$$ With $t = 3$, the answer is $9$.
hints: The goal here is to convert this into an Ito integral i.e. integrating against $dW_s$, as we will be able to apply Ito's isometry. To do this, we can integrate by parts with $u = W_s$ and $dv = ds$.

title: Ito Variance II
statement: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Evaluate $\displaystyle \var{\int_0^t W_s~dW_s}$ when $t = 4$.
solution:
The exact method of the previous question will not suffice, as $W_s$ is now a random integrand. In standard calculus, we know that $\displaystyle \int x~dx = x^2/2 + C$, so a natural starting point is to consider if $d(W_t^2/2) \overset{?}{=} W_t$. By Ito's formula applied to $f(x) = x^2/2$, $$df(W_t) = d(W_t^2/2) = W_tdW_t + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 1 \cdot d[W,W]_t = W_tdW_t + \dfrac{1}{2}dt$$ $\dfrac{W_t^2}{2}$ is close to what we want, but there is a straggling $\frac{1}{2}dt$ out back. To combat this, we can subtract out $t/2$ from the original expression, so that the first derivative is $-\frac{1}{2}dt$, cancelling the back. Therefore, we conclude $$\int_0^t W_s~dW_s = \dfrac{W_t^2 - t}{2} + C$$ Our initial condition is that the integral from $0$ to $0$ must be $0$, so as $W_0 = 0$, we can conclude $C = 0$ too. Now, the goal is to evaluate $\var{\frac{W_t^2 - t}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4}\var{W_t^2}$. By definition, $$\var{W_t^2} = \ev{W_t^4} - (\ev{W_t^2})^2$$ As $W_t \sim N(0,t)$, $\ev{W_t^2} = t$, since it is mean $0$. To compute $\ev{W_t^4}$, we can note that $W_t = \sqrt{t}Z$, where $Z \sim N(0,1)$, as the variance scales quadratically. Therefore, $W_t^4 = t^2Z^4$, so $\ev{W_t^4} = t^2\ev{Z^4} = 3t^2$. The expected value is evaluated using the fact that $\ev{Z^{2n}} = \frac{(2n)!}{2^nn!}$. Plugging these into the variance, $$\var{\int_0^t W_s~dW_s}=\dfrac{1}{4}\var{W_t^2} = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot (3t^2 - t^2) = \dfrac{t^2}{2}$$ With $t = 4$, the answer is $8$.

One can also see this by an alternate form of Ito's isometry. Namely, if $a_s$ is an adapted process that is square-integrable i.e. $\ev{a_s^2} < \infty$ and almost-surely continuous, $\displaystyle \int_0^t a_s~dW_s$ is a mean $0$ martingale, and $$\var{\int_0^t a_s~dW_s} = \int_0^t \ev{a_s^2}~ds$$ Applying this here with $a_s = W_s$ yields a variance of $$\int_0^t \ev{W_s^2}~ds = \int_0^t s~ds = \dfrac{t^2}{2}$$
hints: The method of the previous question will not suffice, as $W_s$ is now a random integrand. In standard calculus, we know that $\displaystyle \int x~dx = x^2/2 + C$. Try evaluating the integral with this as the starting point.

title: Brownian Hitting I
statement: Let $W_t$ be a BM. Let $\tau_{a,b} = \inf\left\{t \geq 0: W_t \in \{a,-b\}\right\}$. Find $\prob{W_{\tau_{a,b}} = a}$ when $a = 4$ and $b = 6$.
hints: In words, we are asking the probability that given the BM hits either $a$ or $-b$, it hit $a$. Since $\tau_{a,b}$ is a stopping time and $W_t$ is a martingale, we can apply OST directly to $W_t$.

title: Brownian Hitting II
statement: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion and $\tau_{a,b} = \inf\{t > 0: W_t \in \{a,-b\}\}$. Compute $\ev{\tau_{a,b}}$ when $a = 3$ and $b = 4$.
solution: To compute the expected of $\tau_{a,b}$, we need to create a martingale out of $W_t$ that has a $\tau_{a,b}$ term in it. For the random walk, we considered $S_n^2 - n$ to compute the corresponding expected hitting time. Therefore, a natural candidate is to consider $X_t = W_t^2 - t$. One can verify that $X_t$ is indeed a martingale by Ito's lemma. Since $X_t = f(t,W_t)$, where $f(t,w) = w^2 - t$, $f_t(t,w) = -1, f_w(t,w) = 2w,$ and $f_{ww}(t,w) = 2$, so Ito's lemma says $$df(t,W_t) = dX_t = -dt + 2W_tdW_t + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot dt = 2W_tdW_t$$ Since there is no $dt$ term in the resulting SDE, $X_t$ is a martingale. Applying the OST, we get $$\ev{X_{\tau_{a,b}}} = \ev{X_0} \iff \ev{W_{\tau_{a,b}}^2 - \tau_{a,b}} = \ev{W_0^2 - 0} \iff a^2\prob{W_{\tau_{a,b}} = a} + (-b)^2\prob{W_{\tau_{a,b}} = -b} - \ev{\tau_{a,b}} = 0$$ From "Brownian Hitting I", we can conclude that the two probability statements are, respectively, $\frac{b}{a+b}$ and $\frac{a}{a+b}$. Plugging these in and moving them to the other side, we get that $$\ev{\tau_{a,b}} = \dfrac{a^2b + b^2a}{a+b} = \dfrac{ab(a+b)}{a+b} = ab$$ Note that this is the exact same result that we obtained when considering random walks! This is not a coincidence: Brownian Motion is just the limit of a scaled random walk, so some properties should look fairly similar. With the specified values, the answer is $12$.
hints: To compute the expected of $\tau_{a,b}$, we need to create a martingale out of $W_t$ that has a $t$ term in it. This will allow us to compute $\ev{\tau_{a,b}}$ when applying OST.
For the random walk, we considered $S_n^2 - n$ to compute the corresponding expected hitting time. Therefore, a natural candidate is to consider $W_t^2 - t$.

title: Powered Brownian
statement: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Find the number of distinct non-negative integers where $W_t^n$ is a martingale.
solution: Let $X_t = W_t^n$. The best way to verify if $X_t$ is a martingale or not is by Ito's lemma. In particular, $X_t$ is a martingale if and only if it has no drift term i.e. the coefficient of $dt$ is $0$. Since $X_t$ is a function of $W_t$, we can apply Ito's lemma with $f(x) = x^n$. Doing this, $$df(W_t) = dW_t^n = nW_t^{n-1}dW_t + \dfrac{1}{2}n(n-1)W_t^{n-2}d[W,W]_t = nW_t^{n-1}dW_t + \dfrac{1}{2}n(n-1)W_t^{n-2}dt$$ Since the process $W_t^{n-2}$ is definitely not $0$, the only way for $W_t^n$ to be a martingale is if the coefficient before it is $0$. This means $n(n-1) = 0$, which occurs exactly when $n = 0,1$. This yields two distinct non-negative integers where $W_t$ is a martingale, so the answer is $2$.
hints: Let $X_t = W_t^n$. The best way to verify if $X_t$ is a martingale or not is by Ito's lemma.

title: Variance of BM Sum
statement: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. For $0 \leq s < t$, compute $\var{W_s + W_t}$. Report the answer when $s = 1$ and $t = 3$.
solution:
Since this is a sum of random variables are that are not independent (the Brownian Motion process has autocorrelation), we should apply the variance of a sum formula. Namely, $$\var{W_s + W_t} = \var{W_s} + \var{W_t} + 2\cov{W_s}{W_t}$$ As $W_a \sim N(0,a)$ for any $a > 0$, the first two terms are $s$ and $t$, respectively. For $\cov{W_s}{W_t}$, the covariance, by "Autocorrelation of BM", is $\min(s,t) = s$. Therefore, $\var{W_s + W_t} = t + 3s$. With the specified values, the answer is $6$.

$$$$

Another approach to this is by the independent increments property. The idea here is to split up the interior into two independent components of the Brownian Motion. As $s < t$, we can write $W_t = W_s + (W_t - W_s)$, as $W_s$ and $W_t - W_s$ are independent. Substituting this in, $$\var{W_s + W_t} = \var{W_s + W_s + (W_t - W_s)} = \var{2W_s + (W_t - W_s)}$$ Since $W_s$ and $W_t  -W_s$ are independent, we can apply variance linearly, as well as the stationary property, to conclude $$\var{W_s + W_t} = \var{2W_s} + \var{W_t - W_s} = 2^2\var{W_s} + \var{W_{t-s}} = 4s + (t-s) = t + 3s$$ so that with the provided values the answer is $3 + 3 = 6$.
hints: Since this is a sum of random variables are that are not independent (the Brownian Motion process has autocorrelation), we should apply the variance of a sum formula.

title: Covariate Brownians
statement: Let $W_1(t),\dots, W_n(t)$ be independent Brownian Motions. Furthermore, let $t_1,\dots, t_n$ and $s_1,\dots, s_n$ be sequences of non-negative real numbers. Compute $\displaystyle \cov{\sum_{i=1}^n W_i(t_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^n W_j(s_j)}$ when $n = 4, t_i = i,$ and $s_i = 2i$.
solution: Since we are considering sums of random variables inside the covariance, it's best to apply bilinearity. This yields $$\cov{\sum_{i=1}^n W_i(t_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^n W_j(s_j)} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \cov{W_i(t_i)}{W_j(s_j)}$$ Since the Brownian Motions are independent, when $i \neq j$, the covariance is $0$. Thus, we only need to consider the $i = j$ terms, yielding $$\cov{\sum_{i=1}^n W_i(t_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^n W_j(s_j)} = \sum_{i=1}^n \cov{W_i(t_i)}{W_i(s_i)}$$ From the result of "Autocorrelation of BM", we know that for a single Brownian Motion $B_t$, $\cov{B_s}{B_t} = \min(s,t)$, so we can conclude the answer is $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n \min(t_i,s_i)$. With the specified values, $t_i = i < 2i = s_i$, so $\min(t_i,s_i) = i$, meaning the answer is is $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$.
hints: Since we are considering sums of random variables inside the covariance, it's best to apply bilinearity. Use the independence of the Brownian Motions.

title: Vasicek Model
statement: Let $W_t$ be a standard Brownian Motion. Let $R_t$ satisfy the SDE $$dR_t = (a - bR_t)dt + \sigma dW_t$$ Assume that $a,b,\sigma > 0$, as well as $R_0 = r > 0$. $\ev{R_T}$ can be written as a function $f(a,b,r,\sigma,T)$. Report the value of $f(0.2, 0.1, 1, 0.15, 1)$ to the nearest thousandth.
solution: When looking to solve SDEs, it is typically useful to consider the dynamics of some function of the process. In this case, we can see that $a$ and $b$ play into the long-term dynamics of the process. Notably, $b$ is the "compound rate" attached to $R_t$, so it would be useful to consider the dynamics of $e^{bt}R_t$. By applying the product rule to $f(t,r) = re^{bt}$, we get, $$d(e^{bt}R_t) = be^{bt}R_tdt + e^{bt}dR_t = be^{bt} + e^{bt}\left[(a - bR_t)dt + \sigma dW_t\right] = ae^{bt}dt + \sigma e^{bt}dW_t$$ $R_t$ has now vanished from the RHS! To solve for $R_t$, we can integrate both sides and multiply by $e^{-bt}$ to isolate $R_t$. Namely, $$e^{bT}R_T - R_0 = \int_0^T ae^{bt}~dt + \int_0^T \sigma e^{bt}~dW_t$$ There are now a couple simplifications that can be made. First, $R_0 = r$ by the question statement.
