title: Triangular Selection
statement: Fix $n \geq 4$. Three distinct vertices are selected uniformly at random from a regular $n-$gon. These points are then connected pairwise via line segments to form a triangle. Find the probability that at least one of the sides of the triangle is also a side of the $n-$gon when $n = 10$.
solution:
As the three points are selected uniformly at random from the $n$, we can just compute the ratio of the number of triangles that satisfy the condition to the total number of triangles that can be formed. This is admissible because each collection of $3$ vertices forms a distinct triangle, making it relatively easy to compute the probability. 

$$$$

As stated previously, every subset of $3$ points forms a distinct triangle, so the number of triangles that can be formed is equal to the number of subsets of $3$ points from $n$, which is $\binom{n}{3}$. As for the triangles that can be formed, by drawing out a simple diagram, we see there are two possible types of triangles: Triangles with $1$ side in common with the $n-$gon and triangles with $2$ sides in common with the $n-$gon. We should count these cases separately, since these types are triangles are formed differently.

$$$$

For the triangles with $2$ sides in common, we must have three consecutive vertices selected. This is because  There are exactly $n$ such possible collections of three consecutive vertices, which correspond exactly to rotating the starting point of the three vertices through the $n$ vertices.

$$$$

For triangles with $1$ side in common, there are two parts:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Pick the side that is common between the triangle and the $n-$gon.
    \item Pick the location of the last vertex.
\end{itemize}

There are $n$ sides of the $n-$gon, so there are $n$ ways to pick the common side. Once the side is selected, we can pick any point besides exactly $4$: The two vertices on the side that was selected, as well as the vertices directly adjacent on either direction of the selected side. We can't do the latter because we would then have $3$ adjacent vertices, and the triangle would share $2$ sides with the $n-$gon. Thus, there are $n-4$ options for the last vertex of this case, meaning that there are $n(n-4)$ total triangles that can be formed sharing $1$ side. 

$$$$

Adding the two cases together, there are $n + n(n-4) = n(n-3)$ total triangles sharing at least one side with the $n-$gon. Therefore, the probability of the triangle sharing at least one side with the $n-$gon is given by $$\dfrac{n(n-3)}{\binom{n}{3}} = \dfrac{n(n-3)}{\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}} = \dfrac{6(n-3)}{(n-1)(n-2)}$$ With $n = 10$, the answer is $7/12$.
hints: As the three points are selected uniformly at random from the $n$, we can just compute the ratio of the number of triangles that satisfy the condition to the total number of triangles that can be formed. This is admissible because each collection of $3$ vertices forms a distinct triangle, making it relatively easy to compute the probability.

As for the triangles that can be formed, by drawing out a simple diagram, we see there are two possible types of triangles: Triangles with $1$ side in common with the $n-$gon and triangles with $2$ sides in common with the $n-$gon.

title: Rizz Party Deck
statement: Seby (group leader) combines $2$ standard decks of cards in preparation for the TikTok Rizz Party, resulting in a stack of $104$ cards. While "Carnival" was playing, Seby was admiring Turkish Quandale Dingle's $\textbf{GYATT}$ so much that he accidentally dropped $15$ cards uniformly at random from the deck. Find the probability that within the remaining $89$ cards, Seby is able to create a standard deck of cards i.e. one of every rank and suit. Round to the nearest ten-thousandth.
solution:
For Seby to be able to make a standard deck from the remaining $89$ cards, no two of the duplicates of any card type could have been removed from the deck. For example, we can't lose both $7$ of hearts. Otherwise, we would be missing a card type in the final deck that we want to form. Therefore, we need to find the probability that $15$ distinct card types fell out from Seby's deck. 


$$$$

As all cards are equally likely to fall out of the deck, we can convert this into a counting problem: We can find the number of ways in which cards can fall out such that a deck can be formed from the remaining $89$ cards, and then divide this by the total number of ways in which $15$ cards can fall out. We treat every card as distinct here. It would be unclear how to compute the number of ways to draw out $15$ cards with indistinguishable cards of the same rank and suit, as we could draw out both cards of one specific rank and suit, which would be difficult to account for. 

$$$$

Since all $104$ cards are distinct, there are $\binom{104}{15}$ ways to pick $15$ cards from the larger deck that fall out. As for the numerator, we need to perform two steps: 

\begin{itemize}
    \item Determine which $15$ rank and suit combinations will fall out of the deck.
    \item Which deck (deck $1$ or $2$) the card of that rank and suit comes from.
\end{itemize}

We have to perform the second step because we treated all cards as distinct in the denominator, so we have to distinguish between the $7$ of hearts (for example) that came from the two decks. There are $\binom{52}{15}$ ways to pick the $15$ card types we remove. From each of the $15$ card types selected above, there are $2$ options for the deck of the selected card, so we multiply the previous quantity by $2^{15}$. Substituting in, the probability is $$\dfrac{2^{15}\binom{52}{15}}{\binom{104}{15}} \approx 0.3078$$
hints: For Seby to be able to make a standard deck from the remaining $89$ cards, no two of the duplicates of any card type could have been removed from the deck. For example, we can't lose both $7$ of hearts. Otherwise, we would be missing a card type in the final deck that we want to form. Therefore, we need to find the probability that $15$ distinct card types fell out from Seby's deck.
It's better to treat all $104$ card types as distinct.

title: Circularly Together
statement: Fix a positive integer $n$. $3n$ people sit around a circular table with $3n$ seats uniformly at random. Among these $3n$ people, there are $3$ groups consisting of $n$ people each. Find the probability that at least one of the three groups sits down with all $n$ people of that group adjacent to one another. Arrangements that are rotations of one another are not considered distinct. Report the answer with $n = 5$ to the nearest ten-thousandth.
solution: Let's first frame this problem probabilistically. Let $G_i$ be the event that all $n$ people of group $i$, $i = 1,2,3$, are seated together at the table. We are looking for $\mathbb{P}[G_1 \cup G_2 \cup G_3]$, since we want the probability that at least one of the three groups sit together. The events $G_1,G_2,$ and $G_3$ are clearly not disjoint (more than one group can sit continuously at the table). Furthermore, they are not independent: The knowledge that all members of group $1$ sit together, for example, increases the probability that the other groups sit together, since there are fewer seats to assign them to. Because of this, inclusion-exclusion is likely the best approach. As the group labels are arbitrary (all $3$ groups have the same number of people), we can say that $$\mathbb{P}[G_1 \cup G_2 \cup G_3] = \binom{3}{1}\mathbb{P}[G_1] - \binom{3}{2}\mathbb{P}[G_1 \cap G_2] + \mathbb{P}[G_1 \cap G_2 \cap G_3]$$ Let's start with $\mathbb{P}[G_1]$. All $n$ people in group $1$ need to be sat together, so the typical strategy for these types of problems is to treat the $n$ people as a block. In this paradigm, we need to create a permutation of the block and the other $2n$ people at the table. This is a circular permutation of $2n+1$ objects, so there are $(2n)!$ arrangements here. However, we also need to account for the number of ways to arrange the people within the block, which is $n!$, since every permutation of those $n$ people will yield a distinct arrangement in the end. Therefore, there are $(2n)!n!$ total permutations for this case. As the permutation is created uniformly at random, we can divide the number of valid permutations by the total number of permutations of the $3n$ people without restrictions. The number of circular permutations of $3n$ people is $(3n-1)!$, so $$\prob{G_1} = \dfrac{(2n)!n!}{(3n-1)!}$$ For $\mathbb{P}[G_1 \cap G_2]$, we take the same approach: Treat the two groups as $2$ blocks. We now are forming a circular permutation of $n+2$ objects, meaning that are $(n+1)!$ distinct permutations here. However, we need to account for the number of ways to arrange the people in each block. There are $n!$ ways to arrange the individuals per group, so we also need to multiply the above by $(n!)^2$, so our total number of arrangements is $(n!)^2(n+1)!$. Therefore, $$\prob{G_1 \cap G_2} = \dfrac{(n+1)!(n!)^2}{(3n-1)!}$$ For the last probability, there are only $3$ blocks to be arranged circularly, so there are $2!$ circular arrangements of the three blocks. However, each block has $n!$ arrangements of the people inside, so the total number of arrangements of this case are $2 \cdot (n!)^3$. Therefore, $$\prob{G_1 \cap G_2 \cap G_3} = \dfrac{2 \cdot (n!)^3}{(3n-1)!}$$ Plugging it all in, the probability of our event is $$\prob{G_1 \cup G_2 \cup G_3} = \dfrac{3 \cdot (2n)!n! - 3 \cdot (n+1)!(n!)^2 + 2 \cdot (n!)^3}{(3n-1)!}$$ As a sanity check, the answer is $1$ when $n = 1$, which makes sense: Each person is their own group, so by definition, all the members of each group sit together. With $n =5$, the answer is $\approx 0.0147$.
hints: Let's first frame this problem probabilistically. Let $G_i$ be the event that all $n$ people of group $i$, $i = 1,2,3$, are seated together at the table. We are looking for $\mathbb{P}[G_1 \cup G_2 \cup G_3]$, since we want the probability that at least one of the three groups sit together. The events $G_1,G_2,$ and $G_3$ are clearly not disjoint (more than one group can sit continuously at the table). Furthermore, they are not independent: The knowledge that all members of group $1$ sit together, for example, increases the probability that the other groups sit together, since there are fewer seats to assign them to. Because of this, inclusion-exclusion is likely the best approach.
There are $(n-1)!$ circular permutations of $n$ objects.
You may want to do some type of grouping/blocking of the people.

title: MGF Moment I
statement: Suppose $X$ is a random variable with MGF given by $M_X(\theta) = \dfrac{1}{1 - \theta^2/2}$ for $|\theta| < \sqrt{2}$. Find $\ev{X^{2k}}$ for all integers $k \geq 0$. Report the answer with $k = 4$.
solution: To obtain the moments from a MGF, we typically evaluate derivatives. However, there doesn't appear to be a nice pattern here with evaluating all the derivatives. If it was something like $e^{\theta}$, it would be easier, but this function isn't nice to take derivatives of. Instead, we should consider the Taylor series expansion of the function, since the coefficients are related to the derivatives. Namely, for $|x| < 1$, we know the Geometric series $$\dfrac{1}{1-x} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} x^k$$ Plugging this in with $x = \theta^2/2$, $$\dfrac{1}{1-\theta^2/2} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\dfrac{\theta^2}{2}\right)^k = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^k} \theta^{2k}$$ Note that there are no odd powers of $\theta$ in this expansion, so all odd moments of $X$ are $0$. As for the even moments, we note that in a Taylor series expansion of a MGF, $$M_X(\theta) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{\ev{X^j}}{j!}\theta^j$$ From this, we can conclude that the coefficient of $\theta^{2k}$ is $\frac{\ev{X^{2k}}}{(2k)!}$. Equating these terms, $$\dfrac{\ev{X^{2k}}}{(2k)!} = \dfrac{1}{2^k} \iff \ev{X^{2k}} = \dfrac{(2k)!}{2^k}$$ Plugging in $k = 4$, the answer is $2520$.
hints: To obtain the moments from a MGF, we typically evaluate derivatives. However, there doesn't appear to be a nice pattern here with evaluating all the derivatives. If it was something like $e^{\theta}$, it would be easier, but this function isn't nice to take derivatives of. Instead, we should consider the Taylor series expansion of the function.
Look at the coefficients in the series and relate them to the moments of $X$.

title: You Win?
statement: You are a winner of a lottery! However, you may not be the only winner. The number of other people who won the lottery is $N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, where $\lambda > 0$ is a constant. Given $N = n$, the person who actually receives all the money is randomly selected from the $n+1$ total winners (you and the other $n$ people). Find the probability that you actually receive the money when $\lambda = 1$, rounded to the nearest thousandth.
solution: Let's first frame the problem probabilistically. Let $W$ be the event that you actually win the money. The probability that you win is clearly dependent on how many winners there are: Given $N = n$, there are $n$ other winners besides you, so there is probability of $\frac{1}{n+1}$ of you winning. Using our events, this means $\prob{W \mid N = n} = \frac{1}{n+1}$. Therefore, the best approach is to condition on the value of $N$ via the Law of Total Probability. Doing the conditioning, $$\prob{W} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \prob{W \mid n = n}\prob{N = n} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{n+1} \cdot \dfrac{\lambda^n}{n!}e^{-\lambda} = e^{-\lambda} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{\lambda^n}{(n+1)!}$$ To evaluate this summation, we must align the indices of the terms inside and then shift the index as necessary. The goal is to apply the Taylor expansion of $e^x$ here. The power of $\lambda$ is $n$, while we're dividing by $(n+1)!$, so it's easiest to multiply and divide by $\lambda$ so that we get $\lambda^{n+1}$ on the inside. Doing this, $$\prob{W} = e^{-\lambda}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{\lambda^{(n+1) - 1}}{(n+1)!} = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}}{\lambda}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \dfrac{\lambda^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}}{\lambda}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \dfrac{\lambda^{n}}{n!} = \dfrac{e^{-\lambda}}{\lambda}\cdot \left(e^{\lambda} - 1\right) = \dfrac{1-e^{-\lambda}}{\lambda}$$ We evaluated the summation by noting that it's the Taylor series expansion of $e^x$ evaluated at $x = \lambda$ without the $n = 0$ term. This is why we subtract $1$ from the sum. The result makes intuitive sense: As $\lambda \rightarrow 0$, the probability tends to $1$, as it becomes very unlikely that there is any other winner. Similarly, as $\lambda \rightarrow \infty$, the probability tends to $0$, as there are typically many other people who won. With $\lambda = 1$, the answer is $1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632$.
hints: Let $W$ be the event that you actually win the money. The probability that you win is clearly dependent on how many winners there are: Given $N = n$, there are $n$ other winners besides you, so there is probability of $\frac{1}{n+1}$ of you winning. Using our events, this means $\prob{W \mid N = n} = \frac{1}{n+1}$.
Apply the Law of Total Probability, conditioning on the value of $N$.
Use the Taylor series of $e^x$ somewhere later on.

title: Zero Square
statement: Let $A \in \R^{n \times n}$ be an $n \times n$ matrix. If $A^2$ is the zero matrix, what is the maximum possible amount of positive entries in $A$? Report the answer when $n = 100$.
solution:
For simplicity of notation, let $0^{n \times n}$ be the $n \times n$ matrix of all zeros. Since $A^2 = AA = 0^{n \times n}$, by the definition of matrix multiplication, we can write $$0 = \left[A^2\right]_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik}A_{kj}$$ We want to maximize the amount of positive entries in $A$. Note that we need at least one negative term in $A$ per summand to balance out all of the positive entries. If all of the entries were positive, the sum would be positive! Since we perform a row multiplied by a column in matrix multiplication, a natural choice is to make either a single row or single column all negative values. No matter which it is, in one of the multiplications, we will row into that row or column somewhere. If you're unclear, draw out a small square matrix with either a row or column of all negative values, and them square the matrix. 

$$$$

The question is: Can we get away with just $1$ row or column of negative values? Indeed we can! The easiest solution is to make all of the other values equal to $1$ that are not in that row/column of negative values. $1$ is arbitrary, but it's an easy number to work with. We make all of them the same value because it makes evaluating the negative row/column easier if we know every other value. 

$$$$

How do we find that last row/column? WLOG, let's assume that row $n$ is all negative values, so that $A_{nj} < 0$ for all $1 \leq j \leq n$, whlie $A_{ij} = 1$ for all $j$ and all $1 \leq i \leq i-1$. By substituting into the prior expression, we see that for all $1 \leq i \leq n-1$, $$0 = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik}A_{kj} = \sum_{k=1}^n 1 \cdot A_{kj} = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}1 + A_{nj} \iff A_{nj} = -(n-1)$$ Thus, a natural candidate is $A_{nj} = -(n-1)$ for all $1 \leq j \leq n$. This ensures the first $n-1$ rows are $0$. How about the $n$th row? This indeed works! $$\left[A^2\right]_{nj} = \sum_{k=1}^n A_{nk}A_{kj} = \sum_{k=1}^n -(n-1) \cdot A_{kj} = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} -(n-1) \cdot 1 - (n-1)A_{kj} = -(n-1)^2 + (n-1)^2 = 0$$ $-(n-1)$ is an intuitive choice as well: It's the sum of the column above it. Therefore, when matrix multiplying, we sum $1 \cdot 1$ $n-1$ times, and then we add in $-(n-1) \cdot 1 = -(n-1)$, which makes the term $0$. By the above, the entire matrix except one row (or column) is positive. This row or column would be $n$ elements, meaning the other $n^2 - n$ elements are positive, which is the answer. With $n = 100$, the answer is $9900$.
hints: Note that we need at least one negative term in $A$ per summand to balance out all of the positive entries. If all of the entries were positive, the sum would be positive! How can this be achieved?
The easiest solution is to make all of the other values equal to $1$ that are not in that row/column of negative values. Work out the negative values from there.

title: Shooters Shoot
statement: Alice, Bob, and Chad are in a shootout on O-Block. Each of them are strapped with guns that have varying accuracies. The three guns respectively have probabilities $1/3, 2/3,$ and $1$ of hitting their desired opponent per shot. If the target is not hit, the bullet goes astray and does not hit anyone else. Going in the order Alice $\rightarrow$ Bob $\rightarrow$ Chad, each person gets to decide if they want to shoot at a given turn, and if so, who they target. This cycle repeats until only person remains. Under the optimal strategy from each player, what is the probability that Alice is the last one alive?
solution:
Since each player plays rationally, everyone would prefer to be left with a weaker opponent than themselves. Thus, Alice would prefer to be left with Bob instead of Chad, and Chad would prefer to be left with Alice instead of Bob. Therefore, Alice's first course of action is to opt out of shooting until either Bob or Chad dies. This happens by the end of the first rotation: If Bob kills Chad (probability $2/3$), Alice and Bob remain; if Bob misses, then Chad always hits his target, and that would be Bob.

$$$$

Summarizing the above, Bob and Chad go against Alice in the end with respective probabilities $2/3$ and $1/3$. Now, we need to find the probability Alice wins against Bob and Chad when it's just two players.

$$$$

If Alice is against Chad, then she must hit her first shot to win, as Chad will kill her next turn. Thus, Alice has probability $1/3$ of winning against Chad.

$$$$

If Alice is against Bob, Bob just shot at Chad and hit, so Alice is up first. We are now looking for the probability that Alice hits her bullet before Bob. We can view this in the same light as flipping coins: Alice and Bob have coins with respective probabilities of $1/3$ and $2/3$ of landing heads per flip, with Alice flipping first, and we want to find the probability of Alice landing heads before Bob. This is exactly the scenario of "Coin Swap IV", so here is the solution to that problem, where $p$ and $q$ are the probabilities of the two coins, respectively, showing heads per player. In this case, $p = 1/3$ and $q = 2/3$.

$$$$

Alice's probability of winning is dependent on what happens in the first turn. Therefore, we should use the Law of Total Probability to condition on what happens on the first flip of each player. Let $a$ be the probability that Alice wins the game. With probability $p$, she flips a head on her first turn and immediately wins. Otherwise, she flips a tails with probability $1-p$. In this case, for Alice to have another shot at winning, Bob must also flip a tails, which occurs with probability $1-q$. Afterwards, the coin would go back to Alice, and the probability of her winning would still be $a$, as the coin just performed one cycle and past outcomes don't influence future outcomes of the coin. Thus, we have the equation $$a = p + (1-p)(1-q)a \iff a = \dfrac{p}{1-(1-p)(1-q)}$$

With the specified values, the probability Alice wins is $3/7$. By the Law of Total Probability, we can conclude that Alice's probability of being the last person standing is $$\dfrac{2}{3} \cdot \dfrac{3}{7} + \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{25}{63}$$
hints: Since each player plays rationally, everyone would prefer to be left with a weaker opponent than themselves. Thus, Alice would prefer to be left with Bob instead of Chad, and Chad would prefer to be left with Alice instead of Bob. Therefore, Alice's first course of action is to opt out of shooting until either Bob or Chad dies.
Once it's down to two players, you can treat this as a two-player coin game, which is relatively easy to solve.

title: First Odd
statement: Every integer from $1$ to $10^{10}$ ($10$ billion) is written out on a (very very long) piece of paper in alphabetical order such that all spaces and hyphens are ignored. For example $7611$ is read as "seven thousand, six hundred eleven", and the spaces are ignored when writing. Scotty, who has too much free time, decides to read out all $10$ billion numbers in order of their appearance on the page. What odd number does he read first?
solution:
This question is a very advanced exercise in alphabet knowledge. The first integer from $1$ to $10$ that appears alphabetically is $8$ (eight). However, after this, the first available suffix word is billion (as opposed to million, thousand, hundred, or any digit $0-9$). Therefore, the integer must start with "eight billion".

$$$$

As for the millions and thousands spot, we see that "eight" is not optimal here, as you'd follow eight by thousand (or million), whereas "eighteen" beats out "eightthousand" and "eightmillion" alphabetically. Thus, "eighteen million" and "eighteen thousand" come next. 

$$$$

We can't repeat this for the last three digits, as having $8$ or $18$ would make the number even, and we want the first odd number. Let's first start at the end. Since $8$ can't be the last digit, we should look for eighty, as that starts with e as well. $80$ itself doesn't work, but looking among the odd digits, we see "five" comes first alphabetically, so the number ends in $85$. However, is there a hundreds spot? We must have a hundreds spot, as the $h$ in hundreds comes before the $y$ in eighty, so "eight hundred" must come before the "eighty five". Thus, our final integer is $$8,018,018,885$$
hints: This question is a very advanced exercise in alphabet knowledge. The first integer from $1$ to $10$ that appears alphabetically is $8$ (eight). However, after this, the first available suffix word is billion (as opposed to million, thousand, hundred, or any digit $0-9$). Therefore, the integer must start with "eight billion".
Think about eighteen as a number.
Do you need a hundreds spot? What number should come in the tens and ones? Compare them.

title: Choccy Break
statement: Rui has a chocolate bar that is arranged into the shape of a $m \times n$ grid of $1 \times 1$ squares. Rui can break up the chocolate bar in any way he wants horizontally or vertically at each step. The goal is to obtain the constituent $mn$ $1 \times 1$ squares. What is the minimum number of breaks Rui must perform? Report the answer for $m = 10$ and $n = 8$.
solution:
In this problem, we initially have one piece of chocolate, and we want to obtain the $mn$ $1 \times 1$ squares of chocolate. When we break up a piece of chocolate into two pieces, our total count of pieces of chocolate increases by $1$: The piece that was broken is now $2$ pieces. This is the key insight we need: No matter how Rui breaks up his chocolate, the number of total pieces he has increases by $1$ at each step! Therefore, to go from $1$ piece to $mn$ pieces, no matter how Rui decides to break it, he will need to perform $mn - 1$ breaks, as the "piece count" must increase by $mn-1$. 

$$$$

In general, with these "devise an algorithm" type brainteasers, the idea is to create and track some metric that changes with each step. With the specified values, the answer is $79$.
hints: Think about the count of the number of pieces of chocolate when a break is performed.
You start with $1$ piece of chocolate and must reach $mn$.

title: Multiplicatively Decreasing I
statement:
You play the following game starting on turn $i = 1$: 

\begin{itemize}
    \item Initialize turn to $i = 1$.
    \item Generate $X_i \sim \unif{0}{\alpha^{i-1}}$, where $0 < \alpha < 1$, independently of other random variables.
    \item You can choose to either receive a payout of $X_i$ (the game ends), or you can choose to reject $X_i$.
    \item If you reject $X_i$, $i$ gets incremented to $i+1$, and the process goes back up to the second step.
\end{itemize} 

Assuming you play optimally, what is your expected payout from this game? Report the answer when $\alpha = 1/2$ to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
This game appears to have a recursive flavor to it, as when we consider a $\unif{0}{\alpha^k}$ random variable, this is exactly $\alpha$ times a $\unif{0}{\alpha^{k-1}}$ random variable. Since we can play this game infinitely, we can relate the expected payout of the next turn given the value on the current turn. For ease of notation, denote $E_z$ to be the expected payout of the game when the first random variable being generated is $\unif{0}{z}$. We are looking to compute $E_1$, as the first value generated in this sequence is $\unif{0}{1}$. There is one key fact here: By the multiplicative property of Uniform random variables stated above, $E_z = zE_1$ for all $0 < z < 1$, as it's the same problem with all Uniform random variables scaled by $z$.

$$$$

The expected payout of this game is dependent on what the first value is, since this influences our decision. Therefore, to evaluate $E_1$, we should condition on the first generated value. If the value generated is $x$, then our optimal strategy says that we should take $\max(x,E_{\alpha})$, since our two options are to cash out (receive $x$), or continue on (the first value generated is now $\unif{0}{\alpha}$, so $E_{\alpha}$ is the expected payout). We have to integrate this with respect to the density of $X_1$. Since $X_1 \sim \unif{0}{1}$, $f_{X_1}(x) = 1$ on $(0,1)$. Performing the integration, 
\begin{align*}
    E_1 &= \int_0^1 \max(x,E_{\alpha})~dx\\
    &= \int_0^{E_{\alpha}} \max(x,E_{\alpha})~dx + \int_{E_{\alpha}}^1 \max(x,E_{\alpha})~dx\\
    &= \int_0^{E_{\alpha}} E_{\alpha}~dx + \int_{E_{\alpha}}^1 x~dx\\
    &= E_{\alpha}^2 + \dfrac{1 - E_{\alpha}^2}{2}\\
    &= \dfrac{1 + E_{\alpha}^2}{2}\\
    &= \dfrac{1 + (\alpha E_1)^2}{2}\\
    &=  \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\alpha^2}{2}E_1^2
\end{align*}

In line $2$, we split the integral at $E_{\alpha}$ because that's where the maximum expression changes. For the third line, we note that if $x \leq E_{\alpha}$, the maximum is $E_{\alpha}$, and vice versa for the second integral. For the second-to-last line, we use the linearity property $E_{\alpha} = \alpha E_1$. This now yields a quadratic equation in $E_1$. Solving this, we get $$E_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\alpha^2}{2}E_1 \iff \alpha^2 E_1 - 2E_1 + 1 = 0 \iff E_1 = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 4\alpha^2}}{2\alpha^2} = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{1-\alpha^2}}{\alpha^2}$$ Since the variables generated are always in $(0,1)$, we can't take the solution that adds the square root. Therefore, we have $$E_1 = \dfrac{1-\sqrt{1-\alpha^2}}{\alpha^2}$$ This answer makes intuitive sense. As $\alpha \rightarrow 1$, the expectation goes to $1$, as the penalty by generating a new value is essentially non-existent, so you are incentivized to generate a large amount of numbers. Similarly, as $\alpha \rightarrow 0$, the expected value tends to $1/2$, as the penalty becomes so large that you should essentially never generate a new value. With $\alpha = 1/2$, the answer is $\approx 0.536$.
hints: This game appears to have a recursive flavor to it, as when we consider a $\unif{0}{\alpha^k}$ random variable, this is exactly $\alpha$ times a $\unif{0}{\alpha^{k-1}}$ random variable. Since we can play this game infinitely, we can relate the expected payout of the next turn given the value on the current turn.
If $E_z$ represents the expected payout of the game when your next value generated is $\unif{0}{z}$, can you relate this to $E_1$?

The expected payout of this game is dependent on what the first value is, since this influences our decision. Therefore, to evaluate $E_1$, we should condition on the first generated value. If the value generated is $x$, then our optimal strategy says that we should take $\max(x,E_{\alpha})$.

title: Deterministic Poker
statement:
Alice and Bob trust each other a lot, so they play a game of deterministic poker. Deterministic poker proceeds under the following rules:

\begin{itemize}
    \item A standard deck of cards is displayed in the center completely face-up.
    \item Alice draws any $5$ cards of her choice from the center, and then Bob does the same.
    \item Alice can discard any amount of her $5$ selected cards, in which they will remain out-of-play. If she discards $k$ cards, she can select any $k$ cards from the center to replace them.
    \item Bob does the same as the above step.
    \item The person with the stronger hand (in the sense of standard poker rules) is the winner. If they have equally strong hands, the game ends in a tie.
\end{itemize}

The cards in the hands of both players are visible at all times. Under optimal play from both players, who has a winning strategy?
solution:
For this question, recall that the order of hands in poker is: Royal Flush (Ace-high straight flush) > Straight Flush (decreasing in power as the high card decreases) > Four-of-a-kind.

$$$$

Since Alice chooses first, if Bob is able to select any type of royal flush, she will never be able to win, as royal flush is the best hand. To block Bob from doing this, Alice must select one card from each suit that is in the royal flush. The best card to select would be the one that blocks the most straight flushes, as it weakens the maximum possible hand Bob can have. The rank $10$ is in the most straight flushes, so Alice should select the $10$ from each suit first. Bob is now limited to straight flushes that are $9-$high at best. The last card Alice selects is irrelevant, as she will be able to discard later if she wants. Since Bob will likely want high ranks, WLOG, suppose Alice takes the Ace of spades as her last card.

$$$$

Since Bob is also playing optimally, he must ensure Alice does not get a royal flush after discarding some of her cards, so he must obtain one card in each suit that is above a $10$ in rank. By doing this, Alice will always be missing a card for the royal flush in any suit. For simplicity, assume Bob chooses all of the kings. As for the last card, Bob knows that the best he can do is obtain a straight flush with high card at most $9$. Therefore, his best choice is to pick a $9$ of some suit. This would allow him to discard the kings on his next turn, and then get a $9-$high straight flush.

$$$$

Alice is now in a great position: She has all of the rank $10$ cards and some other card, so although she can't get a royal flush, she is able to get a $10-$high straight flush by only keeping a $10$ that isn't the suit of the $9$ that Bob selected. She can't keep that suit of $10$, as she would not be able to complete her $10-$high straight flush in that suit. Once she discards the other $4$ cards, she can pick up ranks $6-9$ in the proper suit, and she obtains a $10-$high straight flush. Since Bob can't do any better than a $9-$high straight flush, it's over for him. The correct answer is Alice.
hints: Since Alice chooses first, if Bob is able to select any type of royal flush, she will never be able to win, as royal flush is the best hand. To block Bob from doing this, Alice must select one card from each suit that is in the royal flush.

The best card to select would be the one that blocks the most straight flushes, as it weakens the maximum possible hand Bob can have. The rank $10$ is in the most straight flushes, so Alice should select the $10$ from each suit first. What should her last card be? Does it matter?
What does Bob need to do to block Alice from getting a royal flush? What should his last card be? Does it matter?

title: Shuffling In BIG 2024
statement:
It's BIG $2024$, and Priyanshu is dealing from a deck of $m+n$ cards, where there are $n$ cards labelled $1$ to $n$, as well as $m$ jokers. The deck comes pre-shuffled uniformly at random. Each second, he draws out a card from the top of the deck. Priyanshu plays the following game:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Initialize $S$ as the empty set.
    \item If the card he draws has the value $x$ on it, he removes the card and adds $x$ to $S$.
    \item If he draws a joker, he checks the set $S$. If $S \neq \{1,2,\dots, n\}$, he places all the cards back into the deck and reshuffles the total deck of $n+m$ cards uniformly at random to form a new deck. Otherwise, the game ends. Shuffling the deck takes no time.
\end{itemize}

Note that when he shuffles the deck, the set $S$ remains unchanged. Find the expected duration of the game when $m = 40$ and $n = 60$. Report the answer to the nearest second.
solution:
In this question, we are looking to compute the expected duration of the game, which is taken in turns based on when we hit a joker. Each time we shuffle the deck again, the expected time until we shuffle again is IID to the other times, since the condition to shuffle again (obtain an joker) never changes, and all $m+n$ cards are back in the deck. We also have a stopping time $N$ here, which is the first time at when $S = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$. Thus, we can represent the total duration of the game as $$T = \sum_{i=1}^N T_i$$ In the above, $T_1,T_2,\dots$ is a sequence of IID random variables that represent the times between the $i$th and $(i+1)$st deck of cards (i.e. consecutive shuffles). Our goal is to compute $\ev{T}$. Since $N$ is a stopping time and $T_1,T_2,\dots$ are IID, we can use Wald's identity to conclude $$\ev{T} = \ev{N}\ev{T_1}$$ Intuitively, we can interpret this as: The expected total duration is equal to the expected number of decks we see multiplied by the expected time each deck is being dealt from. 

$$$$

It's unclear how to find $\ev{N}$ yet, since we don't have a direct way to compute the expected number of rounds. However, we can compute the expected duration of each round easily: This is just the expected number of cards dealt until we see the first joker in each deck of $m$ jokers and $n$ other cards. Such a problem format can be efficiently solved by the "First Ace" approach, where we have $m$ dividers (the jokers) and $n$ other cards to be distributed between them. The $m$ dividers, on average, split the deck into $m+1$ equally-sized regions, so there would be $\frac{n}{m+1}$ cards per region in expectation. We must add $1$ to this for the extra second needed to draw the joker itself, so we can conclude $$\ev{T_1} = \dfrac{n}{m+1} + 1$$ Now, we must find the expected number of total decks that are observed until the end of the game. More formally, define an $\textit{iteration}$ as the process of drawing cards until we reshuffle. In phrasing, this sounds similar to the standard "see all sides of a fair die" problem. Intuitively, the number of iterations performed is dependent on $k$: If we've observed $n-1$ of the $n$ distinct values, we will shuffle very frequently , as the last remaining value must come before all of the jokers; conversely, if we haven't observed any values yet, we won't perform as many iterations. Thus, the natural approach is to find the average number of iterations that must be performed when there are exactly $k$ values we haven't observed yet in $S$. 

$$$$

Let $I_k$ be the expected number of iterations we perform to end the game when there are exactly $k$ elements missing from $S$. We want $\ev{N} = I_n$, as $S$ is initially empty, so it has $n$ missing elements. Note that we only care about two types of cards: The $k$ values we haven't observed yet, and the $m$ jokers. We can ignore all of the cards we have already observed, as they don't contribute to the number of iterations we perform. From here on out, we will refer to the unseen card types and jokers as $\textit{useful cards}$. The number of iterations we perform is dependent on the first useful card we observe. There are two cases:

\begin{itemize}
    \item If the first useful card observed is an unseen value, we don't reshuffle. We can then view the remaining deck as $k-1$ unseen values and $m$ jokers, so an additional $I_{k-1}$ shuffles are needed on average. This occurs with probability $\frac{k}{k+m}$, as any of the $k+m$ remaining cards are equally likely to be first, and $k$ of them are unseen values.
    \item If the first useful card observed is a joker, we reshuffle, and there are $k$ unseen values in the deck. Thus, the expected number of shuffles in this case is $1 + I_k$, as we add $1$ for the shuffle performed, and $I_k$ is the expected number of additional shuffles afterwards. This occurs with probability $\frac{m}{m+k}$ by similar reasoning to the first case.
\end{itemize}

By the Law of Total Expectation, we obtain $$I_k = \dfrac{k}{m+k} \cdot I_{k-1} + \dfrac{m}{m+k} \cdot (1 + I_k) \iff I_k = I_{k-1} + \dfrac{m}{k}$$ This is a very simple recurrence relation. By just expanding out backwards, \begin{align*}
    \ev{N} = I_n &= \dfrac{m}{n} + I_{n-1}\\
    &= \dfrac{m}{n} + \dfrac{m}{n-1} + I_{n-2}\\
    &= \dfrac{m}{n} + \dfrac{m}{n-1} + \dfrac{m}{n-2} + I_{n-3}\\
    & \hspace{30pt} \vdots\\
    &= I_1 + m\sum_{k=2}^n \dfrac{1}{k}
\end{align*}

As for $I_1$, we can intuitively note that we repeatedly go through iterations until the first useful card is the last value we haven't observed. The probability that the first useful card is our last value is $\frac{1}{m+1}$, as there are $m+1$ cards left in the deck, and each is equally likely to be in every spot. Therefore, the distribution of the number of iterations until $1$ is the first useful card is $\geom{\frac{1}{m+1}}$, which has mean $I_1 = m+1$. Plugging this in, we can conclude $$\ev{N} = I_n = 1 + m + m\sum_{k=2}^n \dfrac{1}{k} = 1 + m\sum_{k=1}^n \dfrac{1}{k} = 1 + mH_n$$ In the above, $H_n = 1 + 1/2 + \dots + 1/n$ is the harmonic sum of the first $n$ numbers. Plugging in, we can conclude $$\ev{T} = \left(1 + mH_n\right) \cdot \left(1 + \dfrac{n}{m+1}\right)$$ This result intuitively makes sense: With $n = m = 1$, the answer is $3$: On average, it takes $2$ trials for $1$ to be the first card (takes $2$ seconds), and then we pick out the additional joker ($3$ seconds total), and the game ends. With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 463.6$, which rounds to $464$.
hints: In this question, we are looking to compute the expected duration of the game, which is taken in turns based on when we hit a joker. Each time we shuffle the deck again, the expected time until we shuffle again is IID to the other times, since the condition to shuffle again (obtain an joker) never changes, and all $m+n$ cards are back in the deck. We also have a stopping time $N$ here, which is the first time at when $S = \{1,2,\dots, n\}$.

title: Pareto Fisher Information
statement: Suppose that $X_1 \mid \theta,\dots, X_n \mid \theta \sim \text{Pareto}(\theta)$ IID, which means they have PDF $f(x \mid \theta) = \frac{\theta}{x^{\theta + 1}}I_{(1,\infty)}(x)$. If it exists, find the Fisher Information of $\theta$, $I(\theta)$. What is the value of the Fisher Information when $\theta = 7$ and $n = 7$?
hints: As the Fisher Information is additive, we can find the Fisher Information of a sample of size $n = 1$, and then multiply it by $n$ to account for the sample of size $n$. Take the log of the PDF and evaluate the partial derivatives.

title: Freedom Day
statement: It's the $4$th of July, so to be very patriotic, you decide to invest $\$b_0$ in a stock today that doubles in value each day, and then drops the total account value by $\$r$ immediately after each doubling. For example, if $r = 40$ and $b_0 = 100$, you would have $\$160$ in your account tomorrow. You find that after $n$ days, you have $\$0$ in your account. How much money was in the account $0 \leq k \leq n$ days after your initial investment? Report the answer with $r = 1280, n = 8$, and $k = 5$.
solution:
This problem has a recursive flavor to it: The amount of money in your account tomorrow is directly related to the money in your account today. Therefore, the best approach is to set up a recurrence relation that relates the money tomorrow to the money you have today. The only challenge in this question is that we don't know the initial amount of money! If $b_k$ represents the balance in your account $0 \leq k \leq n$ days after the initial investment, we are given $b_n = 0$. Thus, a possible approach is to "reverse the time" and look at the balance of the account going backwards from time $n$. This would allow us to treat the money at the end as the initial condition.

$$$$

To more rigorously state the idea above, we can define the new sequence $a_k = b_{n-k}$ as the balance of the account $k$ days before there is no money in the account. We are given that $a_0 = b_n = 0$. We now want to derive a recurrence for the $a_k$ sequence. As per the question, from day $k$ to $k+1$, the amount of money in the account doubles, and then decreases by $\$r$. Since there was $b_k$ in the account at time $k$, there is $2b_k - r$ in the account at time $k+1$. In other words, we have the recurrence $$b_{k+1} = 2b_k -r$$ However, we can get the recurrence for $a_k$ by rearranging the recurrence here for $b_k$ instead of $b_{k+1}$. The reason is because time works backwards in the $a_k$ sequence, so we need to get the money $k$ days before the end as a function of the money $k-1$ days before the end. Namely, we see that $$b_k = \dfrac{b_{k+1} + r}{2}$$ This is exactly what we described above: A recurrence that works backward in time, rather than forward. As this recurrence holds for all $0 \leq k \leq n-1$ (we fix $b_n = 0$), we can conclude $$a_k = \dfrac{a_{k-1}+r}{2}$$ We have the initial condition $a_0 = 0$, so our goal is to evaluate $a_k$ for all $0 \leq k \leq n$. We should additionally note that the account value $k$ days after the initial investment is $a_{n-k}$, since day $k$ would be $n-k$ days before bankruptcy. By working through the recurrence, we see \begin{align*}
    a_k  &= \dfrac{a_{k-1}+r}{2}\\
    &= \dfrac{\frac{a_{k-2}+ r}{2}+r}{2} = \dfrac{a_{k-2}}{4} + \dfrac{r}{2} + \dfrac{r}{4}\\
    &= \dfrac{\frac{a_{k-3} + r}{2}}{4} + \dfrac{r}{2} + \dfrac{r}{4}= \dfrac{a_{k-3}}{8} + \dfrac{r}{2} + \dfrac{r}{4} + \dfrac{r}{8}\\
    & \hspace{30pt} \vdots\\
    &=\dfrac{a_0}{2^k} + r\sum_{i=1}^k \dfrac{1}{2^i}\\
    &= r \cdot \dfrac{1/2 - 1/2^{k+1}}{1-1/2}\\
    &=r \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2^k}\right)
\end{align*}

The second-to-last line is by the geometric series formula. Now that we have found an explicit formula for $a_k$, since $b_k = a_{n-k}$, we can conclude that the balance in the account at time $k$ is $$b_{k} = r\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{n-k}}\right)$$

This formula satisfies the key property we expect: At time $n$, the balance is $0$. We would also intuitively expect the drop in balance to be smaller earlier on, and larger as we approach time $n$, which does happen here. With the specified values, the answer is $\$1120$.

title: Non-Identically Uniform
statement: Can one create two non-identical loaded $6-$sided dice with the values $1$ to $6$ such that when one throws both dice, each sum from $2$ to $12$ appears with equal probability $1/11$?
solution: For these types of problems, it's best to encode this using the $\textit{probability generating function}$ (PGF) of the random variable. This is because the PGF enables us to evaluate probabilities involving a sum quite easily. The way to think of this is the MGF: The MGF stores the moments, and allows us to find the moments of a product of random variables via multiplication. Namely, if $p_1,\dots, p_6$ and $q_1,\dots, q_6$ are the probabilities of $1-6$ on each die, then we define the PGF by $$p(z) = \sum_{i=1}^6 p_iz^i = p_1z + p_2z^2 + \dots  + p_6z^6 = z\left(p_1 + \dots + p_6z^5\right)$$ We do similar for the other die, with $q_i$ in place of $p_i$ and $q(z)$ in place of $p(z)$. In other words, the coefficient of $z^i$ is the probability that the random variable equals $i$. Therefore, we can get the PGF of the sum of the dice by multiplying the PGFs of the individual dice, since they are independent. We want the sum to be uniform over $\{2,3,\dots, 12\}$, so the PGF of the sum needs to be equal to $$p_S(z) = \dfrac{1}{11}\left(z^2 + z^3 + \dots + z^{12}\right)$$ Therefore, we must find coefficients $p_1,\dots, p_6$ and $q_1,\dots, q_6$ such that $$p(z)q(z) = p_S(z) = \dfrac{1}{11}\left(z^2 + z^3 + \dots + z^{12}\right) = \dfrac{z^2}{11}\left(1 + z + \dots + z^{10}\right) = \dfrac{z^2}{11} \cdot \dfrac{z^{11} - 1}{z - 1}$$ The term on the RHS was simplified via Geometric sum formula. We know the roots of $z^{11} - 1$ are the $11$th roots of unity, which are all complex besides $z = 1$. Therefore, we should try to isolate the $z^{11} - 1$ and see if we can match roots. This yields $$11(z-1) \cdot \dfrac{p(z)}{z} \cdot \dfrac{q(z)}{z} = z^{11} - 1$$ The $z-1$ term on the LHS accounts for the real root. Division by $z$ is okay here, as we were able to factor out a term of $z$ from the PGFs $p(z)$ and $q(z)$ before. Since each of $p(z)/z$ and $q(z)/z$ are degree $5$ polynomials, there are $10$ roots on the LHS, and there are also $10$ roots on the RHS that aren't $z = 1$. Thus, all of the roots of $p(z)/z$ and $q(z)/z$ are the non-real $11$th roots of unity. However, the coefficients of $p(z)/z$ and $q(z)/z$ are real, so their roots must occur individually in complex conjugate pairs. Since these are both degree $5$ polynomials, there would have to be a root in each polynomial that can't be paired up. This is a contradiction, so we can conclude there are no such dice.

title: Partial Die Equality
statement: Can one create two identical loaded $6-$sided dice with the values $1-6$ such that when one throws both dice, each sum from $2$ to $7$ (inclusive on both) appears with equal positive probability? If so, report the probability of rolling the value $1$. If not, report $-1$. Note that other sums besides $2-7$ can appear with positive probability.
solution:
In this problem, let $p_1,\dots, p_6$ be the probabilities of sides $1$ to $6$ appearing on a single roll. The most natural thing to start with is to find the probability that the dice sum to $2,3,\dots, 7$ in terms of the $p_i$. Intuitively, there are $6$ equations here (representing the probabilities of sums $2$ to $7$) and $6$ unknowns (the probabilities), so we should feel hopeful there is a solution. By enumerating the outcomes and using the independence of the dice, we can conclude that that if $s_i$ is the probability that the sum of the two dice equals $i$, \begin{align*}
    s_2 &= p_1^2\\
    s_3 &= 2p_1p_2\\
    s_4 &= 2p_1p_3 + p_2^2\\
    s_5 &= 2p_1p_4 + 2p_2p_3\\
    s_6 &= 2p_1p_5 + 2p_2p_4 + p_3^2\\
    s_7 &= 2p_1p_6 + 2p_2p_5 + 2p_3p_4
\end{align*}

Now, we know that all of these must be equal to one another, so it's easiest to work from the first equation downwards, as the expressions progressively get more and more terms. Setting $s_2 = s_3$ quickly yields $p_2 = p_1/2$. Using this, setting $s_2 = s_4$ yields $p_3 = 3/8p_1$. Iteratively doing this process for the other equations yields the relationship \begin{align*}
    p_2 &= p_1/2\\
    p_3 &= 3/8p_1\\
    p_4 &= 5/16p_1\\
    p_5 &= 35/128p_1\\
    p_6 &= 63/256p_1
\end{align*}

Since the die only takes the values $1-6$, the sum $p_1 + \dots + p_6 = 1$. This allows us to solve for the values of $p_i$ explicitly:

\begin{align*}
    p_1 &= 256/693\\
    p_2 &= 128/693\\
    p_3 &= 96/693\\
    p_4 &= 80/693\\
    p_5 &= 70/693\\
    p_6 &= 63/693
\end{align*}

With the above, we can conclude the answer is $256/693$.

title: Choose Your Order
solution:
In this problem, we must be creative about how to generate an approach. The hardest part about the two methods is that it's unclear how long each lasts, since it's dependent on the sequence of wins and losses that occurred. Furthermore, based on this sequence of wins and losses, it influences the probability of winning in the next turn. Thus, it's not reasonable to compute this explicitly. Instead, we want to draw some common thread connecting the games. 

$$$$

In the worst case, the tournament ends in $2n-1$ turns, as someone must have $n$ points by this time. Therefore, to put the two methodologies on equal footing, we will run the tournament for $2n-1$ turns, regardless if someone has won before this point. Let's call this the "extended tournament". In the extended tournament, even if someone has won before $2n-1$ turns has passed, in method A, the players will continue to alternate turns. In method B, after someone has lost, we will let the loser will serve all remaining rounds. 

$$$$

Why do we construct method B in the extended tournament as above? Our goal is to relate these two tournaments somehow. Since you choose first, in method A, you will have chosen in exactly $n$ of the $2n-1$ turns. Thus, to put the two tournaments on equal footing, we need to ensure that regardless of when someone wins and who winsw in method B, you will have chosen in exactly $n$ of the $2n-1$ games. To do this, we note that in our construction, the number of times you choose is always equal to $n$, regardless if you win or lose and when. 

$$$$

How is the above the case? Suppose you lose in $n \leq k \leq 2n-1$ turns. Under method B, you get to pick while you're winning, so if you lose in $k$ turns, you must have won $k-n$ times, since your friend got $n$ points. Thus, the turns at which you get to select are

\begin{itemize}
    \item The first turn $(1)$
    \item The $k-n$ turns that follow after the $k-n$ wins
    \item The remaining $(2n-1)-k$ turns after you lose
\end{itemize}

Therefore, the total number of times you select is $1 + (k-n) + (2n-1-k) = n$. Similarly, if you are the winner, you select in the first turn and the $n-1$ games that follow your first $n-1$ wins. You don't get to select on the turn after your $n$th win because selection power immediately gets turned over to the loser once a winner is declared. 

$$$$

Why do this entire "extended tournament" construction? Other than just putting the tournaments on equal footing, the extended tournaments and the original ones are equivalent: You win the extended version of the tournament if and only if you win the original version (play until a winner is declared). This is very clear: Since there are $2n-1$ total turns in the extended tournament, the person who reaches $n$ points first can't be overtaken by the other person, as there would be at most $n-1$ other turns for them to win. Thus, we can make a determination on the optimal choice in the extended tournament, and the same result will carry over to the original question.

$$$$

In each extended tournament, with both methodologies, you are now choosing $n$ times, while your friend is choosing $n-1$ times. As the probability of winning is constant per each person that selects, the order in which the turns appear is irrelevant: You have the same probability of winning the tournament under either methodology. This is because you have the same stopping condition (need to obtain $n$ points from the tournament), and both extended tournaments consist of $n$ selections for you and $n-1$ selections for your opponent. Since the counts of how many times each player selects is the same per tournament, the ordering of these selections is irrelevant. Therefore, the answer is "You are indifferent to the two methodologies" (quite counter-intuitive!)

$$$$

If you don't believe in the above statement, consider an extreme case where $p_1 = 1$ and $p_2 = 0$ i.e. you win on every turn you select, and lose on every turn you don't. No matter how you order your $n$ selections in the extended tournament, you always win, as you get to select $n$ times, meaning you have $n$ guaranteed wins.

title: Queen, King, Ace I
statement: Hakim is drawing out cards from a standard deck one-at-a-time without replacement. Find the expected number of cards he draws until he has observed a king $\textbf{AND}$ either a queen or an ace.
solution:
This problem has a similar flavor to the "First Ace" problem, except we are now looking at multiple conditions. Therefore, we are going to apply a modified version of the approach. We will abbreviate the cards as $Q,K,$ and $A$. The biggest observation here is that the stopping condition is modified based on which "card of interest" comes first.

\begin{itemize}
    \item If we see a $K$ before both a $Q$ and $A$, then we continue drawing until we see either $Q$ or $A$.
    \item If we see a $Q$ or $A$ before a $K$, then we continue drawing until we see a $K$. 
\end{itemize}

Therefore, to approach this problem, we should consider it in two stages:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Cards drawn until we observe any of $Q,K,$ or $A$.
    \item Condition the observed "card of interest" to compute the expected number of additional cards that need to be drawn to satisfy our stopping condition.
\end{itemize}

As for the first step, we want the expected number of cards until $Q,K,$ or $A$, so, there are $12$ divider cards in this part. These $12$ dividers cut the remaining deck into $13$ equally-sized regions in expectation, so there are $52-12 = 40$ cards that are distributed to these $13$ regions. This means each region receives $40/13$ cards in expectation, so the expected number of cards until we see the first $Q,K,$ or $A$ is $40/13 + 1 = 53/13$, as there would be one region that comes beforehand.

$$$$

Now, each of the three card types is equally likely be the first divider card to appear, since there are $4$ of each to start. Therefore, with probability $2/3$, $Q$ or $A$ appeared first, and we draw until a $K$ appears. Similarly, with probability $1/3$, $K$ appeared first, and we draw until $Q$ or $A$ appears. Let's compute the expected number of additional cards that need to be drawn in each case.

$$$$

If $K$ appeared first, then we have $8$ dividers: The four $Q$ and four $A$. In expectation, there are $52-53/13 = 623/13$ cards left in the deck, where $8$ are dividers. Therefore, in expectation, there are $623/13 - 8 = 519/13$ cards distributed to $9$ equally-sized regions. By simple division, there are $519/117$ cards per region on average, meaning that the expected number of additional cards needed to be drawn in this case is $519/117 + 1 = 636/117$, as we must add in $1$ for the $Q$ or $A$ itself.

$$$$

If $Q$ or $A$ appeared first, we only have $4$ dividers, which are the $4$ kings. In expectation, there are still $623/13$ cards left, where $4$ are dividers. Therefore, in expectation, there are $623/13 - 4 = 571/13$ cards distributed to $5$ equally-sized regions. By simple division, there are $571/65$ cards per region on average, meaning that the expected number of additional cards needed to be drawn in this case is $571/65 + 1 = 636/65$, as we must add in $1$ for the $K$ itself.

$$$$

Combining all of the above terms, by the Law of Total Expectation, we can conclude that the expected number of total cards that need to be drawn is $$\dfrac{53}{13} + \dfrac{2}{3} \cdot \dfrac{636}{65} + \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{636}{117} = \dfrac{7261}{585} \approx 12.412$$

Intuitively, this is not much larger than the expected time to just see a $K$ $(10.6)$ because it's fairly likely that there is at least one $Q$ or $A$ in the cards that come beforehand. You can view the first term as the expected number of cards to see any divider, and the other terms as the expected number of additional cards needing to be drawn based on the divider observed.

We can look at the problem slightly differently to get an alternative solution. Note that the time until we observe both a $K$ and either $Q$ or $A$ can be expressed as a random variable $\max(X,Y)$, where $X$ is number of cards dealt until first $K$ appears, while $Y$ is the number of cards dealt until either $Q$ or $A$ appears. We take the maximum because both $K$ and one of $Q$ or $A$ needs to appear, so we're constrained by the one that takes longer. To evaluate expressions in the form $\ev{\max(X,Y)}$, we can use the identity $$\ev{\max(X,Y)} = \ev{X} + \ev{Y} - \ev{\min(X,Y)}$$ Intuitively, you can see this by noting that for real numbers $x$ and $y$, $\max(x,y) = x+y-\min(x,y)$, as we add both, and then remove the smaller number, leaving us with the larger number. This approach is valid because computing the waiting time until any card in some collection appears is easy using our basic "First Ace" approach.

$$$$

$\ev{X}$ is the waiting time until the first $K$, which is simple: There are $52$ cards in the deck, of which $4$ are our dividers (kings), meaning there are $5$ equally sized regions in expectation. The other $48$ cards are distributed between these regions. Thus, the expected number of cards drawn until the first $K$ is $\ev{X} = 48/5 + 1 = 53/5$.

$$$$

$\ev{Y}$ is the waiting time until the first $Q$ or $A$. This is the same as above, but there are now $8$ dividers (and hence, $9$ regions) instead of $4$ regions, so there are $44$ cards distributed to these $9$ equally-sized regions in expectation, meaning that $\ev{Y} = 44/9 + 1 = 53/9$.

$$$$

$\ev{\min(X,Y)}$ is the waiting time until you see a $K$ OR your see a $Q$ or $A$. In other words, it is the expected number cards dealt until you see $Q,K,$ or $A$. There are $12$ dividers here. We computed this in the previous solution to be $53/13$, so we can conclude $$\ev{\max(X,Y)} = \dfrac{53}{5} + \dfrac{53}{9} - \dfrac{53}{13} = \dfrac{7261}{585}$$

title: Number of Bernoulli
statement: How many $\bern{1/2}$ random variables can be defined on the sample space $\Omega = \{0,1\}^n$? Report the answer when $n = 3$. Assume a Uniform probability measure.
solution:
Since the probability measure is Uniform on $\Omega$, to define a $\bern{1/2}$ random variable, we must associate exactly $1/2$ of the sample points in $\Omega$ with some event. Therefore, this question is really asking us: In how many ways can we create an event $A \subseteq \Omega$ containing exactly half of the sample points? 

$$$$

There are $2^n$ sample points in $\Omega$, since $\{0,1\}^n$ is all $n-$tuples of binary elements. We must choose exactly half of these elements to be in our event $A$, so we must select $2^{n-1}$ of the $2^n$ elements. The order of selection is irrelevant, as we only care what elements are in the subset $A$, so the number of ways to select $2^{n-1}$ elements from a set of size $2^n$ is $$\binom{2^n}{2^{n-1}}$$ With $n = 3$, the answer is $70$.
hints: Since the probability measure is Uniform on $\Omega$, to define a $\bern{1/2}$ random variable, we must associate exactly $1/2$ of the sample points in $\Omega$ with some event. Therefore, this question is really asking us: In how many ways can we create an event $A \subseteq \Omega$ containing exactly half of the sample points?

title: More Kings I
statement: A hand of $13$ cards is dealt from a shuffled standard deck. To the nearest thousandth, find the probability that there are strictly more kings than queens in the hand.
solution:
Let $K$ and $Q$ be the number of kings and queens, respectively, in the hand. Since there are an equal amount of kings and queens in the deck, and each card is equally likely to be in the deck, $\prob{K > Q} = \prob{K < Q}$. Since there are either more kings, more queens, or an equal amount, we can conclude that $$\prob{K > Q} + \prob{K = Q} + \prob{K < Q} = 1 \iff \prob{K > Q} = \dfrac{1 - \prob{K  = Q}}{2}$$ Our remaining task is to evaluate the probability that there are an equal amount of kings and queens in our hand. To do this, we should break it up based on how many kings/queens there are. There could be either $0,1,2,3,$ or $4$ of each card in our hand. Thus, we break up the event as $$\prob{Q = K} = \sum_{k=0}^4 \prob{K = Q = k}$$ The event $\{K = Q = k\}$ means that there are exactly $k$ queens and $k$ kings in the hand. To have this, there are $3$ steps that must be performed:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Select the $k$ kings from the $4$ possible.
    \item Select the $k$ queens from the $4$ possible.
    \item Select the other $13-2k$ cards from the other $44$ that aren't kings or queens. 
\end{itemize}

There are $\binom{4}{k}$ ways to do each of the first two steps, as the other is irrelevant. Once those are chosen, there are $\binom{44}{13-2k}$ ways to pick the other $13-2k$ cards for the hand of $13$. The total number of ways to draw a hand is $\binom{52}{13}$, so we can conclude $$\prob{K = Q} = \sum_{k=0}^4 \dfrac{\binom{4}{k}^2\binom{44}{13-2k}}{\binom{52}{13}}$$ Substituting in, our final result is $$\prob{K > Q} = \dfrac{1 - \displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^4 \frac{\binom{4}{k}^2\binom{44}{13-2k}}{\binom{52}{13}}}{2} \approx 0.342$$

Since there are an equal amount of kings and queens in the deck, and each card is equally likely to be in the deck, $\prob{K > Q} = \prob{K < Q}$. Since there are either more kings, more queens, or an equal amount, we can conclude that $$\prob{K > Q} + \prob{K = Q} + \prob{K < Q} = 1 \iff \prob{K > Q} = \dfrac{1 - \prob{K  = Q}}{2}$$

title: Tokyo Trains I
statement: Just like in anime, you are taking a train in Tokyo. There are two train lines, say $A$ and $B$. The time (in minutes) between consecutive trains arriving on line $A$ is $\exponential{\lambda_1}$ distributed. Similarly, the time between consecutive trains arriving on line $B$ is $\exponential{\lambda_2}$ distributed, independent of line $A$. You arrive at a uniformly random time throughout the day and board the next train that arrives, regardless of the line. Find the expected amount of time you wait (after arriving at the station) until the next train arrives. Report the answer when $\lambda_1 = 1/10$ and $\lambda_2 = 3/20$.
solution:
Let's frame this more formally. Let $T_A$ and $T_B$ be the amount of time that elapses between your arrival and the next arrival of trains on lines $A$ and $B$, respectively. The key here is the memorylessness property: The amount of time you need to wait for the train is not influenced by how long you've already waited or when your waiting period starts. Therefore, $T_A \sim \exponential{\lambda_1}$ and $T_B \sim \exponential{\lambda_2}$. The time until the next train arrives is $T = \min(T_A,T_B)$, as you board whichever train arrives quicker. We are looking to compute $\ev{T}$. 

$$$$

Since we are looking at the minimum of two non-negative random variables, it's natural to consider the tail expectation formula, as it works well on minimum and maximum order statistics. Namely, we see that \begin{align*}
    \ev{T} &= \int_0^{\infty} \prob{T \geq t}~dt\\
    &= \int_0^{\infty} \prob{\min(T_A,T_B) \geq t}~dt\\
    &= \int_0^{\infty} \prob{T_A \geq t, T_B \geq t}~dt\\
    &= \int_0^{\infty} \prob{T_A \geq t}\prob{T_B \geq t}~dt\\
    &= \int_0^{\infty} e^{-\lambda_1 t} \cdot e^{-\lambda_2 t}~dt\\
    &= \dfrac{1}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}\int_0^{\infty} (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)e^{-(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)t}~dt\\
    &= \dfrac{1}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}
\end{align*}

This is actually very intuitive: The rates at which trains show up per unit time is $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ per line, so the rate at which ANY train show up is $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2$ per unit time. In fact, one can show that $T \sim \exponential{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}$. With the specified values, the answer is $4$.
hints: Let's frame this more formally. Let $T_A$ and $T_B$ be the amount of time that elapses between your arrival and the next arrival of trains on lines $A$ and $B$, respectively. The key here is the memorylessness property: The amount of time you need to wait for the train is not influenced by how long you've already waited or when your waiting period starts.
Use the tail integral formula.

title: Rise and Fall
statement: The price of a stock is initially $\$1$. Each day, the stock rises by a proportion $\alpha$ (new value is $1+\alpha$ times as large) with probability $p$, or falls by a proportion $\beta$ (new value is $1-\beta$ times as large) with probability $1-p$. After $n$ days, what is the expected value of the stock price? Report the answer when $n = 10, \alpha = 0.05, \beta = 0.1,$ and $p = 1/2$ to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
Let's first frame this problem probabilistically. The price of the stock starts at $\$1$. Each time the stock rises, it's price is multiplied by $1+\alpha$, where if it falls, it's reduced by a factor of $1 - \beta$. Therefore, the price at the end of $n$ days is $(1+\alpha)^r(1-\beta)^{n-r}$, where $k$ is the number of days the stock rose in price. The exponent on $1-\beta$ is $n-r$ because the stock either rises or falls each day.

$$$$

The number of days in which the stock rises $R \sim \binomial{n}{p}$, as it rises independently each day of previous days with constant probability $p$. There are also a fixed number of trials, which gives it away that we should use a Binomial distribution. Therefore, we are looking to compute $\ev{(1+\alpha)^R(1-\beta)^{n-R}}$. Let's first try to get all of the expressions with $R$ in the exponent together. This yields $$\ev{(1+\alpha)^R(1-\beta)^{n-R}} = (1-\beta)^n\ev{\left(\dfrac{1+\alpha}{1-\beta}\right)^R}$$ In the above, we abbreviate $f = \frac{1+\alpha}{1-\beta}$. This looks like the direct type of problem LOTUS would apply to, so this is the most direct method forward. Using LOTUS, we get $$\ev{\textcolor{red}{f^R}} = \sum_{k=0}^n \textcolor{red}{f^k} \prob{R = k} = \sum_{k=0}^n f^k \cdot \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k} = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}(pf)^k(1-p)^{n-k} = \left[pf + (1-p)\right]^n$$ In the above we used the Binomial Theorem with $pf$ and $1-p$. Multiplying by $(1-\beta)^n$, our answer is $\left[p(1+\alpha) + (1-p)(1-\beta)\right]^n$. With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 0.776$.

As for a second approach, we can note the expected value expression can be written as $(1-\beta)^n\ev{e^{R\ln(f)}}$. This expected value is now just the MGF of $R$ evaluated at $\ln(f)$! It's best seen by matching up the definition of the MGF of $R$ to this. The MGF of a $\binomial{n}{p}$ random variable is $$M_R(\theta) = \ev{e^{R\theta}} = \left(pe^{\theta} + (1-p)\right)^n$$ Applying $\theta = \ln(f)$, we see that $$(1-\beta)^nM_R(\ln(f)) = (1-\beta)^n\left(pe^{\ln(f)}+(1-p)\right)^n = \left(p(1+\alpha) +(1-p)(1-\beta)\right)^n$$  With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 0.776$.

We can also get a third solution that could be more intuitive for some. Note that the price of the stock on day $k$ is related to the price of the stock on day $k-1$, based on what occurs (rise or fall). Therefore, a natural approach is to apply Law of Total Expectation to what happens between day $k-1$ and day $k$. 

$$$$

Let $S_k$ be the value of the stock on day $k$. If the stock rises between days $k-1$ and $k$ (occurs with probability $p$), then $S_k = (1+\alpha)S_{k-1}$. Similarly, if the stock falls between days $k-1$ and $k$ (occurs with probability $1-p$), then $S_k = (1-\beta)S_{k-1}$. By the Law of Total Expectation, we can conclude $$\ev{S_k} = \ev{(1+\alpha)S_{k-1}} \cdot p + \ev{(1-\beta)S_{k-1}} \cdot (1-p) = \left(p(1+\alpha) + (1-\beta)(1-p)\right)\ev{S_{k-1}}$$ We have the initial condition $S_0 = 1$, as the price starts at $1$. This is a very simple recurrence to solve: $$\ev{S_n} = \left(p(1+\alpha) + (1-\beta)(1-p)\right)^nS_0 = \left(p(1+\alpha) + (1-\beta)(1-p)\right)^n$$ With the specified values, the answer is $\approx 0.776$.

Each time the stock rises, it's price is multiplied by $1+\alpha$, where if it falls, it's reduced by a factor of $1 - \beta$. Therefore, the price at the end of $n$ days is $(1+\alpha)^r(1-\beta)^{n-r}$, where $k$ is the number of days the stock rose in price. The exponent on $1-\beta$ is $n-r$ because the stock either rises or falls each day.
What is the distribution of $R$, the number of days in which the stock rises?
You have two options: LOTUS or MGF. Take your pick.

title: Radial Measure
statement: A uniformly random point is selected from the interior of the unit circle. Let $R_1$ be the distance of the point to the center, and $R_2$ be the (shortest) distance of the point to the circumference. Find $\ev{\min(R_1,R_2)}$.
solution:
In this problem, we are looking to compute the expected value of a minimum of random variables. Therefore, it's best to consider the tail integral formula for expectation, as it works nicely with minima and maxima. Denote $D = \min(R_1,R_2)$. The tail integral formula says that $$\ev{D} = \int_0^{\infty} \prob{D \geq x}~dx = \int_0^{1/2} \prob{R_1 \geq x, R_2 \geq x}~dx$$ We stop the integral at $1/2$ because the maximum possible distance of a point from both the center and circumference is $1/2$, since the radius of the circle is $1$. This occurs at points on the boundary of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = (1/2)^2$. Now, we need to compute $\prob{R_1 \geq x, R_2 \geq x}$. As point selected is uniformly at random from the circle, we can simply computations by computing the area of the event of interest, and dividing it by the total area of the support.

$$$$

The event $\{R_1 \geq x\}$ means that the point is a distance at least $x$ away from the center, so the point lies outside the circle of radius $x$. The event $\{R_2 \geq x\}$ means that the point is distance at least $x$ from the boundary, so the point would need to lie inside the circle of radius $1-x$. The radius would be $1-x$ because the total radius is $1$, and we need a distance from the boundary of $x$. Thus, intersection of this two events is circle of radius $1-x$ that has the radius of radius $x$ cut out of it. This is typically called an annulus. To the find area, we can just subtract the area of the inner circle of radius $x$ from the larger one, which yields an area of $\pi(1-x)^2 - \pi x^2$. The total area of the support is $\pi$, so $$\prob{R_1 \geq x, R_2 \geq x} = (1-x)^2 - x^2 = 1 - 2x$$ Plugging this in, we can conclude $$\ev{D} = \int_0^{1/2} 1-2x~dx = 1/4$$
hints: In this problem, we are looking to compute the expected value of a minimum of random variables. Therefore, it's best to consider the tail integral formula for expectation, as it works nicely with minima and maxima. Denote $D = \min(R_1,R_2)$. The tail integral formula says that $$\ev{D} = \int_0^{\infty} \prob{D \geq x}~dx = \int_0^{1/2} \prob{R_1 \geq x, R_2 \geq x}~dx$$
Think about the event $\{R_1 \geq x, R_2 \geq x\}$ in the plane.

title: Center Square
statement: A point is selected uniformly at random from the square with vertices at $(\pm 1, \pm 1)$. Find the probability that the selected point is closer to the origin than any of the edges. Report your answer to the nearest thousandth.
solution:
At first sight, this doesn't appear too bad, until you realize that the region of interest (the points closer to the origin than the edges) is neither a square nor a circle. This is because the boundary square has flat edges, so the distance from the origin to the edge is non-constant. Therefore, our goal is to determine some boundary functions $f(x)$ that is our "boundary": All points lying on $f(x)$ are equidistant between the origin and one of the edges. By the symmetry of the square, we can determine this function for just one of the $4$ edges, and then we can "rotate it" (this will be made more clear later) to find the boundaries for the other edges.

$$$$

Let's do this for points equidistant from the origin and the $x = 1$ edge. The distance of the point $(x,f(x))$ from the edge $x=1$ is just $1-x$, as it's just a direct horizontal from $(x,f(x))$ to $(1,f(x))$. The distance of the point $(x,f(x))$ from the origin $(0,0)$ is $\sqrt{x^2 + (f(x))^2}$. We must set these equal to get our boundary: $$\sqrt{x^2 + (f(x))^2} = 1-x \iff (f(x))^2 = 1-2x$$ Letting $y = f(x)$, we can conclude the parabola $y^2 = 1-2x$ is the collection of points equidistant from $(0,0)$ and $x = 1$. The points to the left of this parabola i.e. ones where $y^2 < 1-2x$ are the ones closer to the origin than $x = 1$. 

$$$$

Alternatively, if you're well-versed in pre-calculus, you would recall that a parabola is the collection of points who are equidistant from a directrix and a locus, and you can use the formula for $(y-k)^2 = 4p(x-h)$ to get the equation, where $(h,k) = (1/2,0)$ (this is equidistant from $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$) and $p = -1/2$ (downwards-facing parabola).

$$$$

By the symmetry of the square, we can just rotate the boundary of equidistant points for $x = 1$ to obtain the boundaries for the other sides. By doing this, we can conclude:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Points equidistant from $(0,0)$ and $x = -1$: $y^2 = 1+2x$ (reflect $(x,y)$ to $(-x,y)$ from the original)
    \item Points equidistant from $(0,0)$ and $y = 1$: $x^2 = 1-2y$ (reflect $(x,y)$ to $(y,x)$ from the original)
    \item Points equidistant from $(0,0)$ and $y = -1$: $x^2 = 1+2y$ (reflect $(x,y)$ to $(-y,x)$ from the original)
\end{itemize}

The region that is bounded by these $4$ curves is our region of interest. By plotting these out in the plane, we obtain a strange rounded-square looking region. This region is very clearly symmetric about the $x-$axis, $y-$axis, and the diagonals. This indeed makes sense, as the original square has ail of these same symmetries. Therefore, to find the probability of being in this region, we only need to find the probability of being in just one of these $8$ equally-sized regions that would be formed if you draw the diagonals and axes, and them multiply by $8$. We can consider areas because this is a uniformly random selected point, so we divide by the total area of the square at the end.

$$$$

We will compute the area of the octant that is above the $y=x$ line and to the right of the $x = 0$ line. This octant is bounded below by $y = x$ and bounded above by the curve $x^2 = 1-2y$. We know it's this one because this could be rearranged to $y = \frac{1-x^2}{2}$, which is a downwards-facing parabola. What are the $x-$values of this region. In other words, we must find where $$x = \dfrac{1-x^2}{2} \iff x = \sqrt{2} - 1$$ Therefore, the area of this octant is given by $$\int_0^{\sqrt{2} - 1} \dfrac{1-x^2}{2} - x~dx = \dfrac{4\sqrt{2} - 5}{6}$$ Therefore, the total area of our region of interest is $8 \cdot \frac{4\sqrt{2} - 5}{6}= \frac{16\sqrt{2} - 20}{3}$. The total area of the square is $4$, so the probability is $$\dfrac{4\sqrt{2} - 5}{3} \approx 0.219$$

title: Sticky Ants
statement:
A colony of $n$ ants participates in the following game:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Each of the $n$ ants takes a uniformly random position along a stick of length $L$ meters, independently of one another.
    \item At the start, each ant chooses to walk left or right with equal probability.
    \item Each ant walks at a constant rate of $v$ meters per second.
    \item Any time an ant bumps into another ant, the collision is perfectly elastic, so the two ants bounce off each other in opposite directions from which they approached, both still moving at constant speed $v$.
\end{itemize}

Find the expected time until all $n$ ants fall off the table when $n = 100, v = 2,$ and $L = 4$.
solution:
There is quite a bit going on here, so let's start by making some keen observations about the problem itself. Let's consider just a singular ant. Since the placement of the ant on the stick is uniformly random and the direction is also uniformly random, the amount of time (in seconds) it takes the ant to fall off the stick on it's own is $\unif{0}{L/v}$. This is because the maximum amount of time it can take is $L/v$ seconds (ant travels all $L$ meters), and the points of distance $x$ and $L-x$ from the LHS have the same probability density. Since they have the same probability density and the direction is selected uniformly at random, the amount of time it takes to fall off from both positions is the same: $x/v$ and $(L-x)/v$ with equal probability.

$$$$

To prove the above intuition more rigorously, one can formally find the CDF of $T$, but the above intuition is sufficient. Now that we've reduced the first part about the direction, we must interpret the collision. Imagine seeing $2$ identical ants colliding with each other in this manner. Initially, one ant was moving left, while the other was moving right, and the same happens afterwards, since the bounce off each other and change directions. 

$$$$

Therefore, in the thought experiment above, this is no different than the ants phasing through one another and just walking on their original paths without bouncing. Thus, we can view the ants as ghost ants that phase through each other, and the bouncing condition doesn't even matter.

$$$$

If $T_i$ is the time it takes for ant $i$, $1 \leq i \leq n$, to fall off the table, the time it takes for all $n$ ants to fall off is $\max(T_1,\dots, T_n)$. Since we can just view the ants as phasing through one another, the placement of each ant is uniformly random, and each ant moves in the same way (velocity $v$, direction at random), we can conclude $T_1,\dots, T_n \sim \unif{0}{L/v}$ IID. 


$$$$

As we are looking to compute the expected maximum of Uniform random variables, we are able to use our classic order statistics formula: The $n$ Uniform random variables, on average, split up the interval $(0,L/v)$ into $n+1$ equally-sized pieces. As $n$ of these pieces come before the maximum of the random variables, we can conclude that $$\ev{\max(T_1,\dots, T_n)} = \dfrac{n}{n+1} \cdot \dfrac{L}{v}$$ With the specified values, the answer is $200/101$.
